“HMRC should monitor whether people are reading notices rather than simply ignoring the alerts. Those affected first are likely to be digitally savvy, but even they face a relentless stream of app notifications and emails. Important tax notices can easily disappear into digital noise.”

HMRC said it will monitor how the affected taxpayers respond to the new approach, including whether they ultimately view their code online, contact HMRC or request a paper copy in order to inform the wider digital rollout.

articles.title: Citi UK’s risk boss exits in latest executive shake-up
articles.summary:
The chief risk officer of Citigroup’s UK arm has exited the bank, regulatory filings show, in the latest change in the Wall Street bank’s UK leadership. 

Manjira Sen‑Gosain departed as the company’s UK risk boss at the beginning of November, according to an update on the Financial Conduct Authority register.

The move comes after UK boss Tiina Lee announced her departure to pursue a portfolio career as a non-executive director. She is expected to depart around March 2027.

Lee has overseen the US giant’s UK operations across its banking, services, markets and wealth businesses.

Citi declined to comment on Sen-Gosain’s departure.

The lender has faced scrutiny this week after it was revealed it had underestimated its risk-weighted assets by $35bn after recording some trades incorrectly, leading to an emergency capital injection into its UK unit. 

An internal model that had not been approved by regulators was used for the transactions, which led to risk-weighted assets sharply rising when a standard model was applied. The bookkeeping slip was first reported by Reuters.

The $35bn amounts to around 2.7 per cent of Citi’s $1.2tn in total risk-weighted assets reported in the third quarter.

Citi said it had “identified and resolved an internal capital modeling issue at a European trading subsidiary” over the summer. 

Citi UK blunder a headache for Scot boss

The regulatory mishap marks a headache for Citi boss Dame Jane Fraser, who took the reins in early 2021 and installed a turnaround plan on the back of scrutiny from the Federal Reserve.

The US central bank and the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency fined Citi $400m in 2020 and ordered it to fix its risk-management systems.

In May, Fraser told investors the bank’s monitoring, reporting, and stress testing were “faster” and “more dynamic”.

She added the bank had completed around 90 per cent of the work to beef up its risk-management and the remainder was focused on data governance.

Fraser, who is the only Brit to run a Wall Street bank, was awarded a damehood for services to financial services earlier this year. 

Citi’s UK operations are the group’s second-largest market with it employing around 14,000 people across hubs in Canary Wharf, Belfast and Jersey. 

The bank was fined £5m in September for violating UK sanctions on Russia.

articles.title: On this day: The death of Fidel Castro
articles.summary:
On this day, 25 November 2016, Cuban revolutionary Fidel Castro passed away aged 90 years old. Castro became, and remains, the murderous dictator it’s acceptable for mainstream politicians to admire, writes Eliot Wilson

Ten years ago today, Cubavisión, the state broadcaster of the Republic of Cuba, scrambled to broadcast an unexpected address by the President of the Council of State and First Secretary of the Communist Party of Cuba, 85-year old Raúl Castro.

“With deep pain, I appear to inform our people and our friends across America and the world that today, 25 November 2016, at 10:29 p.m., the Commander-in-Chief of the Cuban Revolution, Fidel Castro Ruz, passed away… In compliance with the expressed will of Comrade Fidel, his remains will be cremated in the early hours of Saturday 26; the funeral organising committee will provide our people with detailed information on the organisation of the posthumous tribute to the founder of the Cuban Revolution. ¡Hasta la victoria siempre!”

That last phrase, “Ever onward to victory!”, had been the sign-off of Che Guevara’s letter to Fidel Castro in 1965; the Argentinian revolutionary, iconic on a million posters and T-shirts, had resigned as Minister of Industries and was leaving to spread the gospel of Marxist-Leninist revolution in Africa and South America. Two and a half years later, Guevara was dead, clumsily executed by a half-drunk sergeant from the Bolivian Rangers. But Castro still had a long way to go.

The birth of Fidel Castro

Fidel Alejandro Castro Ruz was born a century ago, the son of a wealthy farmer and self-made businessman, originally from Galicia, and his mistress and housemaid, with whom he had six other children. Castro was educated at Jesuit-run schools on Santiago de Cuba, then in 1945 he enrolled at the University of Havana to read law. Inevitably, as the son of a hard-bitten entrepreneur, he was soon immersed in radical left-wing, anti-American and anti-imperialist student politics.

That Spain, the land of his father’s birth, had been the imperial power in Cuba for nearly 400 years did not faze him. Nor was he held back by any irony in joining the Party of the Cuban People – Orthodox, the slogan of which was Vergüenza contra dinero, “Shame against money”. For the young, revolution is always a cleansing fire.

Castro never lacked ambition. Before he was 21, he was volunteering for a military operation to unseat the President and Generalissimo of the Dominican Republic, Rafael Trujillo; in 1948 he went to Bogotá, to protest at the foundation of the Organization of American States, just weeks after the assassination of the Leader of the Colombian Liberal Party, Jorge Eliécer Gaitán.

Already well known as a left-wing activist, Castro still somehow managed to graduate as a doctor of law and start a legal practice, but his intense focus was politics, and the politics of revolution. When Major General Fulgencio Batista installed himself as President in 1954, practising what he called “disciplined democracy” and fuelled by deals with US sugar and fruit exporters and the Mob, Castro was given his purpose: to oust Batista and “free” the people of Cuba, even if he had to forge a dictatorship to do it.

First impressions on the world stage

A mood was shifting. If the United States had played a many-layered game during the Second World War partly to undermine the British Empire – and it had, successfully – the heady breezes of decolonisation, both physical and economic, were gusting through the Caribbean too. This was America’s back yard, the Monroe Doctrine had said so since 1823; but the people of Cuba, like those of the Dominican Republic, Puerto Rico, Panama, Colombia, Nicaragua or Guatemala, would not in perpetuity accept the substitution of the power of the dollar for the imperial occupation by Spain.

Having spent most of the 1950s waging the Cuban Revolution, Castro arrived in Havana on 9 January 1959 in triumph. Batista had fled the previous month and Castro had wrong-footed his rival against the régime, General Eulogio Cantillo. He had won hearts and minds: the liberal lawyer Manuel Urrutia Lleó was installed as a figurehead President, but it was Castro, initially as Representative of the Rebel Armed Forces of the Presidency, who was making the decisions. A month later, he became Prime Minister, a position he would hold for 17 years before transitioning to President of the Council of State, stepping down only in 2008, into his 80s.

At first it was hard to know what to make of Castro. His image was perfect: tall and imposing, in army fatigues, with a resplendent beard and long cigar, he had charisma to spare and was a gifted orator, though as his rule went on his speeches became endurance tests. In 1960, he harangued the UN General Assembly for four-and-a-half-hours, but his record was probably 1998, when he addressed the Cuban National Assembly for seven hours and 15 minutes.

Castro did not immediately style himself as a Communist, even if the United States still had a cohort who thought that anyone to the left of Adlai Stevenson was a suspected Red. After hosting Castro in Washington in April 1959, Vice President Richard Nixon told the press cautiously, “He is either incredibly naive about Communism or under Communist discipline – my guess is the former”. But 1962 changed everything, made everything startlingly clear.

The Cuban Missile Crisis of October 1962 is often regarded as the closest the Cold War came to running hot. One clumsy move by either side could have brought the tension to a boil. Although Nikita Khrushchev agreed to withdraw the thermonuclear medium-range ballistic missiles from Cuba, which would have cut any warning the United States might have had from hours to minutes or effectively none at all, it showed that Cuba was a dagger at the throat of America and Castro was willing to brandish it. Relations between the two countries went into deep-freeze and have yet to thaw.

Castro’s death and legacy

By the time he died, it was almost impossible to comprehend how long Castro had spent on the world stage. He had been a thorn in the side of the Eisenhower administration; Harold Macmillan was Prime Minister; and the French Fourth Republic was still in its death throes. He was backed by Khrushchev and the Soviet Union. By 2016, there were carefully worded neutral formulations from Barack Obama and Theresa May, and warm tributes from President Francois Hollande and Vladimir Putin.

President-elect Donald Trump hid nothing: “Today, the world marks the passing of a brutal dictator who oppressed his own people for nearly six decades.” His reaction on Twitter had been more concise: “Fidel Castro is dead!”

Most baffling to many is how Castro became, and remains, the murderous dictator it’s acceptable for mainstream politicians to admire and praise. Certainly the United States had been clumsy, aggressive and paranoid in its approach to Cuba. But Castro was a brutal autocrat: 4,000 executions and extrajudicial killings may seem an underachievement in today’s world, but tens of thousands were held as political prisoners in a one-party state, and in the mid-1960s something like one in 400 of the population was incarcerated for political reasons.

And Cuba is a country beggared. Nine-tenths of Cubans live in extreme poverty, pharmaceuticals are frequently absent, rationing of food has been imposed several times, the population is ageing and falling. The Covid-19 pandemic slammed into Cuba violently, slashing the vital tourism sector. Yet Fidel Castro, a dictator for nearly 50 years, is an icon to many.

Sometimes nations have to choose between freedom and prosperity. Sometimes both can be achieved. It is the tragedy of the Cuban people that they have neither. ¡Viva Cuba libre! And soon.

Eliot Wilson is a writer and historian. He is a senior fellow for national security at the Coalition for Global Prosperity and a contributing editor at Defence on the Brink

articles.title: The Debate: Should criminals be paid for appearing in documentaries?
articles.summary:
In Nathan Fielder’s blockbuster documentary You Can See Everything, the payment of Elizabeth Holmes and her partner becomes a crucial plot plot. Is it fair to pay criminals to appear in documentaries? We hear the case for and against in today’s Debate

YES: Producers are profiting from Elizabeth Holmes’ story, so why shouldn’t she?

Documentaries about crime are big business. You Can See Everything, Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim’s film about Elizabeth Holmes, is drawing crowds and acclaim. Broadcasters, producers and streaming platforms all profit from stories like hers. Yet the one person we instinctively say should not be paid is the one whose life is on screen.

That instinct deserves scrutiny. When a production company films someone with a conviction, it is using their time, their memories and their labour. Asking them to give that for nothing is not a moral stance. It is extraction. People leaving prison already face closed doors in employment, housing and finance. Denying them fair payment for genuine work only deepens the exclusion that makes reoffending more likely.

There is also a rehabilitative case. Research on desistance, including my own, shows that people move away from crime when they can build a credible new account of who they are, and when others recognise that change. A responsible documentary can be part of that process. It gives people a platform to take responsibility in public, explain how harm happened and show who they are becoming. Paying them treats that contribution as legitimate, rather than as a spectacle others cash in on.

None of this means anything goes. Payment should be transparent and proportionate. Victims should be consulted. Where compensation or confiscation orders are outstanding, those must come first. Programmes that glamorise harm should not be made at all. But a blanket ban punishes the wrong people. It lets everyone else profit from crime stories while silencing those best placed to explain them. If we believe people can change, we should be willing to pay them to tell us how.

Dr Natasha Du Rose is a senior lecturer in criminology at London Metropolitan University

NO: Payment turns crime into a commodity and compounds the harm felt by victims

On paper, this appears to be a simple question. At its core, however, we are drifting into much murkier waters.

Documentary has travelled a long way since John Grierson described it as the “creative treatment of actuality”. We are now firmly in the age of “docu-tainment”. You Can See Everything puts this debate front and centre. One of the film’s key figures, Billy Evans, reportedly received payment for his participation, although it has since been reported that he donated the fee. Evans is not himself a criminal, but as the husband of convicted fraudster Elizabeth Holmes, any discussion of who profits from these stories quickly becomes ethically complicated.

More interestingly, maybe we should ask if You Can See Everything is a documentary at all? It is a highly stylised, performative work in which Nathan Fielder is not simply documenting reality but actively shaping it. Fielder is an actor, and that blurring of performance and actuality makes the question of payment even harder to untangle.

My answer is still no. Criminals should not profit from appearing in successful documentaries. Payment further risks turning crime into a commodity and compounds the harm experienced by victims.

But focusing solely on whether offenders get paid may distract us from a bigger question. True crime is already a lucrative industry. Streamers, distributors and production companies routinely profit from criminal acts. If criminals should not benefit from these stories, perhaps we should ask what responsibility the industry has to direct some of those profits towards victims, support services and crime prevention.

Nina Jones is an academic at the University of Birmingham with a specialism in documentary filmmaking

THE VERDICT

It’s not often we need to start this section with a spoiler warning, but we couldn’t resist framing this week’s debate around You Can See Everything, a breakout documentary from Nathan Fielder about convicted fraudster and Theranos founder Elizabeth Holmes, which has sparked a number of questions about the ethics of crime-based entertainment.

The payment of Holmes and her partner Billy Evans for their participation becomes a key plot point in the film, with the audience forced to confront in-cinema that they may inadvertently be financing the couple (and potentially even their new business venture). That makes for uncomfortable viewing, and while Dr Du Rose is right that the alternative also raises unease – people, especially potentially vulnerable people, should be paid for their labour – overall we feel compelled to side with Ms Jones. Surely such payment will only fuel the worrying commodification of crime. Many documentarians consider it an editorial breach to pay subjects at all, let alone criminal ones.

articles.title: Asian stock markets lose steam amid renewed AI fears
articles.summary:
Asian markets suffered yet another sharp sell-off on Wednesday, following Wall Street lower on renewed AI trade fears.

South Korea’s Kospi tumbled 6.1 per cent, dragging the index back below 5,000 points, after heavyweights SK Hynix and Samsung Electronics shed more than 10 per cent.

The chipmakers account for around half of the Kospi’s market capitalisation and have been key beneficiaries of the soaring demand for memory chips. The blue-chip index has lost 14.1 per cent over the last month.

Japan’s tech-heavy Nikkei 225 slid 2.7 per cent, led by semiconductor supplier Tokyo Electron and chipmaker Kioxia, which fell 12.5 per cent and 14.1 per cent respectively.

OpenAI backer Soft Bank fell 14.8 per cent, extending its near 70 per cent decline since June.

Taiwan also lost its early-week gains, sinking 4.8 per cent.

Running away

Asia’s short-lived Tuesday rally was brought to an end by investors increasingly questioning the sustainability of the AI boom and rising debt levels.

The region is home to a number of key suppliers of the AI infrastructure build-out, particularly in South Korea and Taiwan. Both markets are increasingly concentrated in a handful of star chipmakers.

Fresh US tariff threats also exacerbated losses, after reports emerged that the Trump administration is preparing to announce new plans for tariffs for several countries, including China.

The new import taxes will impact 16 economies and are in response to what the White House has said is excessive production in those regions, which had led to a flurry of goods at lower prices that undercut US companies.

“Asia Pacific bourses confirmed the renewed hardware fragility overnight… erasing the prior session’s relief bounce across memory and foundry supply chains,” said Patrick Munnelly, partner at Tickmill Group.

“Fresh US tariff threats exacerbated margin and deployment worries for global chipmakers, leaving Hong Kong as a rare regional outperformer.”

Wall Street points to further losses

Wall Street closed lower on Tuesday, after a blistering rally caused by the reinstatement of Jensen Huang as Nvidia chief executive ran out of road.

The S&P 500 closed 0.5 per cent lower, while the Nasdaq 100 fell 1.9 per cent by closing bell.

The losses also caused Anthropic to fall below its IPO price of $83 for the first time since its blockbuster debut last week.  The Claude maker lost 6.5 per cent, closing at $81.9.

Futures point towards the S&P 500 losing a further 0.8 per cent when New York markets open while the tech-focused Nasdaq 100 is expected to drop 1.4 per cent.

articles.title: Unilever’s McCormick food megamerger set to get green light
articles.summary:
Unilever’s $65bn tie-up between its food arm and spice giant McCormick is poised to be waved through by regulators after the consumer staples giants promised to offload Colman’s mustard to alleviate competition concerns.

The Competition and Markets Authority said on Wednesday that the consumer staples giant’s promise could “substantially lessen competition”, having ramped up an investigation into the deal it last week.

Watchdog officials had raised concerns that the merged entity would become the largest food company in the world and bring together the two largest suppliers of dry ingredient mixes and sauces.

They dialled up their probe into the merger as a result, demanding the firms commit to what are known as ‘material undertakings’, which tend to involve problematic parts being spun or sold off.

Unilever and McCormick had vowed to sell the 200-year-old Colman’s, which as well as making its English mustard also produces a range of dry ingredients and sauces, in August. But the CMA only ran the rule over the vow as part of the second phase in its probe last week, City AM understands.

Ellie Yoo, senior director of mergers at the competition watchdog, said McCormick had “offered proposals which we believe has the potential to resolve our concerns”.

“We’ll look carefully at their proposals before deciding whether to accept them,” she added.

‘Reasonable grounds’ to believe Unilever deal will get green light

The consumer goods behemoths had argued that Unilever’s planned sale of Colman’s would be sufficient for the watchdog to wave the deal through, a person familiar with their position said. But any sale of the mustard brand would still leave the merged company, which will retain the name McCormick, boasting Knorr, Schwartz, French’s mustard and sauce brand Maille.

Unilever took many of its shareholders off guard in March when it announced the $65bn merger between its food arm and Frank’s hot-sauce maker McCormick. The FTSE 100 firm, which owns household-name brands like Dove, Sure and Vaseline, had been gearing up to spin off part or all of the underperforming division before the New York-listed firm approached it with an outright offer.

The deal represents one of the largest in stock market history, and precipitated a sharp drop on both firms’ shares when it was confirmed in March.

The CMA’s announcement brings the megamerger one step closer to completion. A person familiar with the matter said there were “reasonable grounds” for believing the Unilever’s undertaking would be accepted by the competition authority.

The regulator is now poised to consult on the provision, before deciding whether to clear the merger.

articles.title: National Express owner faces UK slump ahead of London Stock Exchange exit
articles.summary:
National Express owner Mobico Group saw profit surge in the first half of the financial year despite a slowdown in its home market ahead of an exit from the London Stock Exchange.

The FTSE 250 transport group recorded an operating profit of £191.1m for the six months to September, up sharply from £14m a year earlier.

The jump was driven by surging passenger numbers in Spain and a near £72m accounting boost from restructured rail contracts in Germany. This helped push revenue up 13.5 per cent to £1.4bn.

But in Britain, National Express coach revenues fell 13.1 per cent and operating losses widened to £4.9m amid fierce competition and fewer rail strikes to boost demand.

Overall coach passenger numbers dropped 16.2 per cent as the group trimmed unprofitable routes but airport transfer revenues were up 1.4 per cent.

Mobico is folding the UK coach arm into its Spanish division Alsa in a bid to overhaul ticketing technology.

The company also booked a £15.4m loss on its West Midlands bus arm ahead of its £24m sale to the regional transport authority, a deal that will offload a £55m pension deficit.

Mobico to steer out of LSE

Despite the headline profit uplift, legacy liabilities and £232m in debt repayments due next summer left Mobico’s cash flow in negative territory.

The board greenlit a buyout offer last month from a consortium led by its largest shareholder, Spain’s Cosmen family, following persistent balance sheet pressures threatening refinancing headaches.

The deal represents a 93 per cent premium to Mobico’s share price before takeover talks began in August and values the entire business at £2.3bn including debt.

The consortium intends to combine Mobico with its existing bus networks in Malta and Cyprus while maintaining operations across the UK.

“The proposed transaction… is an opportunity for the business to benefit from a more sustainable capital structure and greater financial flexibility, which can support continued investment and growth,” Phil White, non-executive chair of Mobico, said.

Mobico is set to exit the London Stock Exchange in the first half of 2027.

articles.title: Easyjet speeds up scrapping old planes as fuel price hurts profit
articles.summary:
Easyjet is speeding up the scrapping of its ageing fleet as the British airline looks to new planes to swerve soaring fuel costs.

The London-listed firm said it would accelerate its upgrade programme by retiring more than 50 of its old Airbus A319 aircraft over the next two years in favour of larger, fuel-efficient alternatives.

The firm’s pre-tax profit tumbled almost 90 per cent to £71m in the year to end September as surging oil prices ate into its bottom line. But total revenue continued to rise, up 6 per cent to £3.8bn.

“This year was challenging for airlines due to the Middle East conflict and its effect on demand and fuel prices, which materially impacted our financial performance,” chief executive Kenton Jarvis said.

The company said it had hedged almost 70 per cent of its fuel contracts below the current spot price of jet fuel, in a bid to mitigate the cost impact.

Easyjet is due to exit the stock market next year after a proposed £5.7bn takeover by private equity firm Apollo was approved by shareholders earlier this month.

Battle to buy the business

Easyjet’s exit from the London Stock Exchange, where it has been listed for more than a quarter of a century, follows a bitter battle between private equity firms seeking to snap up the airline.

Earlier this year, Castelake had a preliminary £5.5bn offer accepted by the FTSE 250 carrier after having several earlier offers rejected. But it was trumped just days later by New York-headquartered Apollo, prompting the board to withdraw its support of Castlelake’s bid and endorse the more valuable bid.

The successful proposal, which valued the carrier’s shares at 715p each, was endorsed by Easyjet founder, Stelios Haji-Ioannou who will roll his stake into the new ownership vehicle.

Apollo has committed to avoid any job cuts for a full year after the deal is tied up. But Easyjet itself is planning a wave of redundancies before the deal in a bid to bear down on costs amid the ongoing Iran conflict.

As part of the deal, Easyjet’s current shareholders will have the opportunity to roll their shares into the newly formed ownership entity. A City AM analysis of takeover documents found investors who opt to retain their stake in the carrier risk having their stake seized from them unilaterally and are highly unlikely to be paid a dividend.

articles.title: Pets at Home profit jumps as ex-Waitrose boss leads turnaround
articles.summary:
Pets at Home has returned an uplift in profit as former Waitrose boss James Bailey defies wider high street gloom with his turnaround of the retailer and vet group. 

The FTSE 250 firm will become a “complete pet care specialist” with the help of its recently-launched insurance offering, Bailey told shareholders on Wednesday, as he unveiled the group’s new strategy. Its stock gained more than eight per cent following the update.

Pets at Home saw revenue jump by 3.9 per cent to £809m in the six months to the end of October and lifted its pre-tax profit from £36.2m to £52.2m. The group expects its full-year profit to land at the top end of market consensus, which is pitched between £90m and £101m.

Bailey, who spent two decades at Sainsbury’s before becoming managing director of Waitrose, was parachuted into the pets retailer in March after predecessor Lyssa McGowan quit with immediate effect in September last year.

McGowan departed after roughly three years in the role after the group cut its profit forecast for the second time that year. Pets at Home had been struggling to find new sources of revenue after the lockdown-era surge in demand for pet products died out.

Bailey said on Wednesday that the group’s growing revenue and profit “build confidence” in its turnaround plan, which will see the company push to improve service across its three arms: retail, veterinary and insurance. 

The Pets at Home boss said: “Today we are announcing a refreshed strategy focused on ensuring we have three sector-leading, complementary businesses across Retail, Vets and Insurance, through which we can continue to deepen our relationships with UK pet owners by better understanding and meeting their needs.”

High street green shoots

Bailey’s new strategy will encourage employees to improve customer service and cut complexity across the business to create “a simpler, more reliable and more productive operating model”.

“This cultural and organisational shift will be critical in ensuring we meet evolving customer needs and unlock the significant opportunity we have to drive greater share of wallet,” the group told shareholders.

Pets at Home says its insurance offering, which launched in August, will help it become “a complete pet care specialist with an offer spanning products, complementary services and colleague expertise”.

The company expects the pet care market, which is already valued at £15bn, to grow by a further three or four per cent every year. The UK’s “broadly stable” number of pet owners are looking towards more premium products to pamper their cats and dogs, the group added.

Pets at Home struggled after the surge in pet-buying caused by the Covid-19 lockdowns, as it rushed to cut prices in a bid to boost sales after this demand receded. But Bailey said he is confident the group can still cash in on this era of pets.

He told City AM: “That cohort of pets is still out there, they’re just middle-aged pets at the moment. They’re super healthy, jumping around in the garden, [but] they’ll begin to age over the next two to three years.

“What we’d normally see when that happens is increased visits to the vet, an increased interest in things like health supplements to make sure they stay fit and healthy, and a switch into more senior food products and different accessories. […] We’ll still be there for those pets.”

Analysts at stock broker Shore Capital said: “Sales momentum has returned, market share is improving and, most importantly, the combination of growth and cost discipline is beginning to rebuild Retail profitability.”

There remains “work to do,” the analysts added, though they said the group’s “direction of travel is very encouraging”.

Pets at Home’s nascent resurgence, and its leadership by a former Waitrose boss, comes as the high street looks to its middle-class stalwarts to drive footfall. 

Upmarket retailer Marks and Spencer has seen an influx in popularity in recent months, as its newly-chic fashionwear and viral bakery products look to be driving younger shoppers back to the high street.

articles.title: Energy bills set to rocket 26 per cent in major blow to UK households
articles.summary:
Energy bills for households across Britain are set to rocket from the start of next year, in a further blow to households struggling with the cost of living.

Bills will surge by 26 per cent from 1 January, energy regulator Ofgem has confirmed.

Ofgem said the energy price cap will rise from £1,723 to £2,166 for typical annual energy bills.

The increase, which leaves the cap at its highest level in more than three years, comes on top of already high energy costs. The price cap increased by 4 per cent at the start of last month.

It’s the first time the price cap has surpassed £2,000 since July 2023.

Brits will pay an average of 32.6p per kilowatt hour for electricity. The daily standing charge is at 54.7p per day.

The average cost of gas will be 10.9p per kilowatt hour, while the daily standing charge will reach 29.6p per day.

VAT will not be charged on energy bills during the period, following the government’s scrapping of the surcharge from 1 October 2026 to 30 June 2027. 

The government also announced that around 20m households will receive £100 toward their energy bill in January in the Autumn Budget.

Fallout from the Middle East

But five per cent VAT must still be paid for gas, while the regulator admitted that as “wholesale gas prices have gone up” due to the war in the Middle East, and winter energy use is higher, Brits may not see “much of a reduction in their bills”.

The cap will cover the period of 1 January until 31 March, and reflects the cost of usage for the average household.

Ofgem looked at energy costs from August to the end of November 2026 to calculate January’s cap, during which time wholesale gas prices shot up as a result of the war in Iran.

Around 10 million households on fixed tariffs will not be affected by the cap increase. 

Households under pressure

But the price has been met with backlash from the industry, who have argued it “could not have come at a worse time”.

Dhara Vyas, chief executive of Energy UK, said: “This is the biggest increase in the price cap since following Russia’s invasion of Ukraine… and with household energy debt already at record levels.

“Customers across Great Britain are once again experiencing the impact of our exposure to volatile fossil fuel markets, as conflict in other parts of the world dramatically increase our energy costs at home.”

Clare Maio, head of energy and natural resources at KPMG UK, argued the “latest rise reinforces the need to break the structural link between imported gas prices and energy bills”.

Maio added that UK businesses will face “similar pressures” to households, urging the government to find a way to lower business energy costs if the UK is “to drive growth and competitiveness”.

articles.title: Heathrow third runway planning to stay on bills for 20 years
articles.summary:
Passengers face paying higher fares to travel from Heathrow for the next 20 years, even if Andy Burnham abandons plans to build the third runway.

Under fresh plans proposed by the aviation watchdog, the two firms bidding to manage the multi-billion-pound project will be allowed to recoup the roughly £400m associated with the planning process for this and last year.

The proposal builds on a previous Civil Aviation ruling to allow Heathrow and rival bidder Heathrow West to recoup early stage planning. It suggests airlines face having to add as much a total £700m onto cost onto a their tickets, regardless of whether the plan goes ahead.

Incumbent operator Heathrow Airport Limited (HAL) has asked the regulator to recoup as much as £304m during the first half of 2027 to maintaining the option of submitting a planning application, known as a Development Consent Order (DSO). Meanwhile rival bidder Heathrow West Limited expects expenditure of just £46m during 2026 and roughtly £35m before June next year.

Under the watchdog’s proposal, which is subject to a public consultation, the figures represent the ceiling for costs before July next year, and each line item the suitors bid for will have to be approved by watchdog officials.

Airports generate the majority of their revenue via what are known as passenger charges, which are bolted onto the fares paid by travellers. This plan would add as much as 70p onto those charges for the next two decades.

Heathrow third runway comes under pressure

Tim Johnson, director of consumers and markets at the CAA, said the plans strike “a balance where the conditions for credible expansion proposals can come forward but only where there is clear evidence that costs are efficient, appropriately justified and delivered”.

According to the watchdog’s plan, both Heathrow and rival proposer Heathrow West will be able to recoup their costs, even if one or neither end up tabling a DSO.

The third runway expansion, which is expected to cost up to £50bn and not be operational until 2039, has come under revived pressure since the departure of Keir Starmer from Downing Street. Many in the sector had regarded it as a fait-a-complis, until Andy Burnham made a string of media appearances in which he refused to give it his full-throated supported and branded it a “matter for London and Londoners”.

Since then, Chancellor John Healey has said the government supports the expansion, even as several high-profile airlines and aviation figures warn costs associated with the more expansive HAL scheme would leave the airport unaffordable for many passengers.

This this week, the Transport Committee is due to publish an eagerly anticipated report into the planning process. The paper is expected to be highly critical of the plan’s environmental impact and limited economic impact.

articles.title: Exclusive: World Darts Championship offers private hospitality suites for first time
articles.summary:
The World Darts Championship at Alexandra Palace will offer private suite hospitality for the first time this year as the sport looks to capitalise on a commercial boom.

The move is part of an expansion of capacity as the wildly popular festive competition relocates to Ally Pally’s Great Hall, boosting crowd numbers from 3,000 to 5,000 per session.

That also means an increased corporate offering for the championship, which has sold out of all 180,000 general admission tickets to see Luke Littler defend his crown.

The Professional Darts Corporation has teamed up with existing hospitality provider Pitch Experiences to offer two 10-person hospitality suites, City AM can reveal. Renderings of the private hospitality suites show plush seating and a private oche and darts set-up.

PDC chief Matt Porter called the offering “the natural next step” for the organisation. “The bigger venue means more opportunity to build on the success to date,” he added. “The bigger venue and greater ticketing and hospitality options is the logical progression for a sport that’s getting bigger and bigger.”

Pitch Experiences chief Neil Bailey said that adding private suites showed “where the market is going” following the steep rise in popularity of darts.

“Fans want more interesting and different ways to enjoy events,” he added. “The hospitality industry and venues can never stand still.

“Change and innovation is essential to maintain engagement and build and deliver top-class guest experiences. We have launched this brand new concept to unprecedented demand.”

Luke Littler fuels World Darts Championship boom

The growth of darts, and in particular the year-end World Championship, has been turbo-charged by the emergence of Littler, who reached the final as a 16-year-old and has won both editions of the tournament since then.

Fulham Pier, home to the football club’s new Riverside Stand, will join the bandwagon next year by hosting drinks-inclusive watchalong events for the Premier League of Darts, taking place over a number of Thursdays in February and March.

The PDC is expected to make around £15m in ticket sales for this year’s World Championship, which has remained at Alexandra Palace despite rumours of a move away from north London to a bigger venue.

The tournament expanded from 96 to 128 players last year, meaning more sessions of darts and more tickets for fans, although all went in September’s ballot. Only hospitality remains available, with the private suites joined by specialist tables also provided by Pitch Experiences.

articles.title: Doctors warn of lead exposure health risks after controversial Army detonation in Iowa
articles.summary:
The U.S. Army blew up about five tons of lead azide, a toxic bomb-making chemical, in a controlled detonation at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown on Wednesday, raising concerns over airborne heavy-metal exposure.

The mission was reportedly necessary because the substances were "unstable" and liable to explode if tampered with.

While a Trump administration official reported that the detonation exceeded expectations by achieving maximum mitigation, the Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) warned that residents within 20 miles should continue to shelter in place to avoid inhaling lead dust, and should follow EPA safety guidance "until given the all clear by officials."

IOWA RESIDENTS NEAR AMMUNITION PLANT TOLD TO VACATE BEFORE ARMY DETONATES 5 TONS OF BOMB-MAKING CHEMICALS

"[The] EPA has been on the ground in Iowa BEFORE the controlled detonation, we will be here DURING the detonation, and we will be here for as long as necessary AFTER detonation to ensure communities are safe," the Environmental Protection Agency said prior to the blast.

The agency predicted a brief increase in lead in the air above Middletown, as officials in Iowa and Missouri warned of potential exposure to toxic lead dust.

According to Mayo Clinic, even small amounts of lead can cause serious health problems. Long-term buildup of lead in the body can get stored and slowly re-enter the bloodstream over time.

AGGRESSIVE CANCER TYPE LINKED TO COMMON CHEMICAL EXPOSURE IN NEW STUDY

At very high levels, lead can damage the kidneys and nervous system in both children and adults, leading to complications in the brain, seizures, neuropsychiatric symptoms and unconsciousness.

Children under 6 years old are the most susceptible, as lead poisoning can severely impact development of their bodies and brains.

According to the Iowa Farm Bureau, Iowa leads the nation in producing corn, pigs, eggs, ethanol and biodiesel — commodities that end up in everyday household products." The state also ranks No. 2 in soybean production and cover crops.

One Iowa farmer, Doug Seyb, spoke with PBS about his concern that the detonation could impact his nearby farm, including his cows out at pasture and local ponds that fill the farm's water tank.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES

The public fears that lead could eventually enter the food supply through crops grown in contaminated soil and livestock raised on contaminated water.

Dr. Stephanie Widmer, New York City emergency medicine physician, medical toxicologist and Fox News medical contributor, confirmed that lead being dispersed into the air is "not a small deal."

"Lead has no beneficial role in human physiology," she said. "In fact, lead in the human body can really mess with biology."

People who eat fresh produce already take in trace amounts of heavy metals like lead, which is widespread in soil — but detonating a "tremendous amount" of the toxic metal raises the risk of dangerous exposure, Widmer warned.

AGGRESSIVE CANCER TYPE LINKED TO COMMON CHEMICAL EXPOSURE IN NEW STUDY

"If there is an enormous amount that is going to be contaminating the food supply, the water, the air that people are breathing in, this is very concerning," she said.

Widmer suggested that Americans near the detonation site should continue to listen to guidance to shelter in place, keep windows closed, and turn on ventilation or air purifying systems.

"We know that lead is dangerous for humans, but we don't know how much, or if any, lead they're being exposed to," she said. "It could be none. It could a ton."

The EPA reported no levels of lead in the air 30 minutes after the detonation, but Widmer noted that just because the blow is over doesn't mean there is no lingering impact.

"Lead inhalation is one of the most efficient ways that lead can be dispersed into the human body," she said, adding that even if it's not inhaled, it can be dispersed into the soil. "It can stay in soil, it could stay in water," the doctor said.

"The very concerning thing is that lead can have negative effects on the human body without even showing any symptoms," she said. "There's still going to have to be testing. Follow-up is really key here."

Symptoms in adults can include the following, according to Cleveland Clinic.

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

Among children, lead exposure can cause the following effects.

Besides breathing in the toxic lead dust dispersed through the air, fallen particles contaminating water and soil can also pose a health risk, experts say.

Those who believe they have been exposed to lead, even without showing symptoms, should visit a healthcare provider for a blood test to check for exposure and lead levels, Widmer advised.

Fox News Digital's Greg Norman-Diamond contributed to this report.

articles.title: Putin's war death toll reportedly tops 700,000 as Russia scrambles for recruits
articles.summary:
The Kremlin on Wednesday dismissed a new investigation estimating that at least 700,000 Russian troops have died in President Vladimir Putin's war against Ukraine, as experts warn that mounting military losses are undermining Moscow's ability to sustain its offensive.

The findings, published Monday by independent Russian news outlets Meduza and Mediazona, are based on leaked Russian government records and statistical analysis.

"The only entity that can officially disclose casualty figures is the Russian Defense Ministry," Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told reporters Wednesday, according to The Moscow Times.

PUTIN'S WAR MACHINE TIED TO TROUBLING RECRUITMENT OF YOUNG WOMEN AS NEW DEALS EMERGE

Peskov urged reporters to disregard other figures but offered no updated official death toll.

The investigation draws on records obtained by the hacking groups Belarusian Cyber Partisans and Silent Crow after they breached Russia's federal statistics agency, Rosstat.

Researchers identified at least 490,000 registered military deaths by late September 2026. However, delays in registering fatalities and soldiers who remain officially listed as missing but are believed to be dead led researchers to estimate that the actual toll had likely reached 700,000 or more by that time.

Keti Korkiya, a research analyst at the Foundation for Defense of Democracies (FDD), told Fox News Digital that she considered the estimate of more than 700,000 Russian military deaths plausible, noting that Britain's defense chief had already put the death toll above half a million in September. "The biggest uncertainty is how many of the soldiers still listed as missing have died," Korkiya said.

"Russia can keep fighting despite these losses," she added. "It still recruits tens of thousands of men a month, and this week the Duma approved a budget that devotes 35% of next year’s federal spending to defense. The war is straining Russia’s economy, but that pressure is unlikely to force Putin to stop fighting anytime soon."

UKRAINE'S ATTACKS ON RUSSIA ARE PUSHING PUTIN CLOSER TO NEGOTIATING TABLE, TRUMP NATO AMBASSADOR SAYS

The findings also raise questions about Russia's ability to replenish its forces nearly five years into the war.

A European intelligence source who spoke to Fox News Digital last week described Russia's efforts to replenish its forces as a form of "hidden mobilization," with recruiters approaching people on the streets, including homeless individuals, and offering them military contracts.

The source said Russia continues to recruit prisoners and target people struggling with financial difficulties, including those with outstanding debts or unpaid child support, effectively offering military service as "a kind of a social deal."

The recruitment strategy, the source said, is increasingly geared toward "more quantity, less quality."

The mounting losses have yielded limited territorial gains for Moscow, according to a separate July 1 report by the Washington-based Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS).

UKRAINE HITS PUTIN'S PRIZED BRIDGE IN RECORD DRONE BLITZ AS KREMLIN TELLS LAWMAKERS TO PREPARE FOR 'VICTORY'

The report, authored by Seth G. Jones and Riley McCabe, estimated that Russia had suffered approximately 1.4 million battlefield casualties, including as many as 450,000 deaths, by mid-2026.

Ukraine has also suffered significant military losses. The same CSIS report estimated that between 125,000 and 150,000 Ukrainian troops had been killed between February 2022 and June 2026, with total military casualties reaching between 525,000 and 625,000.

Despite mounting military and economic pressures, the researchers warned that Putin was unlikely to abandon his ambitions in Ukraine without facing additional costs.

"Without greater costs in blood and treasure, Putin is likely to keep fighting," Jones and McCabe wrote.

Korkiya said Putin's decision to continue fighting reflects his belief that Moscow can outlast both Kyiv and its Western allies. "Putin has had opportunities to stop the fighting. When Ukraine agreed to a U.S. proposal for a 30-day ceasefire, he chose to keep fighting," she said.

"He still believes Russia can bear these losses longer than Ukraine and its allies can hold out. So far, even the deaths of hundreds of thousands of his own soldiers haven’t changed that calculation."

Latvian President Edgars Rinkēvičs echoed that assessment in an interview with Fox News Digital on Monday, arguing that Western leaders risk underestimating the ideological and religious beliefs driving Russia's war.

"We are too pragmatic and rational in the West," Rinkēvičs said.

RUSSIA COULD LAUNCH NUCLEAR-CAPABLE SATELLITE WITHIN WEEKS, WESTERN INTELLIGENCE WARNS: REPORT

He pointed to the concept of Russia as the "Third Rome" and the belief in its historical mission to serve as the protector of Christianity, arguing that such ideological convictions also drive Moscow's foreign policy and its war against Ukraine.

"Russia is using all the diplomatic kind of decoys simply to prolong the war," Rinkēvičs said.

The Latvian president suggested that a potential diplomatic opening could emerge in the spring or summer of 2027, provided Ukraine withstands Russia's winter campaign.

"Currently, Russia explores diplomatic efforts in order to prolong the war, not to end," he said.

Meanwhile, Ukraine continues to target Russian military assets deep inside the country.

Ukraine's General Staff said Wednesday that its forces had damaged five Russian military aircraft at the Savasleyka airbase in Russia's Nizhny Novgorod region, including three MiG-31 fighters and two Su-34 fighter-bombers, according to an official Ukrainian military statement.

Russia did not immediately comment on the Ukrainian claims, Reuters reported Wednesday.

The ongoing fighting has also heightened concerns about the war spilling into NATO territory.

Poland's military reported Tuesday that a Russian drone had briefly entered Polish airspace during an overnight attack on western Ukraine. The incident came four days after three Russian cruise missiles landed in Poland.

Reuters contributed to this story.

articles.title: Can hackers still read Gmail after a password change?
articles.summary:
You change your Gmail password after noticing something suspicious. You sign out of unfamiliar devices and figure your account should be safe again. But what if someone could still read your Gmail after a password change? That's the unsettling claim behind Remus Stealer, a malware service being marketed to cybercriminals. Its developers claim they can keep accessing Gmail messages even after someone resets their password and revokes existing sessions.

However, security researchers have not independently verified those claims, and Google disputes the suggestion that the malware exploits a Gmail security flaw. The company says this type of attack targets infected devices rather than Gmail itself. Google also warns that changing your password may not solve the problem if malware remains active on your computer. Here's what the investigation uncovered and how to protect your inbox.

Missed CyberGuy LIVE? Watch the replay and discover 5 ways to travel smarter and save money.

Our free CyberGuy LIVE class, 5 Ways to Travel Smarter and Save Money, has ended, but you can still watch the full replay. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you through five practical ways to protect your phone and personal information, avoid common travel scams, find better deals, save money on bookings and use technology to make your travels easier and less stressful. No technical experience is needed.

Watch the free replay + downloadable checklist now at CyberGuyLive.com.

CHEAP ANDROID PHONES FOUND WITH MALWARE ALREADY INSTALLED

Security researchers at Hudson Rock examined promotional materials for Remus Stealer, a type of malware designed to collect sensitive information from infected computers. In a November 9 report, the company described a new feature advertised in version 1.3.9 of the malware. The developers claim it allows criminals to open a compromised Gmail inbox directly from their control dashboard. The promotional screenshots show lists of emails and individual messages. There's also a "Mail" option connected to records of infected devices. According to the developers, criminals can retrieve email verification codes without collecting browser cookie files.

The developers make an even more concerning claim. They say changing a Google password or revoking existing sessions won't necessarily stop someone from accessing the mailbox. They also advertise a way to share mailbox access with other criminals through links. Think about what that could mean if the claims prove true. Someone with access to your Gmail could potentially read private conversations or collect password reset messages for other accounts. However, these claims come from the people selling the malware. Independent researchers have yet to demonstrate that the feature works as advertised.

Hudson Rock contacted the malware developer and spoke with someone who claimed to have used the Gmail feature. That person said they could still access an inbox after closing the browser, resetting a session and changing the Google account password. The developer also described a technique involving browser memory but didn't provide enough technical information to verify it. There are important limits to the investigation.

Hudson Rock did not reverse engineer the feature or conduct controlled testing after a complete account recovery. Researchers also couldn't independently verify the customer's claims. Most importantly, the investigation never established that criminals could retrieve newly arriving emails after someone had properly secured their Google account. The screenshots demonstrate that the service advertises a Gmail-reading interface. They don't prove that Remus can defeat Google's protections after a full recovery. There's also no evidence in the report of a previously unknown Gmail security vulnerability.

Researchers also could not rule out other explanations, including incomplete session revocation, previously collected messages or unauthorized access that remained active through another route. Without controlled testing, there's no way to confirm exactly how the advertised feature operates.

NEW AI MALWARE RANKS VICTIMS BY HOW MUCH THEY'RE WORTH

We reached out to Google about the research, and the company rejected the suggestion that the reported activity involved a vulnerability in Gmail. A Google spokesperson said: "Attacks involving infostealer malware that target session tokens on personal devices are not new, and there is no Gmail or Google vulnerability at play here. We routinely upgrade our built-in defenses to protect users against session theft and automatically secure accounts when we detect suspicious activity. Users can invalidate stolen sessions by removing malware from the affected device and revoking active sessions via g.co/mydevices."

Google explained that this kind of attack targets infected personal devices rather than exploiting Gmail itself. The company also highlighted something especially important for anyone recovering from malware. If the infection remains on a computer when someone resets their password, the malware could capture the new login session. That means a fresh password alone may not solve the problem. Google recommends removing the malware before signing back in on the affected device. From a separate, trusted device, you should also change your password, revoke suspicious sessions through Google's device activity page at myaccount.google.com/device-activity and review your account using Security Checkup at myaccount.google.com/security-checkup. The infected computer should remain disconnected until the threat has been removed.

The company says it regularly strengthens its defenses against stolen sessions. Those protections include frequent cookie rotation and additional authentication checks when someone attempts sensitive account changes. Google also highlighted Device Bound Session Credentials, a Chrome security technology designed to make stolen session cookies harder to reuse on another device. This protection applies to supported Chrome sessions, with availability depending on the platform and service. These protections help reduce the risk of account theft, although they don't eliminate every possible malware attack.

You probably open Gmail every day without typing your password. That's because your browser remembers that you've already signed in. Behind the scenes, browsers and applications use session cookies or authentication tokens to maintain access to accounts. These digital credentials help keep you signed in without repeatedly entering your password. Unfortunately, criminals know how valuable that information can be. Infostealer malware can target stored authentication data on an infected computer. If an attacker obtains a valid session, they may be able to access an account without entering the password again. That can also undermine the protection you'd normally expect from two-step verification because the legitimate account holder has already completed the sign-in process.

However, a stolen session doesn't automatically give someone unlimited access. Google can invalidate sessions, and some sensitive actions require additional verification. Google's documentation explains that changing a password generally revokes OAuth access and refresh tokens used by applications with Gmail permissions, although certain exceptions apply. Google also notes that password changes sign people out of most devices, but some trusted devices and third-party connections may remain signed in. Those exceptions do not prove that Remus uses any of these methods. The concern with an infected computer is that malware may capture fresh authentication information when you sign in again. That's why securing the computer and reviewing account access are essential parts of recovery.

An unfamiliar Google security alert deserves attention, especially if you haven't signed in from a new device. You should also investigate password reset messages you never requested. These can indicate that someone is attempting to access another account connected to your email address, although an unexpected reset message alone doesn't prove an account has been compromised.

Other warning signs include missing messages or people telling you they received strange emails from your address. Check your Sent folder for messages you didn't write. You might also discover forwarding rules or account recovery settings you don't remember changing. If something looks suspicious, open your Google account directly rather than following a link in an unexpected message.

If you suspect that someone has accessed your Gmail, take action promptly. The goal is to secure your account while preventing malware from stealing fresh login information. Google emphasizes that removing the infection and revoking compromised sessions are both essential. You can begin securing your account from a trusted device while keeping the suspected infected computer offline.

If you believe your computer has been infected, disconnect it from the internet. Use a separate, trusted device to begin securing your important accounts.

Strong antivirus protection with real-time scanning can help prevent infostealers from gaining access in the first place. However, no antivirus program can guarantee that every threat will be detected. Get my picks for the best 2026 antivirus protection winners for your Windows, Mac, Android & iOS devices at CyberGuy.com

Use a trusted device to secure your Google account. If you suspect that malware stole your login information, change your password promptly and make sure the infected computer cannot capture another session. Do not sign back into Google on the suspected infected computer until you have removed the malware.

Google notes that several sessions can appear under the same device name. Review each one and sign out of any you cannot confidently identify. If you've already changed your password while malware was still running, make sure the infected device has been cleaned or remains offline, then change your password again from a trusted device and review active sessions once more.

A criminal who gains access to your Gmail may change settings so incoming messages get forwarded to another email address. That could allow someone to receive copies of new messages even after you change your password. Google requires verification when someone adds a new forwarding address, but you should still check for forwarding that may have been configured without your knowledge.

To check your Gmail settings on a computer:

Some third-party applications can access parts of your Google account after you grant permission. If an unfamiliar app has access to your Gmail, it deserves a closer look.

You can also read my CyberGuy guide on apps accessing your Google account for additional instructions.

Google recommends several protections that can make account takeovers harder.

Passkeys offer stronger sign-in security, but they cannot remove an existing infection or automatically prevent theft of an already authenticated session. Google's Advanced Protection Program adds stricter account safeguards, including tighter restrictions on third-party access.

Remember how many online services use your email address for account recovery. If criminals accessed your mailbox, they may have seen verification messages from other services. Review important accounts for unfamiliar activity. Pay particular attention to unexpected password changes or security alerts.

If you reused your Google password anywhere else, change those passwords too. Use unique credentials for every important account, and consider a password manager to keep track of them. For additional protection, my CyberGuy article on identity thieves who don't need your password explains other ways criminals try to get around traditional account security.

For years, changing your password has been one of the first things I've recommended when an online account gets compromised. I still believe that's essential. But this investigation highlights something many people overlook. If malware is running on your computer, it may be able to steal fresh login information after you've changed your password. What concerns me is how much of our digital lives depend on a single Gmail account. Think about the personal messages sitting in your inbox and the accounts that rely on your email for password recovery.

Someone who gains access could potentially create problems well beyond your inbox. Google's response makes an important distinction. This is a threat involving malware on infected devices, not a newly demonstrated vulnerability in Gmail. We should also remember that the most alarming claims about this malware have yet to be independently verified. There's a big difference between what criminals advertise and what security researchers can actually demonstrate.

My advice is to take account security seriously without panicking over an unproven claim. Keep strong antivirus protection running on your devices and pay attention to suspicious account activity. If you suspect an infection, make sure the malware has been removed before trusting a fresh login. Then change your password from a trusted device and revoke any suspicious sessions. Those extra steps can help prevent someone from regaining access to your account.

If you discovered that a hacker had been reading your Gmail, would changing your password restore your confidence, or would you feel compelled to abandon that email address entirely? Let us know by writing to us at Cyberguy.com

articles.title: Tech billionaire plans 1,000-year floating city at sea
articles.summary:
How frustrated would you have to be with government red tape to decide the ocean looks like a better place to build a factory? Tech billionaire Palmer Luckey has an answer. He wants to create a massive floating industrial city where American companies could operate beyond certain state and local restrictions.

The project is called SLAB, and Luckey says it would have a design life of 1,000 years. That's a pretty extraordinary promise for something sitting in the middle of the ocean. However, the reasoning behind the project may be even more surprising than the structure itself. We discussed Luckey's ambitious plans in detail on "The CyberGuy Report Podcast" at cyberguy.com/podcast. So, what exactly is he planning to build, and could moving American industry offshore really solve the problems he's trying to escape?

Missed CyberGuy LIVE? Watch the replay and discover 5 ways to travel smarter and save money.

Our free CyberGuy LIVE class, 5 Ways to Travel Smarter and Save Money, has ended, but you can still watch the full replay. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you through five practical ways to protect your phone and personal information, avoid common travel scams, find better deals, save money on bookings and use technology to make your travels easier and less stressful. No technical experience is needed.

Watch the free replay + downloadable checklist now at CyberGuyLive.com.

CEO SAYS DOING BUSINESS IN STATE ‘SUCKS’ AS COMPANY HEADS TO TEXAS AMID CALIFORNIA EXODUS

Palmer Luckey, the founder of Oculus and co-founder of defense technology company Anduril Industries, has revealed plans for a floating industrial platform called SLAB. In a November 18 post on X, Luckey explained that he began developing the project after Facebook acquired Oculus in 2014. He used some of the money from that sale to pursue an idea that has fascinated technology entrepreneurs for years.

The concept is known as seasteading. It involves building permanent structures on the ocean where people can live or operate businesses outside some of the restrictions that apply on land. Luckey's version focuses heavily on American industry. He wants to create a place where companies could conduct activities that face significant regulatory hurdles on the mainland. The illustration accompanying his announcement shows an enormous platform rising above the ocean with buildings and industrial facilities on top.

AMERICA'S REDDEST STATE CHASES BILLION-DOLLAR BOOM AS OTHERS SOUR ON MASSIVE EMERGING INDUSTRY

Luckey believes government regulations have made it unnecessarily difficult for certain industries to operate in the United States. His proposed solution is to move some of those operations offshore. He specifically mentioned metal processing and oil refining. He also identified desalination and medical research as possible activities for SLAB. In his announcement, Luckey described the project as a way to strengthen American industry by creating a "relief valve for ill-considered or outdated rules and regulations."

His argument is that companies could operate more efficiently if they avoided certain state and local restrictions. He also wants the offshore platform to be cheaper than building comparable facilities on land, although he has not publicly demonstrated that the economics would work. There is also a more controversial possibility. In a separate exchange on X, Luckey suggested that offshore facilities could provide access to medical treatments currently prohibited in the United States. That raises difficult questions about patient safety and whether those activities could legally take place offshore.

Luckey says he and several close friends funded SLAB at a $1 billion valuation back in 2017. However, that figure refers to the project's reported valuation at the time. It does not establish that $1 billion has been spent building it. He also says the project has made significant progress, although considerable work remains. So far, he has not publicly disclosed a confirmed construction schedule or a precise location for the proposed platform.

Interestingly, Luckey only decided to discuss SLAB publicly after learning that journalists were preparing to describe it as a floating AI data center. He pushed back on that description, saying the project was much older and considerably more ambitious. His comments suggest that data centers could be part of the broader concept, but SLAB was conceived for other industrial activities as well.

This is where Luckey's proposal runs into some complicated legal questions. According to the Bureau of Ocean Energy Management, most coastal states, including California, have jurisdiction over submerged lands extending approximately three nautical miles offshore. Beyond that boundary, federal authority becomes especially important. The United States has a territorial sea extending 12 nautical miles from its coastal baselines. It also maintains an exclusive economic zone extending up to 200 nautical miles offshore.

The National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration explains that the federal government retains authority over certain offshore structures and activities within that zone. Consequently, moving a business beyond California's coastal boundary would not automatically eliminate federal oversight. Environmental requirements and maritime regulations could still apply. The legal picture would also depend on whether SLAB floats freely, anchors to the ocean floor or operates under a particular country's registration. Luckey has yet to explain exactly how the platform would navigate those requirements.

Building a permanent industrial community offshore presents extraordinary engineering challenges. Saltwater gradually corrodes exposed structures, and powerful storms can place enormous stress on offshore installations. Maintaining a facility for centuries would require substantial engineering and ongoing repairs. Then there is the expense of running an industrial operation at sea. Workers would need transportation to the platform, while supplies and equipment would have to travel across the water.

That makes Luckey's goal of operating more cheaply than comparable land-based facilities particularly ambitious. A 1,000-year design life is also a target rather than a demonstrated lifespan. Until Luckey releases detailed engineering evidence, there is no way to independently verify whether SLAB could meet that goal.

California has long been associated with technological innovation, yet it also has extensive environmental and land-use regulations. Some businesses argue that permitting requirements make industrial development more expensive and time-consuming. Luckey's proposal brings that debate into focus. Moving industrial activity offshore would be a drastic response to regulatory frustration. However, the idea also raises a question worth asking: Have some regulations become so burdensome that entrepreneurs would rather build at sea than navigate the approval process on land?

Of course, industries involving hazardous chemicals or experimental medical treatments require serious oversight. Those protections help prevent accidents and protect public health. At the same time, regulations can become unnecessarily complicated or outdated. Governments need to examine whether their approval processes encourage responsible innovation or create obstacles that serve little practical purpose. Luckey has not identified the specific California laws he hopes to avoid. For now, his project highlights a broader argument about how America regulates industrial development. Whether SLAB becomes a functioning offshore community remains to be seen.

I find the whole idea fascinating, but something about it also strikes me as completely absurd. Have we really reached a point where building a giant industrial platform in the ocean sounds more appealing than dealing with government regulations on land? California, in particular, should be paying attention. This is a state that helped create Silicon Valley, yet we're now talking about taking American industry offshore to escape regulatory headaches. I'm certainly not suggesting we eliminate important environmental or safety protections. But there's a point where excessive regulation can start working against the very innovation we should be encouraging. I'd much rather see American businesses building here, creating jobs and developing new technology without unnecessary roadblocks. Luckey still has a tremendous amount to prove before SLAB becomes reality. But the fact that he's seriously pursuing this idea should give policymakers something to think about. For more on this story and our discussion about the future of American innovation, listen to The CyberGuy Report Podcast at cyberguy.com/podcast/.
