Internal records show the facility suffered from insufficient appropriately trained personnel capable of conducting animal procedures at the required biocontainment level, an absence of adequate contingency planning, unclear protocols and prolonged confinement of flying fox bats without proper enrichment.

RIDGLAN FARMS BEAGLES BEGIN LEAVING WISCONSIN FACILITY AFTER RESCUE GROUPS STRIKE DEAL FOR RELEASE

After a single flying fox tested positive for Hendra virus, staff were forced to kill all eight bats housed together because the room could not be elevated to Biosafety Level 4 (BSL-4) containment. A ninth flying fox housed separately at BSL-4 was later killed after also testing positive.

The primary investigator alerted the NIH to the infections in May 2023, leading the ethics board to suspend the study weeks later. However, the NIH’s Office of Laboratory Animal Welfare (OLAW) did not receive even a preliminary report of the suspension until April 2024 — more than 10 months after the shutdown, according to records.

The documents show the Australian bat study was not an isolated incident. At Newcastle University in the United Kingdom, where researchers conducted NIH-funded brain and stroke research on nonhuman primates, a 2025 federal review ordered the facility to reevaluate its personal protective equipment standards, tuberculosis screening and emergency procedures for testing potential human exposures to the deadly Herpes B virus.

Following past international scandals — including a shuttered Colombian facility that received $17 million in U.S. funding while keeping monkeys in squalor — the NIH pledged to implement "enhanced oversight" of foreign institutions in line with Government Accountability Office (GAO) recommendations.

However, PETA’s review of 124 federal files obtained through the Freedom of Information Act (FOIA) shows the NIH’s oversight relies almost entirely on self-reporting and scripted virtual site visits.

Records show that virtual visits were announced months in advance, allowing overseas facilities ample time to prepare. At Newcastle University, the facility received notice in May 2025 for a virtual visit that did not happen until December. 

Notification letters outlined prearranged planning sessions, document reviews and camera tours where foreign personnel controlled what government monitors could see on screen.

The format gave federal regulators no ability to conduct unannounced walk-throughs, inspect arbitrary rooms, review records in real time or conduct confidential staff interviews, according to records. 

Out of 70 annual reports examined regarding active NIH-backed animal research across foreign labs between 2023 and 2025, 67 self-reported zero violations, reflecting a system almost entirely dependent on foreign labs self-policing their own programs.

HARVARD-CHINA LINKS UNEARTHED AS CONGRESS FINDS 140 PAPERS CO-AUTHORED BY CCP MILITARY UNIVERSITIES

The records also document widespread administrative failures, including grants flowing to institutions that lacked basic federal authorization:

The NIH awarded a $13 million tuberculosis vaccine adjuvant contract to the University of Sydney in 2022, but the animal testing was outsourced to the Centenary Institute in Australia, an entity lacking the required NIH Foreign Animal Welfare Assurance. 

The unauthorized setup went unnoticed by the NIH for years until the university inquired about the death of an experimental mouse in 2025.

HUNDREDS OF ACTIVISTS FACE PEPPER SPRAY IN VIOLENT CLASH WITH DEPUTIES AT WISCONSIN BEAGLE RESEARCH FACILITY

The NIH also confirmed that it could find "no records of an assurance" for multiple foreign entities carrying out U.S.-funded animal studies, including Australian biotech firm Kinoxis Therapeutics, which conducted opioid withdrawal experiments on 80 dogs, 314 rats and 1,485 mice under a grant active through May 2026. 

Similar record absences occurred for grants involving animal testing at institutions in Canada, Kenya and Israel.

At the Research Center in Clinical Biochemistry and Immunology in Argentina, the NIH funded a multi-year Chagas disease study. A 2026 preprint co-authored by the lead researcher detailed mice experiencing continuous whole-body tremors and hind-limb paralysis — conditions mandating euthanasia under the approved protocol.

However, the lab reported that untreated animals died over an extended 120-day timeframe and admitted it does not generate animal monitoring or veterinary records, leaving federal regulators with no documentation of how animal deaths were tracked.

WHITE HOUSE REBUKES CBS INTERVIEW AFTER HOST BATTLES NIH DIRECTOR OVER LOSS OF TRUST IN PUBLIC HEALTH

In her letter Monday to Bhattacharya, Dr. Magnolia Martínez, PETA’s lead projects manager and congressional liaison, argued that the NIH's foreign monitoring regime is fundamentally broken.

The organization noted that an Animal Welfare Assurance represents a baseline administrative requirement that does not ensure animal welfare or clinical applicability to human health, urging the agency to halt funding foreign animal tests and redirect resources toward human-biology-based research methods.

The U.S. Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) on Monday told Fox News Digital the NIH "received the report today and will investigate its claims thoroughly to determine whether any animal welfare policies were violated."

"Under the leadership of Director Dr. Bhattacharya, the agency has taken unprecedented steps to strengthen oversight and increase transparency in research conducted by foreign institutions," HHS press secretary Emily Hilliard wrote in a statement.

Lawmakers in Washington are similarly ramping up efforts to cut off foreign funding through the CARGO Act, emphasizing that American taxpayers should not be underwriting unaccountable and hazardous research in foreign jurisdictions.

Fox News Digital reached out to bipartisan sponsors of the CARGO Act — including Sens. Rick Scott, R-Fla., Cory Booker, D-N.J., and Dina Titus, D-Nev. — asking whether the newly revealed foreign laboratory failures will prompt renewed legislative action and oversight hearings to permanently ban federal funding for overseas animal experiments.

articles.title: Google AI smartwatch could flag high blood pressure
articles.summary:
When was the last time you checked your blood pressure? If you're like a lot of people, it probably happened during your last doctor's appointment. And if you feel perfectly healthy, you may not give it another thought. That's what makes high blood pressure so concerning. You can have it for years without noticing anything wrong.

Now, Google researchers are exploring a way to uncover that hidden danger using something many of us already wear on our wrists. In a new study recently published in Nature, researchers demonstrated an artificial intelligence system that can identify signs of hypertension using standard smartwatch sensors. It works in the background without requiring calibration with a traditional blood pressure cuff.

The technology uses sensors that already exist in consumer smartwatches. That could make early detection much more accessible. However, the research also reveals a limitation that anyone relying on a smartwatch for health information should understand.

Missed CyberGuy LIVE? Watch the replay and discover 5 ways to travel smarter and save money.

Our free CyberGuy LIVE class, 5 Ways to Travel Smarter and Save Money, has ended, but you can still watch the full replay. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you through five practical ways to protect your phone and personal information, avoid common travel scams, find better deals, save money on bookings and use technology to make your travels easier and less stressful. No technical experience is needed.

Watch the free replay + downloadable checklist now at CyberGuyLive.com.

SMARTWATCH AFIB ALERT SENDS DAD TO ER BEFORE HEART SURGERY

Your smartwatch already knows quite a bit about your body. It can track your heart rate throughout the day. Depending on the model, it may also detect irregular heart rhythms.

Google's new AI takes the information collected by those sensors and looks for signs of something harder to detect: ongoing high blood pressure. According to Google Research, the system analyzes two types of sensor data.

The first sensor uses light to detect changes in blood volume beneath your skin. It's the same basic technology many watches use to monitor your pulse. The second sensor measures movement. Researchers found that it can also capture incredibly small vibrations caused by your heart pumping blood. You wouldn't notice those vibrations. However, the AI can analyze them alongside your pulse patterns to look for signs associated with hypertension.

The system collects information over multiple days. It then combines those patterns with your height to estimate the likelihood of sustained high blood pressure. Unlike a traditional monitor, the smartwatch doesn't produce a reading such as 120 over 80. Instead, it looks for signs that your blood pressure may be consistently elevated. What's interesting is that you wouldn't have to do anything differently. You could go about your day while your smartwatch quietly looks for potential warning signs.

Google worked with researchers from Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center and Harvard Medical School to develop and test the system. First, researchers trained the underlying AI using nearly 500,000 hours of smartwatch sensor data collected from 2,109 consenting participants. They then evaluated the hypertension detection system in a clinical study involving 196 participants across five U.S. locations. None of those participants had known cardiovascular disease or were taking blood pressure medication.

During the study, participants wore a consumer smartwatch for seven days. Researchers compared the AI's findings with results from 24-hour ambulatory blood pressure monitoring. That medical test uses a cuff to measure blood pressure repeatedly throughout the day and night. Doctors use it to help confirm hypertension.

During initial screening, the results showed:

For comparison, initial blood pressure screenings performed in medical offices identified 55.3% of participants with hypertension in the study. That's an encouraging result. However, the difference between the smartwatch and office screening was not statistically significant, according to a Nature Portfolio summary of the findings. There's another number worth paying attention to.

That's a number worth paying attention to. After all, we're talking about a condition that can lead to a heart attack or stroke, often without any warning signs.

Researchers also looked at a smaller group of 48 people who had elevated blood pressure readings during their initial doctor's visit. In that group, the AI correctly identified 78.4% of those with ongoing hypertension. It also correctly ruled out the condition in 90.9% of those who didn't have it. Those results are encouraging, but there's still work to do. Google needs to test the technology on more people before we can know how reliably it can detect high blood pressure.

MICROSOFT AI BEATS DOCTORS IN SIMULATED DIAGNOSIS TEST

Here's where things get interesting for people who already own a Google smartwatch. Google introduced its Health Guardian features in September 2026. Among them is a blood pressure trends feature available through the Google Health app.

According to Google's September announcement, blood pressure trends are available at no additional subscription cost on eligible Pixel Watch 3, Pixel Watch 4 and Pixel Watch 5 devices. Availability depends on your region.

The feature analyzes pulse and movement patterns over time. Then, it provides a monthly assessment of whether your blood pressure trend appears high. Google says these existing Health Guardian capabilities are informed by clinical research, including work connected to its newly published findings. However, there's an important difference between the experimental system described in Nature and the feature available on your watch today.

The existing Pixel Watch feature is intended for general wellness. Google specifically says it cannot diagnose hypertension or serve as a medical screening tool. It also cannot tell you your actual systolic or diastolic blood pressure numbers. According to Google's support documentation, the feature provides a monthly trend assessment such as "High" or "Not high."

And a "Not high" result doesn't guarantee your blood pressure is normal. Google also warns users against relying on these estimates to change medications or treatment plans. Meanwhile, the newly published research remains exploratory. Google has not announced that the experimental hypertension screening system will become a commercial diagnostic feature.

Google has some competition in this area. Apple has already introduced FDA-cleared hypertension notifications for compatible Apple Watch models. As we previously reported in Apple Watch gets FDA-approved hypertension alerts, the feature looks for patterns associated with chronic high blood pressure. It uses information gathered by the watch's optical heart sensor over 30-day periods.

The feature supports Apple Watch Series 9 and later models, along with Apple Watch Ultra 2 and later models, subject to software and regional availability. If the watch detects concerning patterns, it can notify you. However, Apple also makes clear that the feature cannot diagnose hypertension. And it may miss cases. Apple recommends checking your blood pressure with a traditional cuff and discussing the results with a healthcare professional if you receive an alert.

So, while Apple and Google are approaching this technology differently, the current guidance remains clear. A smartwatch alert can give you useful information, but you still need an accurate blood pressure measurement.

High blood pressure has earned the nickname "silent killer" for a reason. According to the World Health Organization, more than one billion adults worldwide live with hypertension. Many have no idea they have it.

Meanwhile, untreated high blood pressure can damage blood vessels and increase the risk of a heart attack or stroke. Younger adults can be particularly vulnerable to missed diagnoses because they may feel healthy and see little reason to get checked. Now, consider what could happen if a smartwatch noticed concerning patterns before someone developed symptoms.

That person might decide to schedule an appointment and have their blood pressure checked. If doctors confirm hypertension, earlier treatment could help reduce the risk of complications. Of course, researchers still need to determine whether smartwatch-based screening actually improves diagnosis rates and long-term health outcomes.

COULD A PAINT-ON ELECTRONIC TATTOO SPOT HEART ATTACKS?

If your smartwatch warns you about possible high blood pressure, don't ignore it. But don't assume the watch has diagnosed you, either. The next step is to check your blood pressure using a validated upper-arm cuff.

The American Heart Association recommends automatic upper-arm monitors for home measurements because they provide more reliable readings than typical wrist or finger monitors. If you're using Google's blood pressure trends feature and receive a "High" result, Google recommends checking your blood pressure twice a day for seven days and sharing those readings with your doctor.

Make sure you follow your monitor's instructions and use the correct cuff size. Also, keep an eye on how you're feeling. If you experience emergency warning signs such as chest pain or difficulty breathing, seek immediate medical attention rather than waiting for another smartwatch assessment.

And remember, even if your watch never sends an alert, you should continue getting your blood pressure checked. For another way to track your readings, see our article on how to monitor blood pressure with your Apple Watch using a compatible blood pressure monitor.

One of my biggest questions about this technology comes down to how much confidence people will place in the results. Let's say your smartwatch tells you everything looks normal. Would you still bother checking your blood pressure? That's where the research raises an important concern.

In Google's initial screening study, the AI missed a meaningful number of people who actually had hypertension. And while the results compared favorably with initial office screening, the study was relatively small. Researchers will need more evidence before the technology can become a dependable part of routine medical screening.

Google's findings suggest that everyday wearables could eventually help identify people who might otherwise go undiagnosed. For now, though, a reliable blood pressure cuff and a conversation with your doctor remain essential.

I like where Google is going with this. Most of us probably don't think about our blood pressure until we're sitting in a doctor's office with a cuff around our arm. So the idea that a smartwatch could spot a potential problem before we even know something's wrong is pretty exciting. But there's one number in this study that concerns me. The AI missed roughly one in three people who actually had high blood pressure. That's a lot, especially when you consider the serious health risks involved. I think this technology has tremendous potential, and I'm looking forward to seeing how Google improves it. But for now, I wouldn't rely on my smartwatch to tell me whether my blood pressure is normal. I'd still want to check it with a traditional cuff.

Would you trust your smartwatch to warn you about high blood pressure? Let us know by writing to us at Cyberguy.com.

articles.title: Zelenskyy hails ‘exemplary Ukrainian operation’ sinking Russian warship off Libya
articles.summary:
The war between Russia and Ukraine continues to spill outside the countries' boundaries, as Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy shared a video of a drone striking and sinking Russian weapons ships off the coast of Libya.

"We continue our operations in designated waters," Zelenskyy wrote early Monday morning in a statement on X. "We are responding to Russia’s aggression. We are developing Ukraine weapons. Glory to Ukraine!"

The strikes come as President Donald Trump is pushing for peace, but Ukraine has remained steadfast in not only fighting off Russian gains in south and east of Ukraine, but also taking the fight to Russia "in designated waters" around the globe.

RUSSIAN WARSHIP SINKS OFF LIBYA AS SUSPECTED UKRAINIAN STRIKES TAKE WAR BEYOND BLACK SEA

"An exemplary Ukrainian operation in response to Russia’s war," the post began. "I thank the warriors of the Security Service of Ukraine and all our Defense Forces of Ukraine who took part in carrying out these tasks. I received detailed briefings on the operation’s steps yesterday and today – the targets we set were achieved. It all took place off the coast of Libya.

"Our warriors deployed seven Ukrainian-made naval drones. Despite all the enemy’s efforts to counter the attack, the Russian corvette Merkury was sunk. It’s one of their newest ships, commissioned in 2023, during the full-scale war. A Ka-27 combat helicopter was also destroyed along with the corvette. Our second target was the Russian dry cargo vessel MV ANGARA, which the enemy used to transport weapons. Result: target hit."

UKRAINE POUNDS BLACK SEA FLEET’S ‘LAST MAJOR STRONGHOLD’ WHILE PUTIN FLEXES NAVAL POWER IN PACIFIC

Sunday's drone strike hit the Russian vessel while it was docked at the Benghazi naval base in eastern Libya – a region controlled by military commander Khalifa Haftar, whose Libyan National Army maintains ties with Russia. The Institute for the Study of War reported that the Merkury had stopped at Benghazi for several days under a cooperation agreement to refuel and resupply while escorting Russian cargo vessels capable of carrying military supplies back to Russia.

Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov called the Baltic Sea incident part of a "dangerous trend of increasing terrorist activity" and urged regional nations to warn Kyiv against such operations. Russian, Estonian and Finnish vessels fought the blaze after the Sparta II drifted into Finnish waters before a Russian vessel began towing it away Sunday.

UKRAINE'S ATTACKS ON RUSSIA ARE PUSHING PUTIN CLOSER TO NEGOTIATING TABLE, TRUMP NATO AMBASSADOR SAYS

Osama Hamad, prime minister of Libya's eastern-based government, said he asked the United Nations to investigate "suspicions that the boats had been launched from western Libya" and to verify whether Ukrainian military experts are operating there. Western Libya is governed by the internationally recognized Government of National Unity in Tripoli, which did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

UKRAINE’S DRONE REVOLUTION SHOWS RUSSIA IS DANGEROUSLY UNPREPARED. BUT, SO IS AMERICA

The Benghazi operation follows earlier maritime incidents far outside the Black Sea theater.

UKRAINE'S ZELENSKYY ON DEFYING US IN ATTACKING RUSSIAN OIL: 'OUR RESPONSE MUST BE PAINFUL'

The expanding naval strikes come as U.S.-backed peace talks between Moscow and Kyiv resumed this month after a nine-month pause. The sticking point remains Russian annexation of occupied Ukrainian in exchange for potential NATO-like security guarantees. Zelenskyy had told Fox News of some potential negotiation of land for security, but has since balked at giving up on the land bridge sought by Vladimir Putin to connect Russia to the Black Sea.

The overland route connecting Russia to the Black Sea coast and Crimea runs through occupied southern Ukraine – specifically the Zaporizhzhia and Kherson regions – alongside the 19-kilometer (12-mile) Crimean Bridge across the Kerch Strait.

UKRAINE RELEASES VIDEO SHOWING DAMAGE TO PUTIN'S PRIZED BRIDGE FOLLOWING 'UNPRECEDENTED OPERATION' IN CRIMEA

Ukraine strategically struck the Crimean Bridge while Trump was getting ready to meet with Putin and China's Xi Jinping. The meeting came thereafter and did not result in any movements toward peace.

Mykola Bielieskov of the National Institute for Strategic Studies in Kyiv told Reuters that Ukraine is seeking leverage through "horizontal escalation."

"Since neither side is able to compel the other to accept terms of settlement through the battlefield only, both try to find new ways to pressure each other," he said.

Reuters contributed to this report.

articles.title: Did GTA 6 really recreate Charlie Kirk's assassination?
articles.summary: Just days after its release, Grand Theft Auto 6 has become a vehicle for political misinformation. Viral footage falsely claims the game features a mission recreating Charlie Kirk’s assassination, while pro-Russian accounts are sharing fake screenshots containing anti-Ukrainian messages. Meanwhile, Russia’s own Defence Ministry has exploited the game's popularity to promote military recruitment. Vedika Bahl explains how GTA 6 is being used to push real political agendas in Truth or Fake.

articles.title: Campaign rules for influencers? French regulator targets content creators
articles.summary: Ever since 1965 when the French first got to cast a ballot by universal suffrage for their president, they've valued campaign rules that guarantee ‘equal time’ for candidates. But what does equal time mean when you're closing in on 2027? Last week a bombshell announcement ahead of next Spring’s presidential elections: major online content creators will have to respect the same balanced air time rules as traditional TV and radio broadcasters during the campaign period. Here at France 24, we’re already testing the stopwatches and combing ove the guest list spreadsheets. Should podcasters, YouTubers and influencers be subjected to the same rules as us?

articles.title: EU says 'strongly' rejects premise of new US tariffs
articles.summary: The EU said Wednesday that it rejected the premise of new tariffs on its exports proposed by the United States and expected Washington to stick by a deal struck with Brussels last year. The US unveiled proposed tariffs on 14 economies including the European Union and China, after a months-long probe into alleged excess production. FRANCE 24's Dave Keating reports from Brussels.

articles.title: In boost for Netanyahu, judges question corruption trial charges
articles.summary: Judges in the long-running corruption trial of Israeli caretaker Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu handed his defence a major boost on Wednesday in recommending the prosecution drop one of the cases in which he is accused of bribery. The recommendations, which came as Israel's longest-serving prime minister fights for his political survival, were immediately cheered by Netanyahu's right-wing allies who demanded the trial be brought to an end. FRANCE 24's Noga Tarnopolsky reports from Jerusalem.

articles.title: Poland says will create no-fly zone at Ukraine border after repeated airspace violations
articles.summary: Poland will soon create a no-fly zone near the Ukrainian border, a deputy defence minister announced on Wednesday, after several incursions into its airspace it blamed on Russia. Poland backs Ukraine as it fights off Russia's near five-year invasion and has repeatedly accused Moscow of seeking to target Kyiv's supporters with drone incursions and other methods. The no-fly zone is intended to allow Polish forces to quickly identify any Russian military aircraft and shoot them down if necessary. FRANCE 24's Selina Sykes reports.

articles.title: US unveils proposed tariffs on major partners, including EU and China
articles.summary: The United States on Wednesday unveiled proposed tariffs on 14 economies including the European Union and China, after a months-long probe into alleged excess production -- the latest move by US President Donald Trump to remake Washington's trade relationships. The duties, proposed at up to 20 percent, come over allegations the economies "are promoting production and capacity divorced from the realities of demand and market principles," a senior US official said on condition of anonymity. FRANCE 24's Camille Knight.

articles.title: The ‘French Milei’? Presidential candidate David Lisnard aims to reshape France’s right wing
articles.summary: Having secured reelection victory Wednesday as leader of France's mayors, Cannes Mayor David Lisnard turns once more to build on his recent bid for the Élysée. As his Nouvelle Énergie movement gains momentum, questions swirl over whether his campaign will reshape the French political landscape, or if his party will ultimately cosy up to the far right ahead of France’s 2027 race to the polls.

articles.title: Turkey's deadly factory blast: 'Investing in safety costs more than letting people die'
articles.summary: An explosion at a steel factory on November 9 in Turkey's Aliaga, near Izmir, killed 19 people. This tragedy follows several others and highlights the issues surrounding workers’ safety in Turkey, our Observers say. They also condemn the repressive responses from the government and the company.

articles.title: Paris takes on masculinist movements
articles.summary: As masculinist movements face their first major trial in Paris, the city has announced several initiatives to combat this ideology. The campaign aims to call attention to the real-world danger posed by misogynist groups online. FRANCE 24's Gabrielle Nadler takes a closer look.

articles.title: 'Free' land and thriving businesses: French village defies rural decline
articles.summary: As France's mayors gather in Paris for their annual convention, the decline in living standards and public services in both urban and rural areas is high on the agenda. Rural mayors, in particular, are concerned about the shrinking populations of their communities. But one small French town bucking the trend is Parlan, in the Cantal region, where the population has doubled and local services have flourished thanks to an offer of virtually free plots of land.

articles.title: Moldova launches national preparedness campaign after drone incursions
articles.summary: Moldova is urging its citizens to prepare for emergencies as the war in neighbouring Ukraine brings new risks across its border. The “Moldova Ready” campaign, launched in Chisinau, includes a display of the remains of a drone carrying 52kg of explosives after it crashed in the country last month. FRANCE 24's Daniel Whittington reports.

articles.title: Top Spanish court closes case against Catalan separatist leader
articles.summary: Spain's Supreme Court has applied a controversial amnesty law to former Catalan separatist leader Carles Puigdemont, closing criminal proceedings against him over his role in the region's failed 2017 independence bid. The ruling, which comes ahead of a snap general election on Sunday, marks the final step in the implementation of the amnesty law, passed by parliament in 2024.

articles.title: Huang's return fails to dispel doubts as Nvidia shares drop
articles.summary: A rally sparked by Jensen Huang's return as Nvidia's chief executive faded on Tuesday, with the company's shares falling as doubts persisted over the probes he faces and the fate of the AI investment boom. After vaulting more than 30 percent on Monday following Huang's shock comeback, Nvidia fell almost six percent Tuesday. Huang resigned on November 12 over extramarital affairs, including one with a suspected Chinese spy.

articles.title: US unveils proposed tariffs on major partners, including EU and China

The new tariffs will need to undergo a period of public comment before taking effect. The new levies target some of the United States' largest trading partners. FRANCE 24's International Affairs Editor Kethevane Gorjestani tells us more.

articles.title: Iowa: Toxic dust fears as US Army blows up 10,000 pounds of explosives

articles.title: US Army detonates lead explosives in Iowa despite contamination fears

articles.title: 'It can take years': Why the AI Riemann proof is far from settled

articles.title: Tusk government ‘facing armageddon’ as European court resumes cases against Poland
articles.summary:
Europe’s top human rights court resumed proceedings against Poland on Wednesday, putting fresh pressure on Prime Minister Donald Tusk to deliver on his promise to restore the independence of the country’s courts.

The European Court of Human Rights said it has around 1,600 cases pending over judicial changes introduced by Poland’s former nationalist Law and Justice government. It suspended proceedings in 2023 to give Warsaw time to restore judicial independence.

Tusk’s promise to restore the rule of law helped unlock billions in frozen EU funding following his return to power in 2023. But his efforts have been hampered by two successive PiS-backed presidents, most recently Karol Nawrocki.

Justice Minister Waldemar Żurek has estimated that compensation payments could exceed €12 million. Speaking by phone Wednesday evening, he said the bill could grow considerably as judges appointed under the disputed system continued to hear cases, creating fresh grounds for compensation claims.

“So we’re facing armageddon,” Żurek said. He blamed PiS for undermining Poland’s judicial system and accused Nawrocki of obstructing efforts to repair it.

The decision comes amid a wider confrontation between Tusk and Nawrocki over Poland’s courts, including the Constitutional Tribunal.

At the heart of the ECHR cases is a 2017 overhaul that gave lawmakers greater control over judicial appointments. Nawrocki vetoed a bill in February aimed at reversing those changes, arguing it would usher in a “new phase of chaos.”

Nawrocki’s office did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

The ECHR has already sided with applicants ranging from a distributor of sex-enhancing supplements to former Polish President and Nobel Peace Prize winner Lech Wałęsa.

Wałęsa had won a defamation case against a former associate who accused him of collaborating with the communist secret police, only to see that victory overturned years later by a newly created chamber of Poland’s Supreme Court.

The ECHR awarded him €30,000 in damages in a landmark 2023 ruling that prompted the suspension of similar cases. It twice extended the suspension but let it expire Monday.

Another bill addressing the status of thousands of judges appointed under PiS-era rules has been on Nawrocki’s desk since Nov. 9. Żurek said it would address the ECHR’s main concerns but that he feared another politically motivated veto.

articles.title: “Les COP, c’est une blague” : les critiques enflent contre les sommets climatiques après l’échec à Antalya
articles.summary:
Le processus des Nations unies pour coordonner la réponse mondiale au changement climatique se fissure discrètement depuis des années. Aujourd’hui, même ses partisans historiques se rebellent ouvertement et exigent une refonte des négociations internationales.

L’élément déclencheur : l’échec retentissant des négociateurs à conclure un accord mondial dimanche. De l’Afrique à l’Europe, les représentants des pays ont exprimé leur méfiance face à un processus qui a permis aux pays riches en pétrole de passer outre les appels à inclure dans le texte final une mention sur la sortie progressive des énergies fossiles — une mesure que les scientifiques réclament depuis des années.

Les divisions se sont avérées si profondes lors des pourparlers à Antalya, en Turquie, que les gouvernements n’ont pas pu conclure d’accord de haut niveau pour la première fois depuis 2009. Cela a conduit les ministres, les négociateurs et d’autres responsables à réclamer des changements dans un processus qui, depuis des décennies, nécessite un consensus entre près de 200 pays pour avancer.

“Si nous parvenons à donner le meilleur de nous-mêmes, à nous organiser, au cours des douze prochains mois, la COP31 nous paraîtra rétrospectivement comme un moment cathartique de prise de conscience”, a positivé Rachel Kyte, envoyée spéciale du Royaume-Uni pour le climat, lors d’un entretien accordé à POLITICO, ajoutant que les pays devaient corriger le processus qui, ces dernières années, a peiné à produire des résultats.

Ceux appelant à une refonte du processus réclament une réforme du format COP, voire sa suppression pure et simple, sans que l’on ait réellement d’idées sur la manière de mettre en œuvre l’une ou l’autre de ces options. Reste que l’échec des organisateurs à négocier un accord final a libéré un flot de critiques.

Selon ses détracteurs, le processus actuel, dans lequel les pays pétroliers font obstacle aux initiatives visant à mentionner explicitement les énergies fossiles, n’est plus viable dans un monde qui se dirige à toute vitesse vers une aggravation des conditions climatiques.

“Nous avons tous été pris en otage par les producteurs de pétrole, mais aussi par les plus grands consommateurs de pétrole”, a pointé auprès de POLITICO le ministre panaméen du Climat, Juan Carlos Navarro.

La faute aux producteurs d’énergies fossiles, mais pas que

Ces négociations chaotiques en Turquie interviennent onze ans après que, pour la première fois, tous les pays se sont mis d’accord sur la nécessité de lutter contre le changement climatique en signant l’Accord de Paris. Depuis, des progrès poussifs ont laissé les pays à la traîne par rapport à leurs objectifs. Au point que l’ONU a annoncé le mois dernier qu’il n’y avait plus aucun espoir d’éviter un réchauffement de 1,5 °C.

L’échec de ce week-end contraste fortement avec les négociations de l’année dernière au Brésil, où les gouvernements étaient parvenus à un accord malgré les attaques à distance contre le processus du président Donald Trump, et sa décision de retirer les Etats-Unis de l’Accord de Paris.

Alors que les négociations entraient en prolongation le week-end dernier, l’Arabie saoudite et un groupe d’autres pays producteurs d’énergies fossiles se sont battus pour empêcher que les négociations ne reprennent les termes convenus il y a trois ans lors de la COP28, qui appelaient à accélérer la sortie des énergies fossiles.

“Ce que nous voyons ne doit pas devenir la norme”, insistait le 18 novembre Jiwoh Abdulai, ministre de l’Environnement et du Climat de la Sierra Leone, avant l’échec des négociations. “Il y a un manque de confiance. Je pense que l’essentiel est de trouver un mécanisme permettant de rétablir la confiance.”

Certains responsables estiment que les politiques climatiques peuvent être menées par d’autres moyens, par exemple via des accords commerciaux et des partenariats d’approvisionnement en minerais. Une grande partie de ce travail est déjà en cours, consolidant des changements concrets dans l’économie mondiale et dans la lutte contre les gaz à effet de serre.

“Les COP, c’est une blague et ce depuis des années. Elles devraient être supprimées”, a tancé mardi sur X Rohan Patel, ancien conseiller à la Maison-Blanche en matière de politique climatique et énergétique sous Barack Obama. “Au mieux, cette conférence apporte un élan moral à un problème qui ne cesse de s’aggraver et auquel nous avons tardé à nous attaquer à bien des égards. Mais en général, c’est un énorme fiasco et tout le monde le sait bien (même ceux qui y participent chaque année).”

D’autres pays ont joué un rôle dans cet échec. Les gouvernements des pays riches ont refusé d’accorder des financements aux pays pauvres pour leur permettre de s’adapter au réchauffement climatique. De grandes puissances comme la Chine sont restées en retrait. Plusieurs diplomates ont déploré en privé l’absence des négociateurs américains, qui, historiquement, ont toujours fait pression sur les récalcitrants pour qu’ils fassent des compromis.

Des participants de longue date ont estimé que les négociations se sont trop concentrées sur l’élaboration de déclarations de haut niveau, au détriment de progrès concrets pour réduire les émissions de gaz à effet de serre. D’autres ont suggéré que l’échec du week-end dernier pourrait servir à revoir le processus et à le rendre plus efficace dans un monde fragmenté.

“Je reçois des appels de partout, me disant : ‘C’est une occasion à ne pas manquer, il faut la saisir’”, a confié Rachel Kyte, l’envoyée britannique. “Donc, tout bien considéré, ça a été une décision difficile [de rejeter l’accord], mais je pense que c’était la bonne.”

Des progrès passés inaperçus

Par ailleurs, de nombreux diplomates soulignent avoir constaté des progrès discrets à Antalya, mais ils ont été éclipsés par les dernières heures catastrophiques des négociations.

L’Allemagne, la France et les Pays-Bas ont publié des feuilles de route détaillées pour abandonner le pétrole, le charbon et le gaz. Le fait que 130 pays, dont l’Union européenne, se soient opposés au texte après le retrait de la mention sur la sortie des énergies fossiles a mis en évidence une large coopération, ont soulevé certains. Plus de 80 pays ont signé un engagement lors de la COP31 visant à électrifier 35% de leur consommation finale d’énergie d’ici 2035, bien que celui-ci n’ait jamais été adopté en raison de l’échec des négociations.

En outre, les particuliers achètent de plus en plus de véhicules électriques et les pays développent rapidement leurs capacités de production d’énergies renouvelables. Cette tendance va se poursuivre, a affirmé la semaine dernière l’Agence internationale de l’énergie. Toutefois, celle-ci a également souligné que la demande d’énergie croît, ce qui signifie que la consommation de pétrole, de gaz et de charbon se poursuivra pendant des décennies.

“Le sujet, ce n’est pas des feuilles de papier. C’est décarboner réellement l’économie mondiale”, a résumé dans son podcast Christiana Figueres, qui a dirigé les négociations de l’Accord de Paris en 2015.

Chris Bowen, le ministre australien du Changement climatique et de l’Energie, qui a coprésidé la COP31 avec la Turquie, a jugé que les négociations de cette année s’étaient déroulées dans un climat particulièrement tendu. La sécurité énergétique constituait une préoccupation majeure, étant donné l’angoisse des populations face aux pénuries d’approvisionnement en carburant et à la flambée des prix due à la fermeture du détroit d’Ormuz. Les guerres au Moyen-Orient et en Europe ont encore davantage mis à rude épreuve la coopération internationale.

Les pays économiquement dépendants des énergies fossiles, comme l’Arabie saoudite et la Russie, ont adopté des positions intransigeantes face au désordre mondial. L’Union européenne, le Royaume-Uni et des dizaines d’autres pays ont considéré qu’il valait mieux rejeter un mauvais accord plutôt que de faire marche arrière.

“Il est profondément décevant qu’aucun consensus n’ait été trouvé lors de la COP31. Ce moment, après l’été que le monde vient de vivre, appelait à faire preuve d’ambition. Au lieu de cela, on nous a présenté un accord qui constitue un recul en matière de climat, et nous ne pouvions pas le soutenir”, a justifié lundi le Premier ministre britannique Andy Burnham devant la Chambre des communes.

Les négociations annuelles constituaient autrefois le mécanisme permettant de parvenir à un accord international sur les moyens de lutter contre le changement climatique. Aujourd’hui, il vaut mieux les utiliser comme une tribune pour faire pression sur les pays afin qu’ils agissent plus rapidement pour réduire leurs émissions, considère Alden Meyer, du think tank E3G.

“Je dirais que la coopération pour mener des initiatives de décarbonation sur le terrain dans tous les secteurs de l’économie revêt une importance bien plus grande que l’existence ou non d’un consensus sur une décision-cadre qui se limite au plus petit dénominateur commun”, a-t-il écrit dans un SMS.

Cet article a d’abord été publié par POLITICO en anglais, puis a été édité en français par Marie Thirion et Jean-Christophe Catalon.

articles.title: Don’t ‘backslide’ on defense spending, senior US lawmaker tells Europe
articles.summary:
A senior U.S. lawmaker has urged the European Union not to cut defense spending in its next seven-year budget as Europe’s leaders struggle to agree on the almost €2 trillion pot of cash.

Brendan Boyle, a Democratic member of the U.S. House of Representatives who will chair its Budget Committee in 2027, warned that Russia was an “enormous threat” to Europe and said the bloc must continue increasing its defense spending.

“This is not a time when we can backslide,” Boyle told POLITICO in an interview, pointing to the approaching five-year anniversary of Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine. Earlier this week, Boyle was also elected president of NATO’s parliamentary assembly, which is made up of delegates from the alliance’s 32 member countries.

His comments come as EU leaders prepare to discuss the bloc’s next seven-year budget at a summit Thursday and Friday. The latest draft defense budget tabled by European Council President António Costa would see tens of billions cut from the European Commission’s earlier proposal, drawing the ire of some EU countries — though the total is still double the previous seven-year budget.

Boyle said he was “heartened” that all NATO allies were now spending more on defense than the alliance’s longstanding 2% of GDP target agreed at the 2014 Wales summit. “I’m glad that that is a floor and no longer considered a ceiling,” he said, while acknowledging that European governments face “similar budget constraints” to the U.S.

He said Europe building up its own defense industry after decades of relying on American weapons was a net positive for the NATO alliance, but warned against the bloc breaking that dependence too fast. EU countries are currently only spending about 15% of their defense procurement budgets on European-made equipment, despite calls from the Commission to raise this to at least half by 2030.

“Where it would become a negative is if suddenly there was a hard turn away from totally buying U.S. systems,” Boyle said. “That would be a mistake.”

articles.title: French presidential hopeful Teddy Riner says Ukraine is ‘not our war’
articles.summary:
PARIS — Teddy Riner, the legendary judoka running for president in France, sparked controversy on Wednesday after declaring that Ukraine was not his country’s conflict.

“I don’t understand why we’re sending troops to Ukraine when it’s not our war,” the five-time Olympic gold medalist told reporters.

Riner was referring to the deployment of French troops in Ukraine, which was criticized by opposition parties for having been decided without parliamentary approval. Deputy Defense Minister Alice Rufo said the troops are “dedicated to training and equipment maintenance.”

“If I become president tomorrow, I would like to be the kind of person who brings people together, who smiles and shakes hands to put an end to this war,” Riner added about Russia’s war in Ukraine.

Russian leader Vladimir Putin also practices judo and was honorary president of the International Judo Federation before launching the full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.

The 37-year-old Riner has unveiled few policy proposals and had not yet weighed in on foreign affairs since announcing his candidacy earlier this month. The two leading candidates for next April’s election in France — far-right chief Marine Le Pen and far-left veteran Jean-Luc Mélenchon — have both been critical of current President Emmanuel Macron’s Ukraine policy. Macron’s government has sent funds and weapons to Ukraine and co-led the coalition of the willing, a group of Kyiv’s most significant allies and supporters.

Riner, however, had been more closely associated with the pro-Macron camp based on early campaign statements, making his Ukraine comments more surprising. Early surveys have shown him polling at about 4%, drawing mostly from voters who opted for Macron in the last presidential election.

Center-right MEP Nathalie Loiseau, who handles foreign affairs policy for presidential candidate Edouard Philippe, seized on Riner’s remarks to attack the election rival.

“Teddy Riner’s world would be so simple: you don’t get involved in anything, you shake hands with everyone, and there’s peace and love all over the world,” she wrote on X.

Riner was speaking from the French mayors’ congress currently taking place in Paris, where he was seeking out endorsements needed to run for president.

He still has a long way to go before actually getting onto the ballot: Riner said he had obtained more than 100 signatures from local officials in support his candidacy — far from the 500 needed to confirm his candidacy under French law.

articles.title: Macron threatens to stop negotiating EU budget after December
articles.summary:
PARIS — French President Emmanuel Macron is threatening to abandon negotiations on the EU’s multiannual budget if countries fail to reach an agreement by the end of the year.

“It is clear for the President that it is not possible to continue these negotiations beyond December” if leaders fail to find an agreement at the European Council on Dec. 17-18, an official from Macron’s office told reporters on Wednesday.

The warning increases the pressure on European Council President António Costa, who chairs the talks, and on other EU countries ahead of an extraordinary summit in Brussels on Thursday and Friday.

Macron is leaving office in spring next year because he cannot constitutionally run for a third consecutive term. He has already told fellow leaders that he would not be in a position to continue negotiating the bloc’s 2028-2034 budget in the new year.

Marine Le Pen, the far-right candidate leading the polls for the 2027 presidential election, has repeatedly accused EU institutions and the French president of deliberately speeding up budget negotiations to leave her out of the process. She pledged to drastically cut France’s contribution to the EU budget and transform the European Commission into a “secretariat” of member countries, if she is elected.

Macron’s office openly criticized Costa’s proposal  to shave another €44 billion off the EU’s planned seven-year budget, even if it shields some of France’s favoured spending items like subsidies to farmers from cuts. Macron had lunch with Costa on Tuesday in Paris.

On Wednesday afternoon, Macron hosted representatives of the country’s top farmers’ organizations at the Elysée. He promised them that “the CAP will be the number one subject and the number one goal for France” at this week’s European Council meeting.

The Elysée official quoted above, who in line with the French government’s communications practices was not named, predicted that the EUCO meeting would not be conclusive and stressed that Costa’s proposal was not addressing French demands, including on raising more own resources levied by the EU directly to finance the budget.

In addition to the cuts, Macron’s office warned that Costa’s proposal offers little certainty that new-EU wide taxes would see the light any time soon, as they would have to be adopted in a separate vote after budget negotiations. While France backs the new digital levy proposed by Costa and the European Commission, it warned that it would be hard to convince all EU countries to get on board.

articles.title: EU weist Trumps Argumente für neue Zölle zurück
articles.summary:
BRÜSSEL — Die EU-Kommission hat die Begründung der US-Regierung für neue Zölle auf Waren aus Europa zurückgewiesen. Die US-Regierung war in einer Untersuchung zu dem Schluss gekommen, Europas Industrie trage zu weltweiten Überkapazitäten bei und drücke damit künstlich die Preise. Washington will deshalb einen neuen, wenn auch nicht zwingend zusätzlichen Zoll von 15 Prozent auf EU-Importe verhängen.

„Wir werden die Ergebnisse prüfen. Gleichzeitig weisen wir die These, dass Europa eine Quelle struktureller Überkapazitäten sei, entschieden zurück. Im Gegenteil: Europa gehört zu den Regionen, die am stärksten von Überkapazitäten betroffen sind“, erklärte Kommissionssprecher Olof Gill am Mittwoch.

„Die EU und die USA teilen die echte Sorge über globale Überkapazitäten, die größtenteils staatlich gefördert werden und sich auf Drittländer konzentrieren. Wir bedauern das Fehlen gemeinsamer Maßnahmen“, fügte er hinzu.

Das Büro des US-Handelsbeauftragten unter der Leitung von Jamieson Greer hatte festgestellt, dass 14 Handelspartner, darunter die EU, China und Japan, Preise künstlich gedrückt hatten, indem sie die Märkte mit Industriegütern überschwemmten. Die Entscheidung folgte auf eine im März eingeleitete Untersuchung nach Abschnitt 301 des US-Handelsgesetzes von 1974

Greer schlug einen Zollsatz von 15 Prozent für die EU vor. Er entspricht der Obergrenze, die im Juli 2025 im EU-US-Handelsabkommen von Turnberry vereinbart wurde.

Greer wird voraussichtlich am Montag per Video an einem Treffen der europäischen Handelsminister teilnehmen. Die EU-Minister dürften dabei mangelnde Fortschritte bei der Senkung der Zölle auf EU-Produkte mit Stahlanteilen zur Sprache bringen. Für einige davon gelten nach wie vor US-Zölle bis zu 50 Prozent.

Die Untersuchung gemäß Abschnitt 301 die zweite abgeschlossene Handelsuntersuchung der USA gegen die EU seit dem Frühjahr. Die US-Regierung hatte bereits einen Zollsatz von 10 Prozent gegen die EU verhängt, weil die EU die Einfuhr von Waren nicht verbiete, die unter Einsatz von Zwangsarbeit hergestellt wurden. Es werde aber nur der höhere der beiden Zollsätze gelten, anstatt dass beide addiert würden, erklärte ein hochrangiger US-Beamter. Außerdem werde die Turnberry-Grenze von 15 Prozent eingehalten.

Der Vorsitzende des Handelsausschusses des Europäischen Parlaments, Bernd Lange, bezeichnete die Schlussfolgerungen des USTR-Berichts als „absurd“.

„Wer nach den Zwischenwahlen ruhigere Zeiten erwartet hatte, hat sich getäuscht. Das hatte ohnehin kaum jemand ernsthaft erwartet“, erklärte Lange. Bei der Wahl vom 3. November hatten die Demokraten im Senat und im Repräsentantenhaus deutliche Mehrheiten errungen.

„Weder das Urteil des Obersten Gerichtshofs noch das Votum der Wähler haben Donald Trump vom Kurs abgebracht. Wenn ein Gericht die Rechtsgrundlage für seine Zölle aufhebt, sucht er sich eine neue. Sein Ziel bleibt dasselbe. Er nutzt Zölle, um Druck auf seine Handelspartner auszuüben und ihnen immer mehr Zugeständnisse abzuringen“, so Lange.

Der Artikel erschien bei POLITICO zuerst auf Englisch.

articles.title: UK will not offer equal tuition fees for EU students, says Burnham
articles.summary:
LONDON — Andy Burnham on Wednesday appeared to rule out students from the European Union being allowed to pay the equivalent of “home fees” while studying at British universities.

During Prime Minister’s Questions, the Labour Party leader suggested equal fees “won’t be put on the table” in negotiations when pushed by leader of the opposition Kemi Badenoch to rule such an agreement out. EU students are currently charged considerably more than domestic students.

In the House of Commons, Burnham told MPs the European negotiating position “is not the British negotiating position, this has not been put on the table.”

The issue of tuition fees has become politically fraught since Friday, when contradictory briefings from London and Brussels left it unclear if the agreements reached at the U.K.-EU summit on food, emissions and youth mobility were contingent on a deal for students.

Burnham insisted that the university deal was not linked to the other agreements. “The deal on tuition fees is not done,” he said. “It’s on a separate piece of paper, a separate deal.”

Under the current scheme, EU students pay international fees — which can sometimes be £20,000 higher than the rate British students pay.

Last week, two EU diplomats, granted anonymity to discuss the plans, told POLITICO London had so far offered fees of £12,000.

In a joint statement released Friday, EU and U.K. leaders said they would “work towards” an agreement on tuition fees. “We will conclude the negotiations within six months from the date of the summit,” they added.

Universities have warned that giving EU students a better deal on fees could impact the financial health of higher education institutions — many of which are already facing a cash crisis.

A statement from the Russell Group — which includes some of the U.K’s top universities — said that any reduction in EU student fees “would put pressure on U.K. student places and take more money out of U.K. higher education, without necessarily achieving the ambition of growing opportunities for EU students to study in the U.K.”

A No.10 spokesperson would not say on Wednesday whether implementation dates for the other agreements would be met without striking a deal on tuition fees.

“We’re moving quickly to ensure the benefits of these deals as soon as possible,” they said.

A spokesperson had said Monday that they were “confident” implementation dates would not change “even if we don’t reach an agreement on the tuition fees issue within six months.”

articles.title: EU rejects Trump’s case for new tariffs
articles.summary:
BRUSSELS — The European Commission on Wednesday rejected Washington’s claim that Europe is fueling global industrial overcapacity, after the Trump administration proposed a 15% tariff on the 27-country bloc.

“We will study the findings. At the same time we strongly reject the premise that Europe is a source of structural overcapacity. To the contrary, Europe is among those most exposed to overcapacity,” Olof Gill, the Commission’s deputy chief spokesperson, said in a statement. 

“The EU and the U.S. share a real concern about global overcapacity, much of it state-driven and concentrated in third countries. We regret the lack of joint action,” he added. 

The Office of the U.S. Trade Representative, led by Jamieson Greer, found that 14 trading partners, including the European Union, China and Japan, had artificially deflated prices by flooding markets with manufactured goods. The decision follows a trade investigation launched in March.

Greer on Wednesday proposed a 15% tariff on the European Union, in line with the ceiling agreed in the transatlantic trade truce struck in July 2025 between U.S. President Donald Trump and European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen.

Greer, who is expected to dial in next Monday to a meeting of European trade ministers, can expect pushback on the excess capacity probe. EU ministers are also expected to bring up the lack of progress on lowering tariffs on EU products containing steel — some of which still face U.S. duties of as high as 50%.

The overcapacity investigation, launched under Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974, is the second of two trade probes initiated in the spring as part of the Trump administration’s mission to rebuild its tariff wall. 

After the “reciprocal” duties Trump imposed in 2025 were invalidated earlier this year by the U.S. Supreme Court, the administration imposed a 10% tariff on the European Union, citing concerns that Brussels had failed to ban the import of goods made using forced labor. The higher of the two tariff rates will apply, rather than the two being added together, a senior U.S. official said. 

The official added that the proposed duties would likely take effect in January at the earliest, after USTR holds hearings and receives public comments.

The chair of the European Parliament’s trade committee, Bernd Lange, lambasted the conclusions of the USTR report as “absurd.”

“Anyone who expected calmer waters after the midterm elections was mistaken. Few seriously expected that in the first place,” Lange said in a statement, referring to a Nov. 3 vote that returned firm majorities for the Democrats in the Senate and the House of Representatives.

“Neither the Supreme Court ruling nor the verdict of the voters has swayed Donald Trump. When a court strikes down the legal basis for his tariffs, he looks for another. His aim remains the same. He uses tariffs to put pressure on trading partners and wring ever more concessions out of them.”

articles.title: Metsola reelection talks in trouble after EU conservatives vote with far right again
articles.summary:
STRASBOURG — Negotiations between EU Parliament’s three main centrist parties that were intended to pave the way for the reelection of President Roberta Metsola are on hold after the European People’s Party again teamed up with far-right forces on green legislation.

The Socialists & Democrats and Renew have been working for two weeks to lock the EPP into a coalition agreement, after the center-right party repeatedly voted through key migration and climate legislation with the far right over the past two years.

The deal is also meant to break the deadlock between the EPP, which wants Metsola to have a third term, and the S&D, which insists it’s their turn to have the top Parliament job. Such a deal would give the Socialists written political commitments in exchange for backing Metsola’s reelection.

Wednesday’s move to freeze talks, confirmed by Renew chair Valérie Hayer’s spokesperson, is unlikely to derail talks for long, as the three groups need to work together to pass laws proposed by Ursula von der Leyen’s Commission and agreed among EU countries. A final deal was expected in two weeks following a meeting between the leaders of the three groups that took place on Tuesday, according two people familiar with the negotiations, granted anonymity to speak freely, as were others in this piece.

Before continuing work on four thematic coalition clusters discussing specific policy files, the S&D and Renew are asking the EPP to commit to adding “strong safeguards in the agreement to prevent, once and for all, this kind of behavior” before returning to the negotiating table, said a third person familiar with the negotiations. A fourth person said the EPP must commit to adding “strong” wording in the agreement committing to a centrist coalition before full talks resume.

But the EPP is unlikely to budge — as it didn’t on the package on environmental requirements for businesses on Wednesday, when it voted with the far right. “There is no exclusivity” on working with the EPP, its leader, Manfred Weber, said at a press conference on Tuesday. 

Environmental deal collapses

After reaching a centrist agreement on the green laws following weeks of talks, the deal fell apart when the EPP decided to support an amendment put forward by the right-wing European Conservatives & Reformists, which called on the Commission to reopen the bloc’s laws protecting wildlife and natural parks. The Socialists said they could not accept this amendment.

It was Weber himself who pushed the EPP to back the amendment despite the Socialists’ opposition, arguing that reopening the laws was part of the conservatives’ political program and warning against falling into the left’s “traps,” according to an internal note from a group meeting on Monday. That was despite Radan Kanev, the EPP’s lead negotiator on the file, urging lawmakers at the same meeting to abstain to preserve the deal with the S&D and Renew.

Weber is walking a tightrope between keeping the EPP anchored in the center while appeasing those internally itching to move further right to deliver on the party’s program. In October, he pushed through a centrist deal on a car package, even though negotiators were ready to team up with the right to weaken carmakers’ CO2 targets further, two EPP officials said.

Spokespeople for Weber and S&D group leader Iratxe García declined to comment.

articles.title: Seabird ‘spies’ could help spot ships that aren’t broadcasting their location
articles.summary:
A northern gannet (Morus bassanus) tagged with biologging devices on its back and tail

Steve Votier

Audio from seabirds fitted with mini recording devices and GPS trackers has been used by researchers to show that marine life can record encounters with vessels that are otherwise difficult to track.

Many large vessels are now legally required to carry automatic identification systems broadcasting their identity and location at regular intervals. Although this has allowed interactions between animals and fisheries to be studied at scale, there are enormous gaps in coverage.

In fact, recent research suggests that three-quarters of industrial fishing vessels don’t use the technology, says Jonathan Rutter at the University of Oxford. This is partly because regulations on the types of vessels that are required to share data vary by country. Large satellite ‘blind spots’ also contribute to the problem, he says, and so does subterfuge for the purpose of illegal, unreported and unregulated fishing (IUU).

Advertisement

Read more

Most large fishing boats go untracked as ‘dark vessels’

Rutter says that being caught as bycatch in fishing is one of the greatest risks to seabird populations, but if fishing vessels are only tracked “with conventional methods, such footprints of risk may be strikingly incomplete”.

The team analysed audio collected from devices attached to seven northern gannets (Morus bassanus) and found that one third of the audio detections couldn’t be matched with vessel tracking data – mostly off the UK coast.

Overall, 12 per cent of the vessel detections made by the four critically endangered Balearic shearwaters (Puffinus mauretanicus) included in the study couldn’t be matched to public data. But given the high vessel density where they were – off the Catalan coast – the researchers estimated that up to 20 per cent of the vessels detected by the four birds weren’t broadcasting their identity.

Tammy Davies at BirdLife International – a global partnership of non-governmental organisations – who wasn’t involved in the study, says the research could “give us a more complete picture of the risks seabirds face at sea” and “ultimately, this could contribute to better assessments of bycatch risk and help identify fisheries and areas where conservation measures are most needed”.

Peter Ejbye-Ernst at the Netherlands Institute for the Study of Crime and Law Enforcement (NSCR), describes the study as “fascinating” from a green criminology point of view, too.

A tagged northern gannet coming in to land in Wales

Steve Votier

“What this study is somewhat proposing is that we can also look outside of humans for witnesses too,” he says, which overcomes a key barrier in observing crime at sea.

In terms of its applications for cracking down on IUU, he says: “There’s a fine line between trying to understand something better and document it and then trying to control it and surveil it.”

There are caveats, as the study has a small sample size and records both false-negatives and false-positives. It also gives very little information on the type of activity vessels were carrying out. But, while the research isn’t a solution to the problem of IUU, it is “part of the toolbox” for understanding what is happening at sea, says Ejbye-Ernst.

The study didn’t differentiate between the size of vessels, but Rutter and his colleagues say this would be a good area for future research.

Powerful images show dark side of South-East Asia’s fishing industry

Photographer Nicole Tung captures the tough world facing South-East Asia’s fishers and their families in this series of images, which won her the Carmignac Photojournalism Award for fieldwork

“Animal-borne audio recorders could potentially be used to investigate other ecological interactions and human activities that are difficult to observe directly, particularly in the marine environment,” says team member Ana Bertoldi Carneiro, also at BirdLife International.

Hugo Tagholm at the charity Oceana says it is shocking that so many of the interactions were with unseen vessels, but he is concerned about attaching devices to seabirds on a broader scale to track this.

“Seabirds are already grappling with the harm caused by overfishing and climate breakdown, we don’t want to put them at even greater risk from vessel operators acting illegally,” he says.

“What we need is mandatory remote electronic monitoring across all fishing vessels, clear and effective laws and catch limits to protect and restore our seas, and truly deterrent sanctions for those breaking the law.”

articles.title: AI’s stunning progress in maths shows how little we understand it
articles.summary:
MARK SYKES/SPL/Alamy

There is a story, possibly apocryphal, that when the mathematician G. H. Hardy was about to undertake a dangerous sea voyage, he sent a postcard to a colleague declaring “I have solved the Riemann hypothesis”. Hardy, a staunch atheist, joked that this would prevent his ship from sinking, as God would never let him claim the credit for such a major result without revealing the details of his proof.

Hardy would probably be both astonished and aghast that we now have what seems to be a proof of the Riemann hypothesis, a problem that has vexed mathematicians since the 19th century, but that no one yet understands it. The consensus among mathematicians is that the proof, produced with the aid of AI, will hold, but that it will take much more work to make it comprehensible to humans.

However you feel about AI, this is a watershed moment, and one that demonstrates just how little we still understand about the capabilities of the technology. As recently as last month, leading mathematician Terence Tao speculated that AI would eventually solve the Riemann hypothesis, but that it may not happen before 2050. Now, some mathematicians are considering whether their hardest and most infamous remaining problems could be settled within months. In a year that has left mathematicians reeling, this may be the knock-out blow.

Advertisement

This is a watershed moment, and it shows just how little we understand about AI’s abilities

For non-mathematicians, the fall of the Riemann hypothesis is harder to interpret. In the past year, AI has seen incredible advances in both maths and coding, but it is perhaps no coincidence that in these arenas, with nothing more than computer code, answers can swiftly be checked and iterated upon, allowing for rapid improvement. When it comes to other human endeavours though, from art to zoology, such verification is far harder, involving either the messy physical world, or unknowable human taste – or both. Whether this verification gap can be closed may become the biggest question of our age. Answers on a postcard, please.

What is the Riemann hypothesis and why is its solution so monumental?

It has been called the hardest problem in mathematics, and now through a combination of human ingenuity and relentlessness, and the computational power of AI, the Riemann hypothesis may have finally been solved

articles.title: Our verdict on Dark Eden by Chris Beckett: ‘Holy cow. Chapter 44!’
articles.summary:
The New Scientist Book Club read Chris Beckett’s Dark Eden in November

Since starting the New Scientist Book Club in May 2023, I have aimed to vary our books as much as possible, moving between science fiction and popular science, older classics and the hottest new titles. Occasionally, though, I’m afraid I let the power go to my head and just choose one of my own personal favourites. That’s what I did in November, with Chris Beckett’s novel Dark Eden, a book I’ve loved ever since it won the Arthur C. Clarke award in 2013.

Set on the planet Eden, a sunless world that drifts alone far outside the Milky Way, this follows the descendants of two astronauts who were marooned there over a century earlier. Now numbering 532 people, they tell each other stories of the world their ancestors came from, and struggle to survive on this dark, cold planet as they await the return of “one of those sky-boats with lights on them”. I think it is all wildly imaginative and original and exciting. So it was with some trepidation that I awaited the verdict of my fellow book club members on our Discord channel. I really wanted everyone else to love it, too!

Free newsletter

Sign up to Book Club

Sign up to newsletter

It started well. “I managed not to stay up all night reading, but the temptation was definitely there – I am hooked,” wrote Dee55. Les was similarly gripped. “Started it? I’ve only gone and finished it, haven’t I? It really got me in, and I found it a fascinating exploration of social anthropology and linguistics in a very small, isolated population. And the world-building was fascinating, too – very different flora and fauna.”

Advertisement

Several other members also cited the strength of the world-building in Dark Eden. I also love the lanternflowers and woollybucks of this planet, and was fascinated to learn, in an essay Chris wrote for book club members, that, when creating a world for a story, he doesn’t “usually seek to make the whole thing scientifically accurate, but I try to make it hang together in a way that feels coherent”. I think he definitely succeeds in that here.

In Dark Eden, I imagined how life might exist on a sunless planet

Dark Eden, the November read for the New Scientist Book Club, takes place on a rogue planet outside the Milky Way. Award-winning author Chris Beckett explains how he thought through the science behind this night world

There were some excellent debates about the language these people have developed – they double up on words for emphasis, for example (“big big”; “cold cold”), use bastardised forms of our words (“Landing Veekle”; “leckytrickity”), and talk about Starry Swirl – the Milky Way they can see in their skies, a wonderfully evocative image.

“I think Beckett has done something really clever here. He’s created a language that feels familiar enough to read naturally, but is sufficiently different to remind us that this is an entirely separate culture that has evolved in isolation,” wrote Maria. “I enjoyed some of the language. Tom’s dick and Harry’s for instance,” wrote Matthew – referring to an exclamation the characters use for emphasis. “It’s contagious… yesterday I found myself saying Wow, it’s hot hot!” added leasabp. Dee55 also admitted to adopting some Edenisms: “My favourite bit of the language is ‘newhairs’! I am already using this for teenagers, but only to myself at present.”

The story’s protagonist is John Redlantern, a young man who decides there must be more to life than waiting for rescue around the Circle of Stones that marks the original astronauts’ landing point on Eden, and tries to spark an exodus from the Family’s small valley to explore the wider planet. John definitely drew some mixed opinions from readers.

“Problem is, I don’t much like our ‘hero’, he’s not a very sympathetic character, more Sméagol than Bilbo,” wrote Matthew. I chatted to Chris in an interview for book club members, and he was certainly aware of this: “He’s an awkward cuss, John, isn’t he? He’s not a particularly nice person,” he told me – before embarking on an enlightening discussion about why he chose to write from various viewpoints, and how hard it was describing the world of Eden from the perspectives of people who have never been anywhere else. “The discipline of just writing it from within the story is if I’m trying to describe the world to readers, I can’t use metaphors and analogies that refer to anything that’s outside of Eden. And that was quite tricky to do.”

Book club member Laura Akers, like others, said she “definitely enjoyed the story more when I realized that John, despite his own intentions, is not intended to be our ‘hero’”.

Overall, I think the book club mostly really enjoyed Dark Eden – I particularly appreciated leasapb’s comment: “Holy cow. Chapter 44!!!”, as I think the ending is fabulous – but one issue that was raised by a few people was the amount the characters have sex with each other. Incestuous sex.

“Certainly one of the odd things I found was the casual attitude to sex,” wrote Alan_P. Maria agreed. “I found the casual attitude towards sex quite unsettling too, particularly because the characters often seem almost childlike in their behaviour and understanding of the world, yet discuss sex so matter-of-factly. I honestly couldn’t bring myself to think too much about the incest!” And while Barbara Howe “loved the worldbuilding, and the story of John’s breakaway family’s trek to find a better place”, she found the “constant and highly unerotic sex… offputting”.

But given that at least some members have gone on to read the sequels, I think this was largely a popular choice – and a welcome change from the Earthly dystopias which seem to be dominating the big new sci-fi novels out this autumn (I’m looking at you, Audrey Niffenegger and Emily St. John Mandel).
