articles.summary:
Josie Ford

Feedback is our weekly column of bizarre stories, implausible advertising claims, confusing instructions and more

Reader Jenny Ozanne writes to tell us of a horrific incident that befell her partner. He had bought Audrey Niffenegger’s novel The Time Traveler’s Wife as a CD audiobook, to listen to on long car journeys.

“After a while, he complained that the plot was completely impossible to follow,” writes Jenny. “It was only when I checked his player that I realized he had accidentally set the CD to ‘shuffle’. “

Advertisement

Jenny raises two points, which Feedback heartily endorses: “I’m still not sure what’s more impressive: the story’s ability to survive total chronological chaos, or the fact that he listened to three random chapters before suspecting anything was wrong.”

Feedback would suggest that The Time Traveler’s Wife might be the ideal novel to experience on shuffle, since the narrative is heavily non-linear. The main character hops uncontrollably back and forth through history. This led us to wonder: would any similarly chrono-displaced stories survive the experience of being played on shuffle, or even be improved by it?

We wondered, for instance, about David Mitchell’s Cloud Atlas. This has six stories set in different periods, including a future in which human clones are used as cheap labour, and a more distant future in which everything has gone a bit Mad Max. The stories are linked by characters in later timelines reading about the earlier ones, and by subtle coincidences. What would it be like on shuffle?

However, after careful reflection, we realised there is only one correct answer to this, and that is Shane Carruth’s 2004 film Primer, which tells the story of two tech bros who invent a time machine in their garage. At first, they use it to go back in time and make money on the stock exchange, only to become caught up in an escalating web of betrayal and deception as they endlessly rewrite their lives.

Primer is so overcomplicated, so mind-wreckingly confusing, that some poor soul once went so far as to draw a diagram trying to convey its timeline. Posted on Reddit by u/Clawz114, the diagram looks like a cross between a metro map and a flowchart of the inner workings of a chemical factory. It is therefore possible that playing the scenes in random order might actually cause the film to make more sense.

The scent of success

It’s that time of year when many of us are thinking, “Oh blimey, I need to buy everyone presents” and then having a meltdown when we can’t think of anything. The last refuge of the true gift scoundrel is, of course, the scented candle. This item might as well come with a note saying, “Sorry, I couldn’t think of anything”.

Readers looking to step up their scented candle game may wish to investigate JD + Kate Industries, which is run by a pair of humour writers with a sideline in themed scented candles. They have taken these tedious items to new and different places.

For instance, consider the Late Bronze Age Collapse scented candle, which “commemorates everyone’s favorite late 13th century [BC] widespread societal collapse”. Happily, it doesn’t smell of violence and decay, but rather of “burning cedar”, since “Lebanese cedar was a popular building material in the Late Bronze Age”.

Those with more contemporary tastes may wish to consider the AI scented candle, which has a little sculpture of a data centre on the top, “surrounded by a post-apocalyptic, bombed-out city”. What does it smell of, you ask? “Diesel generator exhaust fumes”.

Finally, those nostalgic for the headier days of space exploration might appreciate the Apollo 11 scented candle. Disappointingly, this doesn’t smell of moon dust, which, as we understand it, basically smells of burning because it reacts with oxygen on contact. Instead, its scent mimics “a certain powdered orange drink mix often associated with the space program, but that was not brought on Apollo 11. The astronauts brought a generic, grapefruit-flavored powdered drink mix instead, because they selfishly did not consider us and our desire to market candles.”

Feedback has no idea if these candles are any good, but we enjoyed JD + Kate’s website a lot.

By the letter

Let us foray once again into the wonderful world of scientific acronyms. First, two reader claims that, for reasons that will become obvious, we cannot verify.

Michael Berkson tells us: “As a solicitor my late wife was involved in development of insurance for doctors. The firm had to tell the client that they needed to choose a better name. Their original choice was Professional Indemnity Support Scheme.” Michael says the clients were open to replacing “scheme” with “service”, which helps not at all.

Likewise, Jim Taylor asserts that he was once confronted with a military programme intended to ensure that spare parts would always be available for key equipment. It was called the Contractor Repair Advanced Provisioning System.

Finally, a story we can confirm is true because we looked it up. Reader Geraldine Beare is an indexer, which is one of those jobs that we often forget about but would swiftly notice if it wasn’t done. “I am at present indexing a book on goats,” says Geraldine. Through this assignment she has learned the acronym “OMAGOD”, which she recommends saying “quickly, or perhaps in a vaguely Scottish accent”. It actually stands for ovine mouth and gum obscure disease.

Got a story for Feedback?

You can send stories to Feedback by email at feedback@newscientist.com. Please include your home address. This week’s and past Feedbacks can be seen on our website.

articles.title: Basic income trial in Peru aims to prove rainforest protection merits
articles.summary:
A basic income pilot scheme will pay communities in Peru to protect the rainforest there

Andrea Ramos/Cool Earth

A trial seeking to prove the environmental benefits of giving Indigenous populations living in rainforests unconditional cash payments will launch next year amid growing hopes that basic income payments could offer a fresh approach to rainforest protection.

The trial, which will last at least two years and potentially for four, will see almost 400 people living in the Peruvian Amazon receive cash payments equivalent to around £57 per person, per month. The hope is that by providing Indigenous people with income security, they will be less likely to sell or lease land to loggers, miners or agriculture industries that will deforest.

“We are trying to build autonomy into the communities,” says Caterina Cosmopolis at Cool Earth, a UK-based charity that will run the trial. “They can make their own decisions, they can find their own solutions.”

Advertisement

Read more

Ancient human settlements boosted biomass of today’s Amazon rainforest

The trial will build on a two-year pilot that Cool Earth launched in 2023 in which 211 people in three communities in Peru’s Junín province received cash transfers equivalent to £2 per day, to spend however they liked.

The cash payments were supplied alongside a programme of community-led training, covering financial education, climate change, environmental conservation and Indigenous rights.

In October, the University of Bath in the UK published the results of the pilot trial, reporting that the cash payments bolstered food security, improved community wellbeing and led to 90 per cent of participants adopting environmentally beneficial activities such as reforestation or reduced forest burning.

Free newsletter

Sign up to The Earth Edition

Sign up to newsletter

But the evidence for rainforest protection was limited by a lack of rigorous environmental monitoring or the use of control groups during the trial, making it difficult to draw firm conclusions about how effective the basic income was in preventing tropical forest degradation and deforestation.

The second trial is due to launch in March next year across three communities in the Huni Kuin territory of the Peruvian Amazon, where tropical land is under pressure from the expansion of ginger plantations and illegal gold mining. Alongside the community that will receive the cash income – 1040 Peruvian soles, or roughly £228 per person, every four months – there will be two control communities that will receive no payments.

“We are trying to gather more evidence about what the results of cash transfer will be like in different communities,” says Cosmopolis. “If we have the same results, we might be able to say this works – that conservation basic income can work.”

Read more

How Bolivia’s gold rush is poisoning Indigenous communities

The new trial will provide the same additional training on conservation issues, and will more closely monitor the environmental effects of basic income support, says Cosmopolis. She says the first trial saw a steep reduction in Indigenous communities cutting new areas of forest and renting land to loggers, but admits that “we didn’t see if there was more or less deforestation in the area” over the course of the trial. The next trial will feature “a more rigorous impact evaluation”, she says.

Natalie York at the University of Manchester, UK, says the social results of the first pilot seemed positive, but warns that tying environmental performance to cash payments is a delicate task.

“When you start to ask the trial to prove particular environmental outcomes, if the receipt of the payments becomes conditional on that, then it becomes more like a payment-for-ecosystem-services system, which is a very different conservation model,” she says.

Indigenous groups threatened by gold exploration in remote Amazon

Gold mining in the municipality of São Gabriel da Cachoeira would drive deforestation and increase mercury pollution, say ecologists

Meanwhile, Johan Oldekop, also at the University of Manchester, warns that environmental gains aren’t guaranteed, pointing out that while some rainforest cash payment trials have reduced deforestation rates, results aren’t always wholly positive.

In Peru, a scheme already provides direct payments to Indigenous communities in the Amazon on the condition that their forest remains standing. Research indicates that the scheme has had “negligible” environmental benefits on land covered by the conservation scheme, in part because communities often volunteered to protect areas at low risk of deforestation.

Oldekop also says that Indigenous rainforest communities are often financially precarious. He warns that short-lived interventions like temporary cash trials can be destabilising unless they are well designed. “We need really, really strong evidence that you’re not leading to social and environmental harms when you do interventions like this,” he says.

articles.title: Hannah Fry: The bizarre reason humans are so vulnerable to choking
articles.summary:
Fran Pulido

One of the unexpectedly delightful things about becoming a well-known nerd is that other nerds, often with far more interesting jobs than mine, have started hunting me down in social settings to tell me the nerdiest things they know.

It almost always ends up being totally fascinating, and only occasionally mildly traumatising.

At a kid’s birthday party recently, I got chatting to one of the dads, who happens to be an ear, nose and throat consultant. I asked him if he used robotics for his surgeries. He said no, then proceeded to mime what he actually did instead. There followed a series of alarmingly enthusiastic slashing motions, like a scene from a horror movie, while in the background a group of 9-year-old girls sat quietly painting.

Advertisement

Free newsletter

Sign up to Professor Hannah Fry’s column

Sign up to newsletter

But the most bizarre thing about that conversation wasn’t the surgeon’s graphic re-enactment, it was what he went on to say about the totally ridiculous, illogical design of the human throat and what it tells us about the path of evolution.

The story starts by noticing that the human body (if you ignore all the unimportant bits hanging off the sides like limbs) is essentially just one giant tube.

Topologically, this makes perfect sense. Back in the earliest days of animal life, some organisms tried a flat design, like a pancake, with digestion done on one side. Others tried a little pocket, with the same opening serving as entrance and exit. But the one-way tube proved to be the most successful, because it allowed our ancestors to process their last meal while eating their next.

Those early creatures would travel through the world mouth first, which is why the sensory equipment evolved to be gathered around that end, with a brain nearby to make sense of everything.

Hannah Fry: I lost my dad to Alzheimer’s. New research into its origins is amazing

My lovely father died of Alzheimer's last year, and since then, I've been digging into the disease to try to understand what happened to him. I was astonished to discover that scientists think it may start in the nose, says New Scientist's new columnist, Professor Hannah Fry

Now, picture a human standing up, tilting their head back, to make them a nice straight tube, still without limbs (sorry, but this is what happens when you let a mathematician write a science column). The ears, eyes, nose and brain all sit together in a cluster, on what I’m going to call the north side of the digestive tube running through the middle.

So if you were deciding where the lungs should go, you’d surely put them on the same side of the tube as the nose, tucked in next to the spine. That way, you would have a neat tube for air and another for food, both running side by side, and even a first-year engineering student could draw a diagram of it for you.

Except that’s not where the lungs are. They ended up on the belly, or south, side of the body.

Which leaves us with this topological monstrosity, where air that comes in through your nose has to cut straight across the path of your food to get to your lungs. And everything you eat has to cut straight back across the path of your air to get to your stomach.

It would be like plumbing your gas main through the kitchen sink, fitting a little flap on top and trusting you to remember to shut it every time you do the washing up.

The reason for this mess is a fish. More than 420 million years ago, long before anything with a backbone had crawled onto land, a fish started gulping air at the surface. A little pouch on the belly side of its gut, just underneath the mouth, got better and better at soaking up oxygen, and that pouch became a lung. That fish became the ancestor of every mammal, bird, amphibian and reptile on Earth.

And because evolution is about being as lazy as you can possibly be without dying, the lungs stayed exactly where they were.

The extraordinary ways species control their own evolutionary fate

Natural selection isn't just something that happens to organisms, their activities also play a role, giving some species – including humans – a supercharged ability to evolve

So why didn’t the nose move instead? Swivel it round so it sits under the mouth on your chin and you have a much more mathematically pleasing face. Unfortunately, the smell cells are wired straight into the front of the brain, so move the nose and the brain has to come along with it.

There’s just no wiggle room. One end of your airway was anchored by your sense of smell, the other was fixed by an accident over 420 million years ago, and your throat is the bodge job evolution came up with to make it all work.

Snakes have a tube behind their tongue that they can use like a snorkel so that they can still breathe even when swallowing a whole deer in one go. Toothed whales have two completely separate tubes that twirl into position like waterslides. Most mammals, including dogs and cats, have a voice box that sits right up at the top of the throat, poking up into the back of the nose, and tubes for food that flow round either side of the wind pipe to the stomach.

Read more

Why honing your sense of smell could keep you sharp as you age

Human babies start off that way too, which is why they can suckle and breathe at the same time. But in the first six months of life, the human larynx drops down the neck, unplugging the airway from the back of the nose and leaving it wide open to whatever comes in from the mouth.

What’s left is a very human oddity. A single, shared chamber sitting low down at the back of your throat that is great for speaking, but does require your vocal folds to slam shut, the epiglottis to come down like a trapdoor and your airway to be sealed off every time you swallow.

As a result, humans have the questionable honour of being one of the few animals on Earth for whom every single mouthful is a potentially lethal exercise in anatomical coordination. Other animals can choke, sure, but our strange anatomy makes us the most vulnerable to choking of all mammals. Which is how roughly 162,000 people die globally each year.

But evolution, having left us in this mess, did at least make the trapdoor almost impossible to switch off. The surgeon – mid mime – told me that when he is in people’s throats performing surgery, the EEG monitor reading can be measuring almost no brain activity. Still, any little tickle in the throat and those folds will slam shut.

As you can imagine, I spent the rest of the party watching the children eat their cake very, very carefully. None of them choked, which, given the state of the plumbing, is frankly a miracle.

articles.title: Severe eczema healed by novel immune-calming pill in clinical trial
articles.summary:
Eczema causes itchy, inflamed rashes on the skin

Evgeniia Gordeeva/Getty Images

Over a third of people with moderate to severe eczema taking part in a clinical trial have seen their skin completely or almost completely clear up after taking an experimental pill for four months. The drug targets a part of the immune system that causes eczema when it gets stuck in overdrive, and it may be preferable to the current standard treatment, which has to be injected.

“It definitely looks promising,” says Gayle Ross at the Royal Melbourne Hospital.

Read more

Chronic inflammation messes with your mind. Here’s how to calm it

Eczema, or atopic dermatitis, is a chronic skin condition characterised by itchy, inflamed rashes and broken skin that can become infected. It is driven by an overactive immune pathway involving two signalling proteins called interleukin-4 and interleukin-13.

Advertisement

In 2017, the companies Sanofi and Regeneron received approval in the US for their jointly developed eczema drug dupilumab, which blocks interleukin-4 and interleukin-13 signalling. But, although the medication is effective, it has had limited uptake in the US because it must be injected under the skin and costs up to $59,000 per year for those without insurance coverage.

Now, another company, Kymera Therapeutics, has developed an alternative treatment that can be taken in pill form, called KT-621. It targets the same immune pathway as dupilumab but degrades a protein called STAT6 that is activated downstream from interleukin-4 and interleukin-13 in the development of eczema.

Free newsletter

Sign up to Health Check

Sign up to newsletter

In the clinical trial, 244 adults with an average age of 39 and moderate to severe eczema were randomised to take KT-621 at three different doses or a placebo pill every day for 16 weeks.

Those taking the most effective dose experienced an average 72 per cent reduction in their eczema severity on a standard scale, compared to 27 per cent in the placebo group. What’s more, 38 per cent of participants taking KT-621 had completely healed skin or almost completely healed skin by the end of the trial.

“These results exceeded our expectations,” said Terence Rooney, the chief medical officer of Kymera Therapeutics, when announcing the results in a webcast on 23 November. He showed before-and-after photos of one man who had had severe eczema all over his torso at the beginning of the trial, which disappeared by the end.

“It’s obviously early days and the trial had relatively small patient numbers, but [KT-621] looks like it has similar efficacy to dupilumab, which is currently the standard of care for moderate to severe atopic dermatitis, and it would be nice to have an oral option as opposed to an injection,” says Ross.

Read more

You can upgrade your immune system, but not in the way you think

The medication also appeared safe. A small proportion of participants developed conjunctivitis as a side-effect, but it tended to be mild and didn’t cause anyone to discontinue treatment, said Rooney. In fact, since the trial, almost every participant has chosen to continue taking the daily pill as part of an ongoing study, he said.

People taking dupilumab can develop conjunctivitis too, so “we’re pretty used to dealing with that”, says Ross.

Kymera Therapeutics is now planning a larger trial of KT-621 for treating eczema that is scheduled to begin in mid-2027. The company is also currently running a trial of KT-621 in people with asthma, since the condition is caused by the same overactive immune pathway operating in the lungs. It hasn’t yet said how much the drug will cost if it eventually receives regulatory approval.

articles.title: COP31 collapse has shattered the pretence of a global climate consensus
articles.summary:
A closing plenary session at the COP31 climate summit on 22 November

AP Photo/Khalil Hamra/Alamy

A deep rift among nations on how to tackle climate change, and whether the global economy can be weaned off fossil fuels, was exposed after the spectacular collapse of talks at the COP31 climate summit in Antalya, Turkey.

After a tortuous fortnight of negotiations, COP31 ended in disarray late on 22 November after countries including the UK and the EU refused to agree to a political accord that failed to mention fossil fuels.

Read more

Can everyone live a ‘good life’ without destroying the planet?

The Antalya pact would have seen countries officially recognise that the world is on course to exceed 1.5°C degrees of warming and promise to limit the scale of the overshoot as far as possible. It also would have committed nations to increasing the share of electricity in total final energy consumption to 35 per cent globally by 2035, a key target for climate campaigners who see electrification as the route away from fossil-fuel dependency.

Advertisement

But the draft agreement proved unacceptable to many countries, including the UK, the EU and some small island nations, after all mentions of fossil fuels were omitted at the behest of fossil fuel-dependent nations such as Saudi Arabia and Russia.

Failing to mention fossil fuels explicitly in the text would have marked a backwards step for the climate process, the EU argued. At COP28 in Dubai three years ago, nations agreed to “transition away from fossil fuels”, but since then, attempts to strengthen the language or clarify how this transition will take place have been blocked by petrostates.

Alden Meyer at the climate think tank E3G says the talks were subjected to a “brutish” strategy from fossil fuel-exporting states to “systematically block” any reference to the COP28 deal. “They clearly have buyer’s remorse about that agreement. They never were happy about it.”

Free newsletter

Sign up to The Earth Edition

Sign up to newsletter

The EU also took issue with a paragraph inserted at the behest of Saudi Arabia – which leads the 22-member Arab group of countries – calling for the rapid growth of carbon capture and storage technologies to the gigatonne scale by 2035. Carbon capture and storage technologies are expensive and unproven at scale, and many sceptics are concerned that focusing on them will justify the continued use of fossil fuels and distract from the deep emissions cuts necessary for controlling climate change.

Ireland’s climate minister Darragh O’ Brien, speaking on behalf of the EU, claimed the negotiations had been “hijacked by fossil fuel producers” and said the EU would “not accept a COP that greenwashes fossil fuels”.

Parties also vented their frustration at the hosts, Turkey and Australia, with the joint presidency leading to a sluggish and disjointed negotiating process in the final days of the summit. There was also disquiet from lower-income nations over the lack of new climate finance commitments from richer countries.

Fossil fuel-dependent countries have long sought to delay, obstruct and divert climate talks from making a dent in the worldwide consumption of oil, gas and coal. It was oil-exporting countries that insisted all UN climate decisions should be made by consensus when the COP process was established in 1992, a decision that has hamstrung subsequent meetings by effectively awarding veto power to every nation. Other tactics include delaying talks by raising objections and points of order during meetings and flooding the official agenda with additional discussion areas.

Read more

The secret weapon that could finally force climate action

What was new at COP31 was seeing a group like the EU ditching a deal rather than finding a weak compromise in the name of progress, says Joanna Depledge at the University of Cambridge, a seasoned COP observer. “The usual political dynamics were completely upended,” she says of COP31’s endgame. “Usually the EU always backs down at the end. It doesn’t want to be seen as a blocker, but this time it played hardball.”

Many in the climate world are cheering the EU for standing its ground. Bill Hare, the CEO of the influential Climate Analytics think tank, said the deal was “clearly unacceptable”. “The lack of agreement on the main document here shouldn’t be seen as a failure of the COP process, but as a successful defence of the UNFCCC’s integrity against a coordinated attack by a few countries implacably opposed to action on climate change, in particular to any mention of the need to transition away from fossil fuels,” he said in a statement.

But the “no deal” outcome of COP31 is far from good news for those concerned about the world’s direction of travel on climate issues. The global consensus on action is fragmenting, even as climate impacts escalate and the world economy accelerates its embrace of renewable energy and electric technologies. Where does all this leave the COP process?

The debacle underscores the growing scepticism of so-called cover decisions at COPs. With nations at an impasse over even mentioning fossil fuels in any final text, it leaves many wondering what the point of a cover text is at all if it can’t ramp up the ambition signal sent to the rest of the world. Next year’s summit will be held in Addis Ababa, Ethiopia, and the hosts are highly unlikely to want to risk pushing for a cover decision.

With nations unlikely to agree on bold steps unanimously, the next-best thing is for large groups of countries to forge ahead with real-world change regardless. That means COPs will become more focused on the so-called action agenda, where groups of countries voluntarily band together to make pledges and set out roadmaps for adopting cleaner technologies. Yet whether that can be as powerful as all nations standing together under a singular message of ambition is doubtful.

Read more

The looming El Niño could be bad – but much worse is to come

But despite the disarray of the last fortnight, there are still reasons for hope. Meyer points out that progress was made in other areas of the COP, with 70 countries agreeing to accelerate the electrification of their economies, and countries including Brazil, Denmark and Spain presenting their roadmaps for removing fossil fuels from their economies. “In the real world, there’s a lot of progress,” he says.

The collapse of the negotiations might force better planning and strategy from nations going forward, he suggests. “I think, in a strange kind of way, the breakdown in the negotiations may serve as a wake-up call to the vast majority of countries that want to see progress on climate change,” he says.

There is also a clear signal from the wider economy that change is already under way. Renewables continue to grow faster than analyst predictions at every turn, while electric vehicles are hitting adoption tipping points in growing numbers of countries. The Iran conflict has underscored to many governments the security benefits of home-grown power over fossil fuel imports, with solar and nuclear energy the biggest beneficiaries, the International Energy Agency reported last week. Decarbonisation isn’t happening anywhere near fast enough, but the direction of travel is unmistakable.

UN climate summits have been teetering for many years, with the appearance of consensus maintained thanks to delicately constructed phrases and back-room horse trading. COP31 has brought the disputes and distrust out into the open in a spectacular fashion. Perhaps, out of the flames of this summit, a more honest and realistic approach to climate diplomacy can emerge.

articles.title: The BepiColombo spacecraft is finally entering orbit around Mercury
articles.summary:
Artist’s impression of BepiColombo orbiting Mercury

ESA/ATG medialab

After a long and ponderous journey, the BepiColombo spacecraft will finally enter Mercury’s orbit on 21 November. Over the course of the next year, it will investigate the planet’s geology, its tenuous atmosphere and its magnetic field in an effort to understand how it formed and evolved over time.

BepiColombo, a joint mission of the European Space Agency (ESA) and the Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency (JAXA), launched in October 2018. Mercury’s proximity to the sun makes it incredibly difficult to reach without overshooting the planet and falling into the sun, so the spacecraft had to take a long and looping path over the past eight years, flying past both Venus and Mercury several times and using their gravity to make subtle tweaks to its trajectory. In 2024, an issue with the thrusters lengthened that journey even further, pushing the arrival date back from 2025 to 2026. Now, it has finally arrived.

Read more

6 of the most fascinating moments in the life of our solar system

While it is arriving at Mercury as a single spacecraft, BepiColombo actually comprises two separate orbiters: ESA’s Mercury Planetary Orbiter (MPO) and JAXA’s Mercury Magnetospheric Orbiter (MMO, or Mio). In December, the two will split apart and move to different orbits – MPO on a near-circular path that takes 2.3 hours to complete an orbit, and Mio on a more distant elliptical orbit, where it will take 9.3 hours to circle Mercury.

Advertisement

Those split orbits complement the differing scientific objectives of the two spacecraft. MPO is more than twice the size of MMO, and its 11 scientific instruments focus largely on studying Mercury itself. Its instruments include several types of spectrometer to measure the makeup of the surface, a laser altimeter to map its terrain and instruments to study the makeup of Mercury’s extremely thin atmosphere, called an exosphere.

Mio’s more distant orbit will allow it to study a broader area around Mercury. It has five sets of scientific instruments to study the magnetic field and atmosphere of the planet, as well as the solar wind that blows strongly in the area close to the sun.

Free newsletter

Sign up to Launchpad

Sign up to newsletter

Now that the BepiColombo spacecraft are entering orbit, their primary mission is expected to last only one Earth year, which is a little more than four Mercury years. The mission could potentially be extended for another year, but beyond that the combination of limited fuel and extreme temperatures will make it all but impossible to keep going.

Over the course of the year, researchers hope that BepiColombo will provide enough data to solve some of Mercury’s many mysteries. Mercury’s magnetic field is bewildering, because it originates 400 kilometres above the planet’s centre and should have faded away long ago. Its atmosphere must be continuously supplied with material from the surface, but we are unsure exactly how that occurs. And its enormous iron core, much bigger proportionally than the core of any other planet in the solar system, makes its very formation and evolution a puzzle. If all goes well, BepiColombo will start to unravel the convoluted tale of our solar system’s smallest planet.

California has filed a lawsuit against OpenAI for the Hugging Face incident

Chris Jung/NurPhoto/Shutterstock

Can you send a computer to jail? No, obviously not. That’s a stupid question. And yet it is one that AI firms seem to want us to ask when faced with tales of “rogue agents” breaking into other peoples’ computers. As is so often the case with our current AI moment, storytelling has got in the way of reality.

Thankfully, that may be starting to change. This week, California announced that it is filing a lawsuit against OpenAI over an incident that occurred earlier this year, when another AI firm, Hugging Face, was hit by an attack that turned out to originate from OpenAI’s servers.

Read more

The real reasons we keep seeing big tech outages – it isn’t just hackers

In OpenAI’s telling, the Hugging Face hack was “driven by a combination of OpenAI models”, models that were “hyperfocused” on achieving a goal and found ways to “cheat” by stealing the answers for a test from Hugging Face’s servers. It is easy to come away with the impression that seemingly no humans were involved, and certainly not to blame. But in the words of California Attorney General Rob Bonta, the attack “was the predictable result of an internal culture at OpenAI that prioritizes growth and rapid model development over safety and accountability”, and he explicitly dismisses “science fiction fantasies of rogue AI systems run amok”.

Advertisement

Ever since the Hugging Face attack occurred, I have struggled to understand why OpenAI has yet to face legal consequences for what would seem to be a crime – unauthorised computer access under the US Computer Fraud and Abuse Act – if conducted by a human. So far, the legal answer to this seems to be a lack of intent, which the law requires, and it remains an untested legal question whether an AI can have intent, according to an analysis by US firm Ballard Spahr. California is instead bringing a civil suit, alleging that OpenAI created a risk to public safety and violated the state’s Unfair Competition Law, which prohibits harmful or fraudulent business practices even when there is no intent to deceive.

OpenAI has objected to the lawsuit. “This lawsuit appears to single out OpenAI over a challenge that’s been identified by every major AI lab,” said OpenAI spokesperson Drew Pusateri. As legal defences go, “everyone is doing it” doesn’t seem like a very good one to me, but that will be for the courts to decide.

What is clear is that we need an agreed understanding of liability when it comes to AI, but what I don’t think we need are special AI laws when our existing ones work just fine. For example, in 2024, Air Canada was held liable for misleading information given to a customer by its AI chatbot. A tribunal ruled that Air Canada had effectively tried to argue that the chatbot was a legally separate entity that it was not responsible for – an argument that did not wash.

In my view, any similar claims that AI can have its own legal agency should be dismissed. The argument that an AI is a legal actor serves AI companies in two ways, neither of which benefits society at large. The first is that it attempts to swerve responsibility, while the second is that it adds to the story of AI being an all-powerful, unknowable being. That second story is at the heart of the current AI revolution, but it isn’t one we have to listen to.

Read more

How preppers plan to save us if the whole internet collapses

I prefer a different argument. For the past year or so, Arvind Narayanan and Sayash Kapoor at Princeton University have put forward the idea of “AI as Normal Technology” – transformative, yes, in the same way as the internet or electricity, but not something that requires re-engineering the ordinary functions of society. As a normal technology, normal laws can apply. Writing about the Hugging Face attack earlier this year, the pair said that “AI companies should be liable for what their agents do” and, like Bonta, blame OpenAI’s internal culture and lack of human oversight for the incident.

The most high-profile example of existing laws being applied to AI companies is a class-action lawsuit against Anthropic, alleging that the firm used pirated copies of books to train its Claude AI models. Anthropic settled, and is now in the process of paying out to affected authors from a $1.5 billion fund. The wider question of whether training an AI on copyrighted material is illegal or counts as fair use remains open, and I really can’t believe that, four years after the launch of ChatGPT, we don’t yet have an answer to what is probably one of the most fundamental legal disputes of our time. OpenAI has previously said it would be “impossible” to create the kind of AI we have now without using copyrighted material, so this is an existential question for the AI firms.

Existing laws can also be tweaked to make it clear that they apply to AI. The European Union has done just that, updating a 1985 consumer rights directive to produce the 2024 Product Liability Directive, which explicitly makes it clear that software, including artificial intelligence, is a product and that people writing software are liable for any defects. The law doesn’t come into force until 9 December, when EU members must implement it, and it remains to be seen how it might be used against AI companies.

In other words, we don’t have to try to send a computer to jail. We’ve got humans who should be liable instead. As Bonta says, “While the technology OpenAI develops may be new, California’s prohibitions against conduct that harms the public and laws against unfair, deceptive, and fraudulent business practices are not.”

Further AI reading

After much fanfare, Anthropic has listed on the stock market at $83 a share, giving it a valuation of around $1.5 trillion. It is the second big AI firm to go public this year, following SpaceXAI in June.

The Economist has a great piece on whether the AI industry can ever make enough money to survive. It calculates that it must produce $3 trillion in revenue by 2030 to cover the costs of planned data centres. That is roughly equivalent to a tenth of all wages in high-income countries, or similar to the amount spent on food. Are people really going to buy as much AI as they do food?

The Cambridge Dictionary has named “human” as word of the year, as a pushback against the growth of AI. It feels a bit like trying too hard to be relevant, in my view.

As the COP31 climate summit continues, only nine countries have signed a pledge aimed at limiting the environmental impact of AI. As I have written previously, we cannot afford to run this 21st-century technology on a 20th-century energy supply.

articles.title: Huge extinct orca may have eaten other whales
articles.summary: A nearly 8-metre-long species of orca lived in the North Sea over 2 million years ago. Its discovery suggests orcas evolved a diet of marine mammals earlier than scientists thought

articles.title: Woman entered hibernation-like state during winter for more than 30 years
articles.summary: Researchers studying brains donated for scientific research stumbled upon the remarkable case of a woman who went through prolonged periods of reduced activity in which her body temperature dropped to as low as 31°C

articles.title: Cooking pollution dominates air quality at mealtimes in London
articles.summary: Particulate matter from kitchens is the largest source of air pollution during lunch and dinner in the city of London, an analysis shows

articles.title: Otherworldly image of a porcelain crab wins ocean photography contest
articles.summary:
Tammy Nicholas’s winning photograph, Porcelain Crab Feathered Feast

Tammy Nicholas

This exquisite photo of a porcelain crab catching plankton while half-hidden in an anemone was named the overall winner of The Nature Conservancy’s Oceania Photo Contest. The blue of the shadows gives the image an otherworldly feel.

Despite the name and appearance, porcelain crabs aren’t crabs – the similarity is a result of convergent evolution. The photo of the small crustacean was taken on a coral reef off Gili Air Island in Indonesia by Tammy Nicholas.

A shot of a drifter or pelagic crab clinging to a piece of kelp, shown below, won second prize in the wildlife category of the awards. While it looks large, this crab is, in fact, just a centimetre across. The photo was taken near the Poor Knights Islands of New Zealand by Crispin Middleton.

Advertisement

Crispin Middleton’s photograph, named Ocean Drifter

Crispin Middleton

A photograph of water lilies growing in the Cenote Carwash near Tulum, Mexico, shown below, took second place in the prize’s plants and fungi category. Cenotes are sinkholes linked to water-filled caves, and this one got its name because taxi drivers used to clean their cars there. Its Mayan name is Aktun Ha.

Vanessa Torres Macho’s photograph, titled Pendants

Vanessa Torres Macho

Vanessa Torres Macho took this image. The Oceania contest is open only to residents of Australia, New Zealand, Papua New Guinea and the Solomon Islands, but the photographs can be taken anywhere.

A shot of sardines pursued by diving Cape gannets, shown below, took second place in the water category of the awards. This photo, by Justin Tan, was taken off Port St Johns in South Africa during the sardine run, when billions of sardines migrate north along the coast, for reasons that are still not understood.

Justin Tan’s photograph, called Frenzy

Justin Tan

Finally, the first prize in the people and nature category went to this image, below, of a researcher filming juvenile sperm whales and a calf off the island of Mauritius in the Indian Ocean. Photographer Vanessa Mignon says this filming was done under permit, but it is often done illegally.

Vanessa Mignon’s image, Socialisation

articles.title: Turmeric supplements offer little benefit for knee osteoarthritis
articles.summary:
Turmeric capsules are touted as remedies for joint problems

olga Yastremska/Alamy

Turmeric supplements seem to have little to no effect on pain and mobility problems caused by knee osteoarthritis. That’s according to one of the most rigorous assessments of the evidence yet, which focused on four randomised controlled trials comparing the supplements to placebo pills.

Osteoarthritis, which affects more than 500 million people worldwide, is caused by damage to cartilage that cushions the ends of bones, resulting in pain, stiffness and inflammation. Standard treatments include painkillers and anti-inflammatory drugs that can ease symptoms. “But many people see little or no benefit,” says Philip Conaghan at the University of Leeds, UK, who wasn’t involved in the latest review.

Read more

There are only a few anti-ageing supplements that actually work

Turmeric supplements are often touted as an alternative therapy. They contain curcumin, a compound that gives turmeric its yellow colour and is thought to have anti-inflammatory properties. Yet such beliefs are often based on prior flawed studies, says Ivan Shirinsky at the Research Institute of Internal and Preventive Medicine in Novosibirsk, Russia.

Advertisement

Shirinsky and his colleagues analysed results from four randomised controlled trials, collectively involving more than 370 participants with knee osteoarthritis. Participants were randomly assigned to take either a supplement containing turmeric extract or placebo pills two or three times per day, for between eight weeks and three months. Each trial used a slightly different supplement containing a different curcumin dose. “We looked at the most rigorous evidence available,” says Shirinsky.

Among those who took a placebo, knee pain decreased by 1.6 points, on average, on a scale from 0 to 10 by the end of the study. Those taking turmeric supplements experienced an average 2.3-point decrease in pain, meaning the difference between the turmeric and placebo groups was half that required to be meaningful to patients based on prior studies, says Shirinsky.

Free newsletter

Sign up to Health Check

Sign up to newsletter

In line with this, surveys revealed that turmeric supplements had no meaningful effect on participants’ quality of life or their ability to carry out everyday activities such as walking, getting up from a chair or climbing stairs.

“If somebody is taking one of these therapies and thinks it is helping their symptoms, I would never force them to stop,” says Conaghan, since it could be working for some people. “But the evidence suggests it’s not going to help you. I would save your money.”

However, the findings cannot provide a definitive answer, says Shirinsky. “All included studies used different formulations of turmeric, and this reduced the certainty of the evidence,” he says. What’s more, the evidence wasn’t strong enough to make conclusions around turmeric’s potential side effects; curcumin supplements have previously been found to cause liver problems in some people.

Further randomised controlled trials testing a standardised curcumin supplement could address such limitations, but Conaghan doesn’t think this is justified. “There are not enough clues in [existing research] to give me confidence that we should do more trials in this area,” he says. For instance, studies have shown that curcumin isn’t easily absorbed into the blood following ingestion, meaning it is unlikely to reach joints to have an effect, he says.

Journal Reference:

Cochrane Library
DOI: 10.1002/14651858.CD014683

articles.title: A space telescope hunting for dark matter just discovered something unexpected
articles.summary: ESA’s Euclid space telescope has discovered its first previously unknown comet, despite being designed to study distant galaxies and the mysteries of the dark Universe. The icy object is approximately 1.3 billion kilometers from Earth and follows an unusual orbit that takes thousands of years to complete.

articles.title: Physicists trap antimatter in a breakthrough that could explain why the universe exists
articles.summary: Positrons are the antimatter counterpart of an electron. Physicists trapped a positron and cooled it to temperatures near absolute zero. Positron is suspended in a wall-free trap, safely separated from ordinary matter. Team will conduct most precise comparison yet between matter and antimatter. Any difference between the electron and positron could expose cracks in the Standard Model of particle physics.

articles.title: What is a thought made of? Why human consciousness may be beyond AI’s reach
articles.summary: A new theory suggests that the brain may chemically encode and retrieve memories rather than relying solely on electrical signals. Researchers propose that interactions between brain cells and their molecular surroundings could help explain the intimate connection between memory, emotion, and thought. Their findings challenge the assumption that increasingly powerful computers could eventually develop human-like consciousness.

articles.title: Physicists just sent an unblockable message through a brick wall using gravity
articles.summary: Scientists have successfully transmitted a message through a brick wall using nothing but gravity, an old elevator, and an incredibly sensitive detector. By moving a massive counterweight between two positions, researchers encoded the word "Gravity" into tiny changes in gravitational pull. Unlike Wi-Fi or radio signals, gravity passes through ordinary barriers without being blocked, offering a potentially revolutionary way to communicate.

articles.title: Einstein’s 120-year-old theory may be missing something big about the Big Bang
articles.summary: A surprising discovery by MIT and UC Santa Barbara physicists reveals that Einstein’s famous theory of particle motion misses something important when particles travel near the speed of light. Their new calculations show that heavy quarks moving through an ultra-hot plasma experience rare but unusually powerful jolts that Einstein’s traditional model cannot fully explain.

articles.title: New nose drops restore youthful memory and fight Alzheimer’s in aging mice
articles.summary: A revolutionary new nasal treatment has restored youthful learning and memory performance in aging mice while preventing severe cognitive decline in mice with Alzheimer’s-like disease. Developed using technology similar to COVID-19 mRNA vaccines, the nose drops stimulate production of a brain-protecting protein that strengthens neurons and supports memory. Remarkably, the treatment preserved brain function without removing Alzheimer’s-associated plaques, suggesting a completely different way to combat cognitive decline.

articles.title: A black hole the size of an atom could destroy an entire star
articles.summary: MIT scientists have discovered that tiny black holes left over from the Big Bang could slowly devour stars from within, eventually triggering spectacular explosions visible across galaxies. Detecting these unusual cosmic events could reveal the existence of primordial black holes and help solve the mystery of dark matter.

articles.title: 2,200-year-old Roman shipwreck reveals an ingenious waterproofing trick
articles.summary: A 2,200-year-old Roman shipwreck has revealed sophisticated waterproofing techniques involving pine tar and beeswax. Microscopic pollen grains trapped in the ancient coatings are now helping scientists reconstruct where the vessel may have traveled and undergone repairs more than two millennia ago.

articles.title: Ancient rocks from the Moon’s far side rewrite the Solar System’s violent past
articles.summary: Scientists studying ancient rocks from the Moon’s far side have uncovered surprising evidence that challenges decades of thinking about the Solar System’s violent past. Instead of a single catastrophic bombardment, asteroid impacts appear to have declined gradually over billions of years, revealing new clues about Earth's early evolution and the origins of life.

articles.title: Earth's next ice age may have already begun. Global warming stopped it
articles.summary: Scientists have uncovered surprising evidence that Earth’s next ice age may have already begun, only to be stopped by global warming. By studying ancient plants preserved beneath the Barnes Ice Cap in the Canadian Arctic, researchers discovered that the remnants of a massive ice sheet began expanding again about 2,000 years ago, signaling the possible start of a new glacial period. But by the 1960s, rising temperatures had reversed that growth, causing the ice to shrink instead.

articles.title: Earth’s ancient oceans may have fooled scientists about its oxygen history
articles.summary: Earth’s journey from an oxygen-starved world to a planet capable of supporting complex life may have unfolded very differently than scientists once believed. A new analysis suggests that oxygen accumulated in the atmosphere in three major stages, with the oceans taking millions or even hundreds of millions of years to catch up.

articles.title: New gum disease treatment kills bad bacteria while sparing the good
articles.summary: Researchers in Japan have developed an innovative gum disease treatment that uses egg yolk antibodies and near-infrared light to destroy harmful bacteria without harming beneficial microbes. Unlike conventional treatments, the approach preserves the mouth's natural bacterial balance and protects healthy gum cells. In mice, it significantly reduced the bone loss associated with periodontitis, a major cause of tooth loss.

articles.title: A galactic shock wave could rewrite the map of the Milky Way
articles.summary: A surprising discovery suggests the Milky Way may be making stars in places where most galaxies cannot. Scientists found evidence that a massive rotating structure near the galactic center is creating powerful shock waves that trigger star formation rather than suppress it. Even more unexpectedly, part of the Norma spiral arm may not be a spiral arm at all, but a vast region where new stars are being born.

articles.title: Two monster black holes from the dawn of time defy explanation
articles.summary: Astronomers have discovered the oldest known compact pair of quasars, powered by two enormous black holes that existed just 900 million years after the Big Bang. Weighing an astonishing 1.5 billion and 400 million times the mass of the Sun, these cosmic giants somehow grew to incredible sizes far earlier than current theories can explain.

articles.title: Mysterious new viruses reveal a missing link in evolution
articles.summary: Scientists have discovered previously unknown viruses that could help explain how some of life’s earliest biological structures evolved. The surprising findings challenge a longstanding evolutionary theory and suggest that viruses may have hidden capabilities far beyond simply infecting cells.

articles.title: Earth's core may be leaking a 4.5-billion-year-old secret
articles.summary: Scientists have discovered an unusual carbon signature in Hawaiian volcanic rocks that suggests some of Earth's carbon originated in ancient meteorites and later escaped from deep within the planet's core. The discovery raises an astonishing possibility: Carbon essential to life may have traveled from space to Earth's depths before emerging through volcanoes billions of years later.

articles.title: Archaeologists reveal a powerful Iron Age king may have been a woman
articles.summary: Archaeologists have uncovered evidence that Verica, the Iron Age ruler whose exile helped trigger Rome’s invasion of Britain in AD 43, was actually a woman. The discovery challenges centuries of historical assumptions and suggests that a largely forgotten female leader may have changed the course of British history.

articles.title: This tiny spider named after Stephen Colbert has a genome 50% larger than a human’s
articles.summary: A tiny California trapdoor spider named after Stephen Colbert has a genome roughly 50% larger than a human's, despite being only about the size of a quarter. Scientists discovered that its enormous genome contains 4.6 billion DNA base pairs and 52 chromosomes, revealing surprising clues about spider evolution.

articles.title: U.S. loses measles elimination status after 25 years as vaccine myths persist
articles.summary: The United States has lost its measles elimination status after more than 25 years, and a new survey reveals widespread misconceptions about the deadly disease and its vaccine. With measles cases surging, more than one-third of Americans still believe or are uncertain about the debunked vaccine-autism link, while most don't know the disease's risks or how many vaccine doses children need.

articles.title: Common medications may secretly rewire your gut, with effects lasting for years
articles.summary: Medications taken years or even long ago may leave lasting changes in your gut microbiome, according to a study of more than 2,500 people. Researchers discovered that common drugs, including antidepressants, blood pressure medications, and anxiety treatments, can leave microbial “fingerprints” long after patients stop taking them. Surprisingly, some anxiety medications had effects comparable to broad-spectrum antibiotics.

articles.title: Interstellar solar sails hit a bizarre problem at 75% of light speed
articles.summary: Scientists have discovered a surprising obstacle to interstellar travel: at extreme speeds, the light propelling futuristic solar sails could actually begin slowing them down. Once a spacecraft reaches 75% of the speed of light, some scattered light starts producing drag, potentially complicating humanity’s plans to reach distant stars.

articles.title: A mysterious gap hints at black holes born from stars that never exploded
articles.summary: Massive stars may be quietly collapsing into black holes without ever producing the spectacular supernova explosions scientists typically expect. A surprising pattern in 257 black hole mergers suggests these mysterious stellar disappearances could explain the origins of a large population of black holes throughout the universe.

articles.title: DNA’s secret sunscreen may have helped life survive on early Earth
articles.summary: Scientists have uncovered a surprising reason why early life may have survived Earth's intense ultraviolet radiation: a key component of DNA appears to turn potentially destructive damage into something easier to repair. The discovery could help solve a decades-old evolutionary mystery and reveal how life endured the harsh conditions of our planet's earliest days.

articles.title: A 194-year-old tortoise has a remarkable anti-aging secret hidden in its DNA
articles.summary: At an astonishing 194 years old, Jonathan the giant tortoise is the world's oldest living land animal, and scientists may have finally uncovered the secrets behind his extraordinary lifespan. Researchers identified 287 unique genetic variants linked to processes that help repair damaged DNA, control inflammation, regulate insulin, and suppress cancer.

articles.title: Time may be far stranger than we realize. Scientists have a way to test it
articles.summary: Time may be far stranger than we realize, and scientists have proposed a way to detect clocks experiencing multiple flows of time simultaneously. Using atomic clocks with dramatically enhanced sensitivity, researchers hope to reveal a never-before-observed quantum effect that could transform our understanding of time and gravity.

articles.title: A giant star swallowed another star. James Webb reveals the aftermath
articles.summary: Astronomers have witnessed a spectacular cosmic collision in the Andromeda galaxy, where a small star spiraled into a giant star 18,000 times brighter than the Sun, triggering a violent eruption. NASA’s James Webb Space Telescope captured the aftermath just 47 days later, revealing new details about how two stars can merge into one.

articles.title: Who was buried in Westminster Abbey's Roman coffin? A 150-year mystery may be solved
articles.summary: A mysterious skeleton discovered in a Roman sarcophagus at Westminster Abbey may finally be identified after more than 150 years. New dating evidence suggests the remains belonged to a high-ranking medieval abbot who was buried inside a centuries-old recycled Roman coffin.

articles.title: A 50-year-old theory about evolution may have been wrong all along
articles.summary: A decades-old theory suggesting that evolution protects its most important genes from mutations has been dealt a major blow. An extensive new analysis of mutations in bacteria and yeast found no evidence that essential genes mutate less frequently than other genes. Researchers say earlier studies may have been misled by harmful mutations that disappeared through natural selection before scientists could detect them.

articles.title: Even scientists can't agree on what science actually is
articles.summary: Scientists cannot agree on what science actually is, and a new study finds their views are surprisingly more divided than those of the general public. The findings could help explain public frustration with scientific uncertainty and raise questions about how artificial intelligence might reshape future discoveries.

articles.title: Scientists say the human family tree may need a radical rewrite
articles.summary: The human family tree may need a major overhaul. New research from Monash University challenges the traditional classification of our ancient ancestors, arguing that species such as Australopithecus and Paranthropus should be grouped within our own genus, Homo. As scientists uncover more fossils and analyze evolutionary relationships, the boundaries that once separated these ancient relatives are becoming increasingly difficult to defend.

articles.title: After 8 years in space, a groundbreaking X-ray telescope finally opens its eyes
articles.summary: After eight years and 10 billion kilometers in space, a groundbreaking X-ray telescope heading to Mercury has captured its first cosmic observations and is performing even better than scientists expected. The instrument could soon reveal Mercury's hidden chemical secrets and transform our understanding of how the solar system's smallest planet formed.

articles.title: Einstein’s relativity just upended a fundamental rule of chemistry
articles.summary: A surprising discovery at Brown University is challenging one of chemistry's most fundamental textbook explanations. Researchers found direct evidence that Einstein's theory of relativity changes how heavy atoms form triple bonds, causing normally distinct types of chemical bonds to blend together. The breakthrough confirms a decades-old prediction and suggests that traditional chemistry rules don't fully apply to heavy elements such as bismuth.

articles.title: NASA’s Voyager 1 is now so far away that light takes 24 hours to reach it
articles.summary: NASA’s Voyager 1 has reached an extraordinary milestone, traveling 16.1 billion miles from Earth to become the first spacecraft so distant that its signals take a full day to reach us. Nearly 50 years after launch, the aging probe continues its historic journey through interstellar space, pushing the limits of human exploration despite dwindling power and technical challenges.

articles.title: NASA's powerful Moon rocket engine roars through a dramatic 200-second test
articles.summary: NASA has successfully tested a powerful RS-25 rocket engine, firing it for 200 seconds to gather data that could make future Moon missions safer and more reliable. The test supports preparations for the 2028 Artemis IV Moon landing and NASA’s ultimate ambition of sending astronauts to Mars.

articles.title: Scientists turn Moon dust into LEGO-like bricks for future lunar bases
articles.summary: Scientists have found a way to 3D-print Moon dust into LEGO-like bricks, raising the possibility of building lunar bases using materials already on the Moon. The experimental blocks still need to be strengthened, but the technology could transform how humans construct permanent settlements beyond Earth.

articles.title: FCC approves SpaceX plan to put AI data centers in space
articles.summary: The FCC dismissed some of the key concerns raised by opponents, including potential threats to scientific research, because the agency determined they fell outside its regulatory authority.

articles.title: OpenAI says heavy ChatGPT users may hit limits sooner as it merges Chat and Work
articles.summary: OpenAI will introduce a single usage meter across ChatGPT as it combines the Chat and Work experiences.

articles.title: Jensen Huang broke Nvidia’s code of conduct, and his employees may not forget it
articles.summary: Most codes of conduct serve as a reflection of corporate culture. In Nvidia's case, that could have consequences.

articles.title: The canceled Tesla Cybertruck is the fastest-selling used truck in America
articles.summary: The Tesla Cybertruck was the fastest-selling used truck last month, averaging just 39.1 days on the market compared to 65.5 days for trucks overall.

articles.title: Anthropic’s Dario Amodei calls accusations of surrendering human control to AI ‘absurd’
articles.summary: Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei pushes back against rivals’ accusations that he favors surrendering human agency to AI, even as leading AI companies increasingly automate their own research and model development.

articles.title: 1Password said hackers broke into its internal systems, but customer passwords are safe
articles.summary: The password manager maker said an attacker gained access to an employee's corporate account and took some information about customers.

articles.title: Want to buy your kid an AI toy this Christmas? Not in New York
articles.summary: New York has banned AI chatbot toys for five years as new research from Common Sense Media reveals troubling safety failures, including exposure to inappropriate content and risks to emotional development.

articles.title: DOJ accuses former cyber executive of defrauding ransomware victims by secretly paying hackers
articles.summary: U.S. prosecutors accused the former executive of defrauding victims of ransomware by paying the hackers, charging victims more, and pocketing the difference.

articles.title: Character.AI’s plan to auction off users’ private chats challenged by state AGs
articles.summary: The proposed Character.ai bankruptcy sale includes sensitive personal data from more than 21 million U.S. accounts, including 2.1 million registered to minors, the state AGs said.

articles.title: X’s latest update for creators focuses on vertical video
articles.summary: As short-form video ramps up in popularity, X's new creation tools are part of its effort to compete with YouTube and Instagram.

articles.title: WhatsApp now lets you schedule messages in group and individual chats
articles.summary: Users can schedule messages from 10 minutes later to after 14 days.

articles.title: AI data centers are becoming harder to build, and neoclouds are feeling it
articles.summary: ⁠Nvidia has made clear⁠ it won’t backstop an AI data center until it’s nearly ready to run, and that’s landing just as neoclouds report construction delays and more expensive debt. The message to developers is that land, power, and a finished building matter more than a pitch deck.  ⁠Anita Verma-Lallian⁠ has been selling exactly that. […]

articles.title: Allstate suffers multiday tech outage ahead of Thanksgiving
articles.summary: The disruption comes at a particularly bad time for the insurance giant, as millions of Americans prepare to travel for the Thanksgiving holiday weekend.

articles.title: Todoist confirms 6% of customers’ details were stolen in data breach
articles.summary: Todoist said a hacker gained access to its production systems and stole customer data, including email IDs, password hashes, and account creation dates.

articles.title: Amazon and Meta reportedly in talks to lift blockade on AI agent Muse
articles.summary: Amazon and Meta are discussing a potential deal that would end a two-month-long blockade of Muse.

articles.title: Flipkart CEO Kalyan Krishnamurthy to step down next week amid IPO uncertainty
articles.summary: Flipkart's product and technology chief Balaji Thiagarajan will lead the company alongside its board until a successor is found.

articles.title: The questions Jensen Huang and Nvidia will still have to answer about Megaspeed
articles.summary: The central question for investigators is what Nvidia knew about where those chips ended up and whether Huang's affair with a Megaspeed executive gave the company reason to doubt Megaspeed's assurances.

articles.title: Yale’s Sonnenfeld: Nvidia is a ‘detriment’ to US industrial might — not a champion
articles.summary: Yale's Jeffrey Sonnenfeld warns that what the market cheered Monday, Jensen Huang's White House–backed return as Nvidia's CEO and board member, could prove a giant mistake, exposing the directors to "historic" personal liability from a growing pile of lawsuits and raising the question of whether the country is celebrating a company that has helped put advanced chips in its adversaries' hands.

articles.title: Trump reportedly says pardoning Jensen Huang is ‘an option’
articles.summary: Huang faces ongoing questions about his relationship with Alice Huang, an executive with alleged ties to Chinese intelligence who previously worked for a company that has been accused of illegally diverting Nvidia chips to China.

articles.title: Jensen Huang still thinks a succession plan creates unnecessary hierarchy
articles.summary: It's a remarkable stance for a company that spent the last two weeks finding out what happens without its founder.

articles.title: In all-hands meeting, Jensen Huang thanks White House and says he’s in therapy
articles.summary: The Nvidia founder apologized to his staff on Tuesday and said he was grateful for a second chance to lead the company.

articles.title: Even the best AI agents struggle with everyday life
articles.summary: As millions embrace personal AI assistants, a new benchmark reveals that even the most advanced AI models struggle to complete everyday tasks reliably and safely without introducing potential new problems.

articles.title: Walmart teams up with Meta to bring Black Friday deals to AI agent Muse
articles.summary: Walmart now lets customers shop Black Friday deals through Muse, Meta’s AI agent.

articles.title: Maple raises $5.3M to build AI products that protect your data, even from itself
articles.summary: The startup's encrypted AI architecture is designed to prevent even the company itself from accessing users' private data.

articles.title: Anthropic shares fall below IPO price, a worrying sign for AI startups
articles.summary: Anthropic’s post-IPO slump could put pressure on AI startup valuations.

articles.title: UK warns AI-driven cyberattacks are exposing years of weak security
articles.summary: The British cyber agency says that "building strong foundations has never mattered more" as AI hacking tools rely on exploiting simple security flaws.

articles.title: Meta brings its Muse AI assistant directly into Instagram DMs
articles.summary: The new integration gets rid of the need for users to toggle between Instagram and the Muse app when they want to interact with the AI agent.

articles.title: Tidal to ban and remove millions of AI-generated tracks as AI slop inundates music streaming
articles.summary: The company said it will still accept songs that were made with AI assistance, but not fully generated.

articles.title: Why a Crusoe investor is betting on solar and batteries to power future AI data centers
articles.summary: Next-generation data centers will need tens of gigawatts of power every year. One of Crusoe's investors thinks solar and energy storage are the obvious choice.

articles.title: Pinterest will now let parents limit the AI-generated content their teens see
articles.summary: While other social platforms have focused on restricting teens' access to AI chatbots, Pinterest is addressing the AI content filling their feeds.

articles.title: Google’s patent for custom AI video feeds paints a bleak picture of entertainment’s future
articles.summary:
Last year, Google filed a patent for a system called My Channel that's designed to create feeds filled with personalized, AI-generated videos and advertisements based on information the company knows about its users. articles.title: AI may soon change what it means to be a theoretical physicist

He didn’t ask because he needed to know the answer. He had actually solved this particular problem already. But he had never published the solution—which made it a perfect question to test how good AI was at physics.

LLMs have been trained on the whole Internet, so if a physics problem has been discussed online, it’s likely the model already knows about it and may have memorized the answer. So a fair test of AI capabilities needs to focus on problems that have never appeared online.

The model didn’t answer Raju’s problem correctly, but it did better than he expected—well, enough to get him thinking that the experiment should be repeated and formalized. With the help of a colleague, he set out to create a theoretical physics benchmark for AI.

articles.title: What's going on with the Riemann hypothesis?
articles.summary:
Last week, news broke that a mathematician had used AI to help crack one of the biggest outstanding problems in math: a proof of the Riemann hypothesis. The news follows several other major breakthroughs in math that have either been enabled by or managed entirely by large language model-based systems, a development that has left the entire field of mathematics in a state of upset.

It's too early to say much about the proof itself—mathematicians are still in the process of digesting it. But we can say a little about how the proof came about, and what it tells us about the state of math.

Tackling Riemann

The Riemann hypothesis dates from the mid-1800s and was formulated by (you will be surprised to learn) Bernhard Riemann. There's not an obvious way to describe the details of the actual hypothesis simply, but it has implications for the distribution of prime numbers. This gives it significance for areas ranging from number theory to cryptography. As Wikipedia accurately states, "It is considered by pure mathematicians to be one of the most important problems in the field."

articles.title: How brewers can protect beers from smoke-tainted hops

The 2020 Oregon wildfires burned over 1 million acres, destroyed thousands of structures, and killed 11 people. Smoke from the fires spread across the entire region; this "smoke taint" adversely affected not only local wine production, but also hops grown for beer brewing. Since the Pacific Northwest produces more than 95 percent of US hops and about 40 percent of the global supply, the potential economic impact is significant.

That's why Oregon State University (OSU) scientists have been studying how brewers could offset the negative impacts of smoke taint while still incorporating affected hops in their brews. Most recently, they found that it all depends on the quantity of tainted hops that are included and when hops are added during the brewing process, according to a new paper published in the Journal of the American Society of Brewing Chemists.

As previously reported, the chemistry of brewing beer is a very active area of research. For instance, in 2018, OSU chemist Thomas Shellhammer—who also co-authored this latest paper—identified the growing popularity of "dry hopping" (adding hops after fermentation, common for pale ales) among craft brewers as the likely culprit of the exploding beer bottle phenomenon.

Tidal debuted its initial AI policy in July 2026, which included labeling and demonetizing all songs created entirely with AI. That wasn't enough to stem the tide of AI slop, though. Over the past 90 days, Tidal reports that 43 percent of new uploads were completely AI-generated. On November 6, new uploads to Tidal hit a whopping 60 percent AI-generated.

As things stand, Tidal hosts 27 million tracks labeled as AI, all of which were obviously added in the past couple of years. That accounts for 6.3 percent of Tidal's total catalog. On December 9, Tidal will delete all those songs. The streamer notes this will have essentially no negative impact, because 96 percent of AI-labeled tracks got zero plays in the past 90 days. Throughout its announcement, Tidal is careful to stipulate that it's only talking about music that has been fully created by AI. articles.title: Porsche 718 Boxster prototype drive: This electric roadster is real
articles.summary:
Porsche provided flights from Albany, New York, to Los Angeles and accommodation so Ars could drive the 718 EV prototype. Ars does not accept paid editorial content.

It wasn't until I was stuck in traffic on the way back from a run up and down some canyon roads that I realized just how low Porsche's upcoming all-electric 718 Boxster truly is. I was idly looking around at the other cars, doing the math on the EV adoption rate in this small sample of Los Angeles gridlock (roughly 50 percent, impressively) when I noticed that I was eye-level with a Tesla Model Y door handle.

That's not particularly low for a sports car, but it's practically unheard of for an EV. Nearly all modern electric cars are built atop a skateboard-style battery pack, a stack of cells that elevates the seating position by a good 3 inches. In these SUV-heady days, that's usually not a problem, possibly even an advantage. But, in a car like this, the closer you can get your keister to the road, the greater the sensation of speed.

So, for the company's first all-electric sports car, the 718 Boxster that will be fully revealed next year, Porsche engineers put the battery pack behind the driver. That powers a single motor spinning the rear wheels and creates a driving experience that both honors the simple joy of motoring in a mid-engined Boxster while pushing the 718 to new heights of power and performance.

articles.title: Homo erectus lived in the rainforest alongside Denisovans
articles.summary:
Homo erectus was walking around mainland Asia at least 60,000 years more recently than archaeologists thought. A handful of teeth from two caves in southern China's Guangxi Province just filled in a significant gap in the fossil record of a region that's vital to the story of how our genus, Homo, took over the world.

The chemical makeup of the teeth's enamel suggests that, over the course of their lives, these Homo erectus moved across surprisingly large distances and made their living in dense tropical rainforests—an environment we'd previously assumed that only our species had ever gained a real foothold in. And one of the teeth offers a strong clue that Homo erectus probably shared this vast landscape with the Denisovans.

A handful of teeth with a lot to say

Baxian and Naxian are a pair of limestone caves that lie 15 kilometers apart along a karst valley corridor in southern China. University of Copenhagen paleoanthropologist Frido Welker and his colleagues unearthed a total of nine hominin teeth from among the more than 18,000 bones and fragments from non-hominin animals found there. Macquarie University paleoanthropologist Kira Westaway and her colleagues analyzed proteins and chemical isotopes from the enamel of five of these teeth.

articles.title: Amazon says hackers' AI agents found and exploited 0-day with little human input
articles.summary:
Amazon said AI agents recently found and exploited a zero-day vulnerability with no human oversight beyond a simple instruction to get root access on an East Asian university server.

The agents were running on Cairn, an open source AI penetration-testing framework. The hackers, who provided prompts in simplified Chinese and configured the model to the Chinese Standard Time zone, gave the agents a list of IP addresses and the goal: “obtain shell access.” In short order, the agents discovered a zero-day in an open source medical imaging AI application running on one of the target servers. The agents then exploited the vulnerability and gained full control of the system.

“These findings show that agentic offensive operations are already happening, and defenders should prepare for the speed and persistence these tools enable,” Amazon said.
