articles.title: How did the COP31 climate agreement fall apart – and what happens now?
articles.summary:
Chris McGrath/Getty

Two days after the COP31 global climate summit was supposed to finish, the talks in Antalya, Turkey, have come to an end – but not as we might have hoped.

Agreement simply could not be reached. The sticking point was the omission of fossil fuels in draft texts. The European Union led a revolt, shattering the consensus needed to adopt the cover text proposed by the Turkish and Australian conveners.

In a year of unprecedented climate disasters, a supercharged El Niño and as the world heads inevitably past 1.5 °C of warming, the EU and other nations said that the international process did not meet the moment.

Some coverage has suggested the rejection of the cover text is a sign the entire summit was a failure. This isn’t quite right.

These texts have always been add-ons to the formal negotiation process. Countries have regularly agreed these political, overarching statements, particularly since the Glasgow meeting in 2021, but they are not a requirement.

Its failure does not signal the end of the COP process – or the breakdown of the Paris Agreement. What it may mean is that international climate cooperation will look different from this point onwards.

Chris Bowen, the COP31 president of negotiations and Australia’s Minister for Climate Change, speaks to the media after the final session during the second overtime day of the climate talks.
Chris McGrath/Getty

No mention of the ‘F’ word

For many observers, the litmus test for success at COP31 was whether countries could make any headway on the root cause of climate change – fossil fuels. Unfortunately, fossil fuels proved unmentionable.

Three years ago at COP28 in Dubai, countries agreed to “transition away from fossil fuels”, marking the first time fossil fuels had explicitly been mentioned in an official decision text in decades of negotiations.

The Dubai text was hailed as “the beginning of the end of the fossil fuel era”. But there was little sign that hope would be realised in Turkey.

In a repeat of last year’s fraught negotiations at COP30 in Brazil, major fossil fuel producing nations Saudi Arabia and Russia banded together to block any reference in the negotiating outcomes and proposed cover text.

Australia and Turkey proposed a compromise – no fossil fuel language in exchange for support for electrification “with the greatest possible use of clean energy”.

This seemed to get Saudi Arabia over the line but drew backlash from the European Union, Panama, the Marshall Islands, Vanuatu, and Belize, who rejected the cover text.

Brazil took a different approach to the same problem last year. In a bid to break the deadlock, Brazil committed to develop a global strategy to phase out fossil fuels outside the formal negotiating agenda.

The roadmap was launched at this year’s summit in Turkey and managed to attract support from big fossil fuel producers such as India, Germany and Nigeria. Countries across the European Union are launching similar roadmaps.

Frustration over fossil fuels at COP31 is likely to lead more nations to go outside official talks to progress phase-out efforts. Earlier this year, 57 nations attended the first conference on transitioning away from fossil fuels in Santa Marta, Colombia. Another meeting is planned for next year, co-hosted by Tuvalu and Ireland.

Neither the Turkish hosts nor their Australian partners seemed keen to mention fossil fuels. Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan was untroubled by the optics of announcing two huge new oilfields in Turkey in his speech at the summit opening. While Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese highlighted the existential risks to Pacific countries from climate change, he made no commitment to stop approving new Australian coal and gas projects.

Both leaders much preferred to talk about electrification, namely the flagship “35 by 35” electrification pledge. The goal here is to boost electricity’s share of final energy use globally from around 23% at present to 35% by 2035.

Efforts to embed this goal in the cover text failed. But the electrification pledge drew strong support outside official negotiations. More than 75 countries and 180 businesses signed on, including the European Union and China.

Activist Greta Thunberg attends a protest at the COP31 climate summit in Antalya, Turkey.
Burak Kara/Getty

The “COP of action” fails to deliver

This year’s climate summit was billed as an “implementation COP”, focused on delivering the pledges countries had already made to address climate change.

Overseen by Australia in its role as “president of negotiations”, the formal talks largely focused on the actions countries are taking to reduce emissions and adapt to climate change, whether their response is sufficiently urgent and whether funds aimed at supporting the most vulnerable countries are adequate.

It was abundantly obvious that longstanding divisions had not been overcome. Developed countries called for emissions to be cut faster, while developing countries responded by pointing to a lack of financial support to do so.

African countries, in particular, stressed that an “implementation COP” was meaningless if rich nations failed to provide the actual resources needed to act.

Despite the general gloom, these talks did achieve progress in a few areas. Nations moved forwards on supporting a just transition (shifting to clean energy fairly) via a “phased approach”, as well as improving alignment in climate adaptation, which will help the poorest nations to implement their adaptation plans.

But broader efforts to find a way forward on the Paris Agreement’s Global Goal on Adaptation were left unresolved.

Decisions stalled in many negotiating rooms in the face of hard “red lines” declared by different blocs of countries.

Countries failed to reach any agreement on the vital question of cutting emissions, after Saudia Arabia and Russia blocked a proposed decision. Both are among the world’s top fossil fuel exporting nations.

This failure has left the world without any dedicated negotiating process on cutting emissions under the Paris Agreement. It’s possible nations could agree to renew a work program on climate mitigation at next year’s COP32 talks in Ethiopia.

What about money for adaptation?

Who pays for the costs of climate change has long been a contentious point. Developing countries face the brunt of damage from climate change, but have emitted far less – and have much less money to spend on adaptation.

Ahead of COP31, EU Climate Commissioner Wopke Hoekstra said talks on new climate finance commitments were “dead in the water”. He urged delegates to focus on implementing existing pledges rather than try for fresh funding.

The summit failed to meet even these low expectations. No concrete progress was achieved on the goal of tripling funds for climate adaptation pledged last year at COP30 in Brazil.

Ahead of the summit, the Australian government flagged the need to boost global contributions to the official Pacific climate fund.

This, too, didn’t eventuate. Rich nations – including Australia – merely re-announced their existing pledges, leaving the Pacific fund A$450 million short of its 2026 target of $749 million.

Ironically, the most notable pledge came from the Solomon Islands, a small Pacific nation. Prime Minister Matthew Wale pledged $600,000 to the global Green Climate Fund. “The Pacific did not create this crisis,” he declared. “But we will not stand by and wait for others to act”.

A few new commitments arrived by the end of the two week summit from nations such as Canada and Norway.

Press and participants watch as a man dressed as a dinosaur performs as part of the Fossil Of The Day award at the COP31 UN climate summit.
Burak Kara/Getty Images

Defending the science

Unusually, climate science was front and centre at COP31.

This year, a small bloc of fossil fuel-producing countries has been obstructing the publication of key scientific reports from the world’s leading body of climate scientists, the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change.

This year marks the first UN summit since it was officially confirmed the world will overshoot the Paris Agreement’s 1.5°C goal by 2030.

With the collapse of support for the cover text, statements supporting release of the latest climate science didn’t get approval. All that remained were technical conclusions which “expressed utmost concern” that climate impacts will continue to increase with every increment of global warming.

IPCC chair Jim Skea at the opening ceremony of COP31. Previously, he described the stymied outcome of the meeting in Ethiopia as frustrating and disappointing.
Chris McGrath/Getty Images

Australia on the global stage

COP31 gave Australia a unique global role. After being outmanoeuvred in their bid to host the summit, Australia secured a role in overseeing negotiations.

Australian Climate and Energy Minister Chris Bowen and his team had the unenviable task of seeking consensus between 195 countries and the European Union.

After the cover text was rejected, Bowen declared Australia had left “nothing on the field” but had faced “unbridgeable red lines.”

Hours beforehand, Fijian Climate Minister Lynda Tabuya acknowledged Bowen’s efforts, noting the failure was “not yours to carry […] it is the responsibility of all parties.”

Are COP summits still worthwhile?

This year’s climate summit took the unenviable record of the longest ever. With consensus seemingly impossible, some civil society representatives dubbed it “the worst COP ever.”

Outgoing UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres blamed “powerful fossil fuel interests”, including fossil fuel exporters and corporate lobbyists.

Some nations are now calling for urgent reform to negotiations long paralysed by vetoes and disconnected from science.

Unfortunately, any change to official voting processes would itself require a consensus decision.

Consensus is hard to achieve, but powerful. The power of the Paris Agreement draws on the fact it represents the view of nearly every country – big or small, rich or poor.

COP31 President Murat Kurum began the summit expressing hopes this year’s talks would leave a legacy of “working together.”

That was a false hope. A more realistic hope is that the collapse of consensus may be the shock the world needs to change course.

As former UN climate chief Christiana Figueres has said, we should not see the refusal of more than 130 countries to sign an inadequate deal as a failure. Rather, it might be “a sign of courage”.

Jacqueline Peel receives funding from the Australian Research Council. She is affiliated with the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change, serving as a coordinating lead author in Working Group III (mitigation) for the Seventh Assessment Report.

Kathryn Bowen receives funding from Australia's Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade and Department of Climate Change, Energy, Environment and Water, the World Health Organisation, Wellcome, the Global Fund, Green Climate Fund, Global Environment Facility, Asian Development Bank and World Bank. She is affiliated with the Port Philip EcoCentre and the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change where she is a lead author for the Sixth and Seventh Assessment Reports (Working Group II - Impacts, Vulnerability and Adaptation).

articles.title: Why fossil fuel-producing countries are stalling this crucial climate report
articles.summary:
Muhammad Fajri/Getty

After a year of record-breaking weather and a “super” El Niño underway, there’s no doubt climate extremes are wreaking havoc across the globe.

For decades, scientists have warned us this would happen. Their research made the case for reducing fossil fuel dependence. And we’ve relied on their expertise to assess the severity and extent of climate change.

But a small bloc of fossil fuel-producing countries is now obstructing the publication of a key scientific report from the world’s leading body of climate scientists, the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC).

This threatens global cooperation on tackling the climate crisis. And it has created deep concern at the COP31 climate summit, currently in its final hours in Turkey, also known as Türkiye.

A truly global report

First, it helps to understand why this report is so significant. The IPCC is the UN body for assessing the science related to climate change. Established in 1988, it provides political leaders with independent scientific assessments on climate change and strategies for response.

This panel has produced six pivotal reports to date, which have collated and reviewed the latest knowledge on climate change science. And over the past two years, more than 640 experts from around the world have been meeting to write the seventh.

The authors are leading researchers who volunteer their time. More than half of the authors working on the current seventh report, called the Seventh Assessment Report, or AR7, are from developing countries. I am a lead author for the Sixth and Seventh Assessment Reports in the working group that looks at impacts, vulnerability and adaptation.

Work on this seventh report kicked off in December 2024, and its timeline for completion was never officially finalised.

What’s the hold-up?

Originally, the plan was for the seventh report to be released in 2028. But five countries are objecting to this timeline and pushing for a later release in 2029.

India, Russia, Saudi Arabia, Kenya and China are ostensibly arguing that countries from the global south lack the resources and capacity to meet the current deadline.

However, these countries also happen to be among the world’s largest fossil fuel producers.

If recent reports are anything to go by, the evidence of global warming in this seventh report is likely to be alarming. It will highlight the evidence for much greater action, including deep and urgent reduction in fossil fuel production and use.

Extending the release date means IPCC contributors would have even more information they would have to assess. This delay would increase, not alleviate, the demands of authorship and reviewing for those contributors from developing nations.

The disagreement resulted in the suspension of the latest IPCC meeting in October in Ethiopia, with no confirmed timeline for the report release or budget for 2027. This threatens the very existence of the IPCC.

Nations seeking delay argue that tight timelines are unfair to developing countries. But the least developed countries (LDC), a group comprised of 44 nations, expressed “deep disappointment” when the meeting in Ethiopia was suspended.

Why the deadline matters

Every five years, the UN’s climate body does a global stocktake of how effectively the world is responding to climate change.

Intended to ramp up climate action, these stocktakes take a long hard look at the state of the planet, identify the gaps in our approach and suggest a path forward. To be truly effective, these must be based on the latest science.

Delaying the seventh report would mean the most recent science is not fed into the 2028 global stocktake. This has grave implications for future climate action, and any delay in our response could have catastrophic effects on the wellbeing of planetary and human health.

Science vs politics

While major fossil-fuel-emitting countries often attempt to impede phaseout efforts, undermining the IPCC follows a recent trend of discrediting science for political ends.

After a UN report in September found that limiting global warming to 1.5°C was no longer possible, Saudi Arabia jumped to question the credibility of the science, contending the research was not peer-reviewed. In fact, the report had been written over the course of a year by 44 experts, and reviewed by a further 44.

Conflict at COP31

Despite opposition to delaying the IPCC report, those pushing for it have remained unmoved at COP31. Speaking to media at the summit, former US Vice President Al Gore accused Saudi Arabia of trying to sabotage the IPCC’s work.

“Saudi Arabia is trying to destroy the IPCC in order to prevent the next global stocktake from using the accurate scientific data on fossil fuels,” he said.

At climate negotiations where the phrase “fossil fuels” is routinely vetoed from the text, finding a resolution to the IPCC issue has even broader implications. If countries can’t agree on this, how will nearly 200 countries agree on a robust final COP31 outcome?

Seeking resolution

While the clock ticks down on the COP31 negotiations, a resolution to the IPCC issue is unlikely in Turkey. However, it is hoped a timeline and budget can be nailed down at meetings in early December.

As the world’s most authoritative global body on climate change, the role the IPCC plays in driving climate action is critical to our future wellbeing. And the science in this seventh report will be fundamental to a truly effective global stocktake.

In a time when the world often feels divided, settling this issue amicably and in good faith would offer countries a much-needed reminder that we are capable of cooperation in pursuit of a better future.

Disclaimer: the author’s views do not reflect those of the IPCC

articles.title: Alcohol addiction and eating disorders often go hand in hand – here’s why
articles.summary:
Many people aren't aware of the connection between the two disorders. shisu_ka/ Shutterstock

When some people drink, they purposely skip meals in order to amplify the effects of the alcohol or to save calories for their drinks. The practice, sometimes referred to as “drunkorexia”, highlights the crossover that can exist between risky drinking behaviour and disordered eating.

Although this practice has been documented in students and “wine-mom culture”, very little research has actually investigated how common it is in people who are in alcohol treatment services. This is what my research sought to do.

My colleagues and I recently conducted a review which found that eating problems are common among people being treated for alcohol addiction. We also found that the two conditions often share the same underlying drivers.

We reviewed data from 44 studies published between 1988 and 2026. Most of the studies were conducted with women living in high-income countries, including the US, Canada and the UK.

All the studies involved people getting support for their drinking. Some studies also included people getting support for their eating behaviour, while others only asked participants to fill in questionnaires about their eating habits.

Most studies were observational. This meant that rather than testing a treatment, people within these services were observed and asked about their experiences. This means our findings only show a link – we cannot prove cause and effect.

We found that people who are receiving treatment for alcohol use problems have around twice the likelihood of experiencing an eating disorder compared with the general population.

For instance, one of the studies we included in our review found that over two-thirds of women who were receiving treatment for alcohol addiction identified as binge eaters, while between 6% and 39% had bulimia nervosa.

Using food to cope with difficult emotions, manage mood or as a substitute for alcohol was common among both men and women undergoing treatment. Traits such as impulsivity, low self-esteem and negative self-image were common among study participants as well.

Several of the papers also showed that difficulties with mental health, attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) or post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) were linked with increased risk of struggling with both an eating disorder and alcohol addiction.

Our study also showed that people undergoing treatment for alcohol addiction who are struggling with eating problems may be at increased risk of leaving treatment early, against medical advice. This can make recovery harder, increase the severity of challenging eating behaviour and the risk of medical complications.

Being aware of this link is important as it could impact treatment.
Pixel-Shot/ Shutterstock

Overall, our review highlights the distinct link between both alcohol addiction and disordered eating, and the common underlying traits both may share.

Our findings also suggest that asking people undergoing treatment for alcohol addiction about their eating behaviour could support treatment and highlight any challenges a person may be experiencing sooner.

Why this link matters

Both eating disorders and alcohol addiction can affect how the body absorbs nutrients, which may lead to nutrient deficiencies.

Weight gain may also be a problem in alcohol recovery, especially if a person uses sugar or food in order to cope. People who struggle with both of these conditions may also be at greater risk of depression or anxiety.

Using food and drink to cope with stressors, low mood or feeling bad about yourself is common – but many people may not be aware of when this behaviour becomes unhealthy or out of control.

For those undergoing treatment for alcohol use disorder, it may be beneficial to share any questions or concerns you may have surrounding food or eating with your therapist or nurse – including any challenging emotions you may have about food or meals.

Understanding the way both alcohol use disorder and disordered eating are connected means we may be able to better help those undergoing treatment for either condition.

Anna Preece does not work for, consult, own shares in or receive funding from any company or organisation that would benefit from this article, and has disclosed no relevant affiliations beyond their academic appointment.

articles.title: Burnham in Brussels: why party politics still defines the UK’s relationship with Europe
articles.summary:
Andy Burnham has attended his first EU-UK summit in Brussels with major agreements reached on youth mobility, food exports and carbon emissions. Ultimately though, the prime minister will have understood that this was merely the start of new political negotiations. Back home in the UK, he has started a “national conversation” on the future of UK-EU relations that gained momentum rapidly.

Burnham held talks with European Council president Antonio Costa and president of the European Commission Ursula von der Leyen. Both Burnham and Costa come from sister social democratic parties and both are former mayors – Burnham of Greater Manchester and Costa of Lisbon. This could make for smoother meetings in future than in the months and years after the 2016 Brexit referendum.

In the run up to the talks, the prime minister had repeatedly claimed that the Conservatives failed to get a good deal from the EU. As part of former prime minister Keir Starmer’s “reset” of relations with Europe, then-business secretary, Peter Kyle, and European Commission vice-president Teresa Ribera signed a deal committing the UK and the EU to closer cooperation on trade.

Like Costa and Burnham, Ribera is also from a European social democratic party (the Spanish Socialist Workers Party, or PSOE). Senior figures in Labour have long admired the electoral success of social democrats in both Spain and Portugal.

When it comes to claims of the UK having had a bad deal, there is one explanation that is under-discussed. It has its roots in the internal party politics of the centre-right in Europe. Ahead of the 2009 European Parliament elections, the then-Conservative leader David Cameron decided to leave the European People’s Party (a bloc of centre-right pro-European parties).

Cameron went on to set up a new right-of-centre eurosceptic faction with parties from Poland and the Czech Republic. But he underestimated how hurt highly influential EU figures like German chancellor Angela Merkel were by the move. So when it came to negotiating a better deal with the EU ahead of the 2016 referendum, Merkel and other figures had not forgotten Cameron’s betrayal. As such, they felt disinclined to meet him half way.

Burnham is walking a fine line

Youth mobility, migration, food exports and emissions are all important issues. But the broader discussion is increasingly about the politics around Brexit rather than the rights and wrongs of Brexit itself.

The UK is not going to rejoin the EU in the near future. Burnham even said when standing in the Makerfield byelection that first and foremost he wants to sort the consequences of Brexit rather than necessarily the outcome.

Now Burnham is increasingly focused on the claim that Brexit hasn’t worked for British voters – without saying it was completely wrong. He may understand that aiming to reverse Brexit in a binary way could simply open up new problems. It could even finish his premiership in the same way that it ended the tenures of multiple prime ministers before him.

In contrast, however, Burnham understands that he has the political capital to discuss the downsides of Brexit. For now, at least, he can do this in a way that is unlikely to result in much political damage to his government. While not completely without risk, he has calculated that the benefits of discussing Brexit outweigh any costs.

These costs could include the fragile “red wall” of Labour seats in northern England and the Midlands. The party knows all too well that this could flip to Reform UK the next time the country goes to the polls.

But those voters who have already moved to Reform are something of a sunk cost for Labour. For now, it seems Burnham sees more advantages in drawing voters away from the Liberal Democrats and the Greens than he sees disadvantages in alienating supporters of Reform. Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch appears to be sensitive to the fact that many people disapprove of how the Tories handled Brexit – whether they voted Remain or Leave.

At the height of the Brexit chaos, however, Burnham was mayor of Greater Manchester and so can revisit the issue in a fresh way, untainted by the Westminister turbulence of that time.

His predecessor Starmer was frequently seen as being paralysed by caution. Burnham appears to know how to talk about difficult issues lightly and fluently – his own parliamentary seat overwhelmingly voted Leave in 2016.

He may or may not truly want to see the UK rejoin the EU at some point – he has sometimes sent out mixed signals on the issue. But he certainly has the firm aim of removing the toxicity from the issue and having a “national conversation”. To do this, the prime minister will have to consider how Westminster relates to Brussels as well as how it relates to constituencies like his own in Makerfield.

Martin Steven does not work for, consult, own shares in or receive funding from any company or organisation that would benefit from this article, and has disclosed no relevant affiliations beyond their academic appointment.

articles.title: People wade through floodwater because they underestimate danger – how to avoid risk
articles.summary:
A firefighter dealing with an emergency situation in Oxford after significant flooding. Alessia Pierdomenico/Shutterstock

A footpath home disappears beneath brown water. The other side is only a few metres away and someone has already crossed. Turning back means a long detour and you will be late. Would you wade through? This is the kind of everyday decision that flood safety advice must address.

People do not need to be thrill-seekers to enter dangerous water. They may just be trying to get home. But a familiar route can become an unfamiliar hazard within minutes.

Flooding is one of the leading causes of death during climate disasters worldwide. People can underestimate the speed or power of the water, or they might not spot underwater hazards that could mean they trip and fall.

A significant number of deaths are due to avoidable behaviour. There have been some recent UK fatalities during floods, including in 2023, when storm water rose suddenly.

In the US, the second highest cause of deaths during floods is people walking into or near water. The US National Weather Service warns just six inches (15cm) of fast-moving water can knock over an adult.

With the UK likely to see high levels of rainfall this winter, and flood risk increasing, it’s worth asking why people decide to wade through floodwater.

A review of research on behaviour around floodwater identified several reasons. One is just wanting to get to a destination, such as going to work or school. Other factors include people travelling to flooded areas to taking photos of the extremely high water levels. Protecting property or pets and helping others who are in trouble are other reasons. Underestimating danger and being influenced by other people were major themes.

Watching someone wade through flooded water could make you feel reassured, even though their height, strength and route may differ from yours. Previous success at walking through a flooded road can also encourage someone to have another attempt. Yet getting through safely last time tells you little about the current conditions.

Media images of floods sometimes depict people paddling through flooded streets. This can make the scene look recreational. This does not, of course, prove that such pictures cause risky behaviour. But it is a reason for news organisations to explain the hazards of entering flood water alongside them. What looks like harmless fun, of people getting on with life – being resilient despite the flood – in a photograph or clip may conceal a strong current or a missing drain cover. Government advice is not to walk through floodwater and also warns that floodwater could be contaminated.

Read more:
Floods and droughts are both signs of water insecurity – they show up in these four places

Why appearances can be deceptive

Even clear water can deceive us. Refraction, the bending of light as it passes from water into air, makes the bottom of a flood appear closer to the surface. This is why a swimming pool can look shallower than it really is.

In muddy floodwater, the more immediate problem is often that you cannot see the bottom at all. A submerged pavement may end at a kerb, ditch or uncovered drain. Knowing where the path normally goes does not establish that the ground beneath it remains intact. In a recent study of 185 drivers, participants often focused on depth even when asked how they would judge water speed. That study concerned driving, not walking, but it highlights why advice needs to explain both the depth and the flow conditions.

Depth is only part of the danger. Research shows how both water depth and speed of the water flow combine with body size to affect balance. Moving water pushes against the legs and body; as more of it is submerged, buoyancy also reduces our weight pressing feet against the ground, making it easier to slip and fall. For otherwise similar conditions, drag increases roughly with the square of water speed: doubling the speed can mean around four times the pushing force.

You can lose your footing well before the water reaches your thighs. The Environment Agency guidance warns that water around 15cm deep can knock someone over or conceal hazards. This is not a safe wading limit. Even shallower water is not automatically safe, and children or people with limited mobility will face different risks.

Heavy storms hit Monmouth in 2025.

What should make you turn back

Floodwater across your route is itself a reason to stop and find an alternative. You do not need to establish its depth or test its strength with your feet. The government advice is to avoid walking through floodwater altogether.

Rising levels, debris being carried along and water flowing forcefully across a path are additional warning signs. So are heavy rain and flood warnings. These signs call for moving away from danger, not getting closer to investigate. Flash flooding can develop before an official warning arrives.

Still water can also be dangerous. It can hide sharp objects, damaged surfaces and sewage. The advice is to stay away from flooded riverbanks as the ground can become unstable or may have already been eroded away below the water. Keep children away and dogs on leads, and never bypass a closure because another person has done so.

Read more:
A record-breaking El Niño is still developing – likely bringing a cold winter to the UK

How a game can help

People can explore what to do in an emergency through a game, the Flooding Mucky Dip, that I developed with Girlguiding, Global Link Education and the Environment Agency. At the moment, we are trialling it with schoolchildren in Leicestershire and Rutland, but it can be used by people of any age. It uses tubs of deliberately clouded water (with tea and coffee dissolved in it) containing cards representing flood risks. Participants retrieve cards from the “muddy water” and discuss actions.

Read more:
Did the hot summer make more people worry about climate change? Here’s what the latest indications show

Players can pause a story about a flooded school route and consider what a character should choose next and what to do. Children playing the game can then discuss why following a friend might feel reasonable, then identify another, safer, option. If floodwater blocks the way, choosing another route avoids having to discover what lies beneath it. Playing the game can help children, or adults, understand flooding dangers. Adults could use it to check whether their household plan works. It’s useful to help identify the dangers floodwater can bring.

Other work I am doing with colleagues also explores how stories and practical activities can help families discuss disrupted journeys, safer alternatives and who might need assistance.

With more heavy rains expected this winter, learning how best to respond to a flood could help people understand more clearly what dangers could lie ahead, and how to avoid them.

Katie Parsons receives funding from the Environment Agency and the UK Research and Innovation.

articles.title: UK’s nature healthcheck doesn’t stack up in wildlife’s favour – but volunteers are collecting plenty of crucial data
articles.summary:
encierro/Shutterstock

As nature declines over time, it becomes easier to normalise an increasingly impoverished environment.

One way to help counteract this so-called shifting baseline syndrome is the nation’s annual status report for nature, commissioned by the UK government. First published in 2007, this impressive environmental healthcheck explains how and why habitats and the wildlife within them are changing.

It brings together the best data on a diverse set of 28 biodiversity indicators. These cover measures such as air pollution and habitat condition. They show how birds and butterflies are faring and record how much time people spend volunteering in conservation. The report outlines struggles in the natural world as well as some reasons for hope.

Conservation volunteering highlights the best news. The number of hours worked by volunteer citizen scientists to support the natural environment has increased over both the short- and long-term. Between 2000-24, recorded volunteer time in UK increased by an amazing 70%. This shows the public’s keen appetite to engage with nature and do good. This nature data is being used increasingly by conservationists, planners and researchers to help protect and restore nature, to monitor change and to educate.

Read more:
Why grandparents should talk to children about the natural world of their youth

The latest UK biodiversity indicator report draws on a wide range of measures to give an unrivalled picture of how the environment is changing.

The indicators touch on direct and indirect drivers of biodiversity change, on conservation interventions, on data and expenditure, on awareness and nature connection. It allows researchers to track nature and begin to understand what drives the ups and downs and how to limit and counteract harmful change.

Using huge volumes of data generated by monitoring programmes and recording schemes, coordinated by many conservation and research organisations, many of the indicators go back several decades.

But disappointingly, only half of the 28 biodiversity indicators were updated this time, so the picture isn’t complete.

Looking at trends from all of the indicators that use data compiled over decades, 44% were assessed as improving, 44% deteriorating (12% little or no change). Over the last five years, 38% were assessed as improving, 29% deteriorating and 32% as having little or no change. Certainly, some pressures are reducing and some responses are improving. But outcome measures of the state of nature are either deteriorating or flatlining.

The latest statistics on the UK’s wild birds sadly make for grim reading. Nature in the UK is already known to be depleted, but the apparent acceleration of decline in birds is particularly alarming.

Trends are classified as “deteriorating” in most bird groups in the last five years; none are increasing. This nosedive is most evident in farmland birds (such as lapwing, yellow wagtail and starling) and seabirds (such as Arctic skua and Arctic terns).

It isn’t just birds, butterfly populations are in trouble, declining from steadily from 1976 when systematic monitoring began. These include the small tortoiseshell, adonis blue and small pearl-bordered fritillary.

The UK is a world leader in promoting biodiversity targets and indicators. The Environment Act, for example, includes a legally binding target to halt the decline of species abundance and reduce extinction risk, among wider environmental objectives.

Biodiversity indicators form the basis of much of the UK’s international reporting obligations on biodiversity. They are used to measure progress against targets set by the UN’s Convention on Biological Diversity in 2022. The groundbreaking agreement, known as the Kunming-Montreal global biodiversity framework, contains 23 action-oriented targets for 2030 and four overarching goals for biodiversity recovery by 2050.

Soberingly, government reporting earlier this year showed the UK was on track to meet just three of those 23 targets. For 19 targets, progress was being made but not fast enough. Progress for one target on the management and use of wild species couldn’t be assessed because the UK still lacks evidence on benefits to people.

Mixed signals

Protected areas of both land and sea are both vital for nature protection. The news on the area they cover and their condition sends mixed signals. While the total extent on land and sea protected has increased since the 1950s, the increase has been only at sea since the 1990s. The total area of protected land has flatlined and not changed since 2020.

Reliable information on the condition and quality of those sites is lacking, so whether they protect nature in a meaningful way remains open to question. Overall, the UK is way short of reaching the UN’s bold goal to protect 30% of the world’s land for nature by 2030. At sea, that 30% target has just been reached, according to the update, thanks to expanding marine protected areas around UK coasts.

Overall, more money is being spent on nature, both in the public sector and the non-governmental organisations and private sector. Whether that spending is in all the right places and up to the task of protecting nature is debatable. The current evidence on the state of nature says it is not because the loss of nature continues.

But at least with brilliant volunteers, monitoring schemes and comprehensive indicators, it will be easier to track and respond to any potentially insidious change around us.

Richard Gregory works for the Royal Society for the Protection of Birds (RSPB) as the Head of Monitoring Conservation Science.

articles.title: Could an erectile dysfunction drug offer a new way to treat Alzheimer’s?
articles.summary:
Orawan Pattarawimonchai/Shutterstock.com

A drug developed to treat erectile dysfunction might seem an unlikely treatment for Alzheimer’s disease. But researchers are increasingly interested in whether medicines such as Viagra could also help protect the brain.

These drugs affect blood flow and other processes that may play a role in brain health. An experimental drug called AR1001 has produced encouraging results in a large international clinical trial.

In one group of people with early Alzheimer’s, the drug was reported to slow the worsening of symptoms by 31% over a year, compared with a placebo.

AriBio, a South Korean biotechnology company, announced the results at the 19th Clinical Trials on Alzheimer’s Disease conference in Boston, US. A full scientific paper, reviewed by other researchers, has not yet been published.

The phase three trial – the final phase of testing in humans – involved 1,535 people with early Alzheimer’s in 13 countries. Participants took either 30mg of AR1001 or a placebo every day for a year.

Researchers measured changes in memory, thinking and everyday activities. They looked at two groups: everyone who took part in the trial and a smaller group of 604 people who were not taking other Alzheimer’s medicines to ease their symptoms, such as donepezil or memantine.

Only this smaller group saw a 31% reduction in worsening symptoms. Across the whole trial, AR1001 did not produce reliable benefits.

How could erectile dysfunction drugs affect the brain?

Erectile dysfunction drugs work by blocking an enzyme that normally breaks down a chemical messenger – called cGMP – in the body. This allows cGMP to build up, helping the muscles around blood vessels relax. The vessels widen, allowing more blood to flow through them. This is how the drugs help treat erectile dysfunction.

The same chemical messenger also helps brain cells communicate with each other. Researchers think that increasing its levels could help brain cells survive and maintain the connections they need to share information.

These connections are essential for learning and memory. Alzheimer’s gradually damages them, making it harder to remember things and think clearly. Researchers hope that AR1001 might help protect some of these connections and slow the damage caused by the disease.

However, this is still a theory. The clinical trial does not show that these biological changes explain the reported benefits in people.

Some laboratory and animal studies support the idea. In a 2022 study, mice with features of Alzheimer’s disease performed better in memory tests after receiving AR1001. The treatment also reduced levels of amyloid-beta and abnormal tau, two proteins linked to Alzheimer’s.

AR1001 belongs to the same family of drugs as Viagra.
artem evdokimov/Shutterstock.com

Other experimental research in mice has found that AR1001 can increase levels of cGMP and a protein that helps brain cells survive. However, results in animals do not always translate into benefits for humans.

Interest in this family of drugs has also grown following research in people. A 2024 study followed more than 269,000 men with erectile dysfunction. It found that men prescribed these drugs were 18% less likely to be diagnosed with Alzheimer’s than men who were not prescribed them.

But this was an observational study, which means it cannot show that the drugs themselves reduced the risk of Alzheimer’s. The two groups may have differed in other ways that influenced the results.

A complicated relationship

The relationship between erectile dysfunction and Alzheimer’s is complicated. Erectile dysfunction can be associated with conditions such as diabetes, high blood pressure and heart disease, which can damage blood vessels. These same conditions are also linked to poorer brain health and a higher risk of dementia.

This means that some of the apparent link between erectile dysfunction, its treatments and dementia could be down to shared risk factors affecting blood vessels, rather than a direct effect of the drugs.

Erectile dysfunction drugs are not an established treatment for Alzheimer’s, and nothing in these results suggests people should take them to protect their memory.

The latest trial does, however, keep alive an interesting possibility: that drugs that improve blood flow and help brain cells communicate might also slow the damage caused by Alzheimer’s.

Whether this is the case will depend on the full trial results and further research in people, including studies looking at why the apparent benefit was seen only among those not taking other Alzheimer’s medicines.

Rahul Sidhu does not work for, consult, own shares in or receive funding from any company or organisation that would benefit from this article, and has disclosed no relevant affiliations beyond their academic appointment.

articles.title: Resistance training could help boost brain health and confidence in older adults
articles.summary:
As you practise lifting weights, your nervous system gets better at coordinating the muscles you use. Lucigerma/Shutterstock

Think about the last time you stood up from a chair or lifted a heavy shopping bag from the floor. These movements might feel automatic, but they take a surprising amount of coordination between your brain and your muscles.

As you lift the bag, your brain sends signals that tell your muscles when to tighten and how hard to pull. At the same time, signals from your body help your brain tell where your limbs are and whether you’re starting to lose your balance. If the bag is heavier than you expected, you can adjust your grip and shift your weight as you lift.

A recent study involved 162 adults aged 65 and over who showed signs of mild cognitive impairment. This means having more difficulty with memory or thinking than is usual at that age while still being able to manage most everyday tasks.

The researchers compared gentle exercise with a 24-week programme of resistance training, in which muscles work against a weight or against the body’s own weight. The strength exercises gradually became harder. In the second half of the programme, participants began doing some of them on surfaces such as foam pads, which made it harder to keep their balance.

By the end of the programme, the strength-training group scored slightly higher than the gentle-exercise group on two tasks: repeating a string of numbers immediately after hearing it and naming as many words as possible beginning with the letter A in one minute. The groups scored similarly when asked to remember details from a story, both immediately and half an hour later. It’s unclear whether the small differences on the two tests would make a difference in daily life. Whether the programme affects the chances of developing dementia, where changes in memory or thinking interfere with daily life, remains an open question.

Learning to move

When someone first starts strength training, they can get stronger before their muscles grow noticeably. One reason is that the brain and nerves get better at activating the muscles needed for the movement. Think of it as developing a “muscle map”. With practice, it becomes easier to sense where your body is and adjust how much effort you need.

An exercise that challenges your balance may also demand more attention. Whether that extra effort benefits other thinking skills is less clear. In the 24-week study, the researchers compared the whole training programme with gentler exercise, so they couldn’t tell how much the balance challenge itself contributed to the results.

Much of the research on exercise and thinking skills in older age looks at memory or at skills such as planning and switching between tasks. Those tests can tell us how someone performs on a particular task. Other measures are needed to see whether exercise helps someone move more confidently or manage everyday activities on their own.

Practising one task can make a similar task easier. For example, doing squats can help you stand up from a chair because both movements use many of the same muscles. The same principle applies to thinking skills. Strength training might give you practice at remembering the order of your exercises, while a programme designed to improve memory gives you more direct practice at learning new information and recalling it later.

How strength training might affect the brain

Strength training may also affect the brain through changes elsewhere in the body. It can lower blood pressure and help the body respond better to insulin, the hormone that helps control blood sugar. Both high blood pressure and type 2 diabetes are linked to a higher risk of dementia.

Strength training can make everyday tasks, such as carrying the shopping, easier as people get older.
Mangkorn Danggura/Shutterstock

Strength training may also reduce some signs of long-lasting inflammation, which can occur when the body’s immune defences stay active over time. Researchers are still investigating what that might mean for the brain.

Other studies have looked at whether strength training changes the levels of proteins that help brain cells work and form connections. Some have found higher levels of these proteins in the blood after training, but results in people have varied. When muscles tighten during exercise, they also release substances called myokines, which can send signals to other parts of the body. Researchers are exploring whether some of those signals affect the brain.

Beyond the gym

Strength training can help some older adults who have difficulty getting around to move more easily. That might make it easier to walk to the shops or get to a regular social activity. Over time, those outings could provide more opportunities to stay active and see other people. Being physically inactive and being socially isolated are both linked to a higher risk of dementia. What someone can do with their improved strength also depends on practical things, such as how easy it is to get somewhere and how confident they feel going out.

More women than men live with dementia worldwide, yet women are less likely to do regular strength exercises. A review drawing on studies involving more than 2.6 million adults estimated that fewer than one in four did muscle-strengthening exercises at least twice a week. In interviews with women who trained regularly, some described feeling unsure of their abilities or feeling that strength training was seen as something for men.

Having the chance to build strength and confidence earlier in life can help people stay independent as they get older. The benefits can show up in ordinary ways, whether it’s carrying the shopping home or getting out of a chair without help.

Hannah Campbell receives funding from the Economic and Social Research Council.

articles.title: The Hillsborough Law requires public servants to be honest – but what does honesty actually mean?
articles.summary:
A Hillsborough memorial at Anfield Stadium in Liverpool. 4kclips/Shutterstock

The Hillsborough disaster in 1989 ultimately claimed the lives of 97 Liverpool fans. In the weeks that followed, South Yorkshire Police reviewed its officers’ written accounts before passing them to the official inquiry.

The Hillsborough Independent Panel later found that 164 statements had been substantially changed. In 116 of them, comments critical of the force were removed or altered. In 2021, two former officers and the force’s solicitor were tried over those changes. The case collapsed. The judge ruled that the original inquiry wasn’t a statutory one, and the police had no legal duty of candour there.

The public office (accountability) bill, known as the Hillsborough law, currently in the House of Lords, is meant to close that gap. Covering up to 1.9 million public servants, it would require authorities and officials to act with “candour, transparency and frankness” towards inquiries and investigations. Breaching that duty with the aim of obstructing them would be a crime. The bill also creates a new offence of misleading the public, with a maximum sentence of two years in prison.

Honesty has been one of the seven principles of public life since 1995. Hillsborough shows what can happen when a moral duty may be ignored at little cost. But once honesty becomes a legal duty, someone has to decide what it requires. That’s much harder than it sounds.

Honesty is more than not lying

Research on public health communication shows that official messages can fall short of honesty without anyone telling a lie. They might use true statements to create a false impression, which is known as paltering. For example, they can leave out the size of a benefit or the harms, strip out uncertainty, or present risks in whatever form looks most persuasive.

Imagine a council official is asked at an inquiry whether they were warned that a block of flats was unsafe. They reply: “I never received a report saying the building was unsafe.” That may be strictly true. But suppose they had received several emails from residents and a fire officer raising concerns about the building’s fire doors. Nothing they said was false, yet the inquiry would come away with the wrong picture.

The Hillsborough statements fit the same pattern: the deception lay in what had been taken out.

The bill seems to accept this. Its test for “seriously improper” conduct refers to dishonesty “whether by means of falsehood, concealment, obfuscation or otherwise”. It says an “act” includes “an omission or a course of conduct”. And the duty of candour requires officials to correct “any errors or omissions” in what they have already told an inquiry.

As a result of campaigning by families of Hillsborough victims, a number of state-mandated investigations were held into the disaster.
Pete Stuart/Shutterstock

But the bill uses the word “dishonesty” without defining it. Nor does it say what counts as “misleading”. That’s important because the line is blurry.

Every statement leaves something out. The duty of candour asks officials to provide information that’s “relevant to the inquiry or investigation”, but someone still has to decide what’s relevant. Not every omission is a cover-up.

The problem grows when the evidence is incomplete or disputed. To show that someone misled others, a court needs something to compare their statement with. Should that be the truth as it later emerged, or the best understanding at the time? Early in a public health emergency, for example, officials often have to speak before the science is settled.

This is why the difference between misinformation and disinformation matters. Misinformation is false or misleading content shared without meaning to deceive, whereas disinformation is spread on purpose. An official may give an inaccurate account because they were wrongly briefed, or may not have realised a detail mattered. That’s a failure, but not necessarily dishonesty.

Can honesty really be enforced through the law?

The bill deals with this through what lawyers call the “mental element” of an offence. To be guilty of misleading the public, officials must “act with the intention of misleading the public” or be “reckless as to whether their act will do so”. They must also “know, or ought to know, that their act is seriously improper”.

An act is only seriously improper if it “involved dishonesty that was significant or repeated” on a matter of significant public concern, caused or risked harm, and departed significantly from proper conduct.

This leaves courts with a hard task. Proving intent means piecing together what an official knew and believed at the time. Omissions are especially hard to prove. A prosecutor must show that the official had the information, understood that it mattered and chose not to share it.

Draw these boundaries too narrowly and the selective editing seen after Hillsborough could slip through again, because every sentence left in was technically true. Draw them too vaguely and officials may say less, hedge everything and send every statement through lawyers.

Criminal law also has to be clear enough for people to know in advance what’s forbidden. Honesty is a tricky concept, so it’s likely the Hillsborough law will be difficult to enforce.

The Hillsborough law already accepts that dishonesty can mean “concealment” or “obfuscation”, not just “falsehood”. What it doesn’t yet do is say where honest selection ends and dishonest concealment begins. Peers still have a chance to fix this by defining “dishonesty” and “misleading” in the bill or its guidance.

For public servants bound by the law, there is a practical lesson. “Did I say anything false?” is the wrong question. A better one is: “Will the people I’m speaking to come away with an accurate picture?”

Byron Hyde previously received funding from the Wellcome Trust to investigate the seven principles of public life.

articles.title: Climate diplomacy is stuck – these three big changes would get it moving again
articles.summary:
The latest UN climate summit, Cop31, held in Antalya, Turkey, was being branded “possibly the worst Cop in history” even before its sorry conclusion.

I was there, and the conference was badly managed from start to finish: initial traffic jams and queues sapped energy and goodwill, while the final plenary was one embarrassment after another, with the summit president sniping at the UN’s climate chief (to audible gasps from delegates), and the closing “Antalya pact” being comprehensively rejected.

This sad outcome was not merely the fault of the conference’s Turkish-Australian presidency, however. The bigger issue is that climate diplomacy is stuck – and has been for several years. Structural changes are required, three in particular.

1. Climate finance is not an optional extra

First, climate finance – money provided to developing countries to help them tackle climate change – has to be increased, in particular public, grant-based finance from developed states.

This may seem an odd place to start for those weaned on the mainstream western media, where most accounts of Cop31’s failure focused on the stand off over fossil fuels. But climate finance is not an optional extra under the Paris agreement: it is the glue that holds the entire arrangement together. Ensuring adequate finance flows is one of the agreement’s three main stated aims (alongside limiting global temperature rises and supporting adaptation). And these flows are meant to progressively increase in line with mitigation ambitions and adaptation needs.

But in recent years they have not. At Cop29 in Baku, an ambitious new finance goal was planned. But instead, the conference saw a pushed-through decision that failed to offer the “progression beyond previous efforts” required by Paris and drew widespread condemnation from developing states. Nigeria termed the deal “an insult” to the UN Climate Convention.

Actual country pledges and disbursements have been falling short too. This year has seen a 70% drop in total developed country finance pledges. Meanwhile, the UK is cutting its development assistance to 0.3% of gross national income, while halving its climate finance.

The consequences have been profound. By no coincidence, within a year of the finance debacle in Baku the other side of the global climate bargain had unravelled too. The 2025 round of national mitigation plans were barely more ambitious than their previous iterations, mostly late, and collectively non-compliant with the goals of the Paris agreement.

For many developing countries, inadequate climate finance was one of the biggest frustrations at Cop31.
Rehman Asad / Shutterstock

Cop31 continued this pattern. On the conference’s eve, EU Commissioner Wopke Hoekstra declared the prospects for additional climate finance “dead in the water”. New developed world pledges for the Adaptation Fund, which helps countries prepare for and cope with the effects of climate change, totalled just US$50 million, less than half the cost of a single F-35 fighter jet.

The predictable result was deadlock on most key negotiation tracks. Indeed, for many developing countries, as well as NGOs, it was above all this climate finance issue – and not the question of whether “fossil fuels” should be named or not – that most underpinned their rejection of the Antalya pact.

The lesson should be clear: to unblock future climate summits, vastly improved finance offerings will be needed from developed countries. And that means that money will have to be diverted from elsewhere, including from the US$2.9 trillion being spent globally on militaries and war.

2. Climate coalitions need to become alliances

More money will not be enough though. Sharper political strategies are also needed, ones that are appropriate to a geopolitically fractured world and to tackling fossil fuel interests.

Cop30 in Belém, Brazil, brought a big step forward on this, with its recognition that “coalitions of the willing” are needed to overcome the UN’s consensus rules. Right now, these rules effectively give fossil fuel-dependent countries a veto on meaningful action. This led to a new process explicitly focused on “transitioning away from fossil fuels”, which began with a 57-country summit in Santa Marta, Colombia, in early 2026.

The risk, though, is that such coalitions just become new talking shops, and lack teeth. The “national roadmaps” that countries in the Santa Marta coalition are producing seem to illustrate this: the first wave of published roadmaps contains not a single new major policy commitment.

But other coalitions show us what might be possible. On the greenhouse gas methane (the focus of my current research), a powerful network of international partnerships, NGOs, funders and regulatory initiatives has transformed policy and practice over the last five years.

And building on the EU’s world-leading methane regulation, this coalition is now constructing a global marketplace that rewards cleaner producers with preferential market access, in order to help drive down methane emissions.

To really work, however, both this and other such coalitions will need commitment, regulation and enforcement. Voluntary initiatives will not be enough. And over time, such ad hoc “climate clubs” will need to transform into something much firmer – binding, treaty-based climate alliances.

3. Public pressure and protest matter

Last, it should be stressed that progress in international climate politics is not the responsibility of diplomats alone. Whatever they achieve, or do not, always reflects diverse lobbying and social pressures.

And sadly, on this front there has been a sharp regression. Since a peak in 2020, mass climate activism has largely died out. Media coverage of climate change has declined worldwide. And, spurred on by the Trump administration and war, fossil fuel interests are ascendant.

These things will only be changed through education, mobilisation and a widespread taking to the streets.

As Tasneem Essop, executive director of the NGO Climate Action Network, put it during an early Cop31 press conference: “We cannot give up on multilateralism … But if we can’t win back home, we cannot expect to win things in this space.”

Jan Selby receives funding from the European Research Council. He is a member of the Green Party of England and Wales.

articles.title: The efficiency paradox: why greener AI means more waste
articles.summary:
Data centres are getting bigger and more abundant, not necessarily more efficient. cflaten/Shutterstock

AI is increasingly being promoted as a solution to climate change. It can help companies use less fuel, reduce waste and make production more efficient.

For example, AI can help delivery companies plan more efficient routes, reducing the fuel they use and the emissions they produce. Similar savings could be made across other industries and transport networks, potentially reducing the overall environmental impact. But greater efficiency can also encourage more consumption.

AI is being promoted as a climate solution and as a driver of competitiveness, productivity and economic growth. The World Trade Organization estimates that the widespread adoption of AI could increase global trade by around 40% by 2040. This is generally presented as a benefit.

But there is an obvious contradiction here. If AI makes firms more efficient and profitable, it encourages further investment and expansion. Successful firms do not use productivity gains to produce less, but to expand and to make greater profits.

When these dynamics are generalised across the economy, the result is more production, transportation, resource extraction, consumption and ultimately more environmental destruction.

This is capitalism’s efficiency paradox, known as the Jevons paradox. According to William Stanley Jevons, a 19th-century English economist, any increase in resource efficiency generates an increase in long-term resource consumption, rather than a decrease.

Read more:
DeepSeek claims to have cured AI’s environmental headache. The Jevons paradox suggests it might make things worse

New technologies can help businesses produce more goods using less energy, materials and labour. But by making production cheaper and faster, they can also encourage businesses to make and sell more, increasing the total amount of resources that people use.

Industrial efficiency gains have been a defining feature of capitalism since the Industrial Revolution. Steam-powered textile mills and coal mines in the late 18th century, the Bessemer steel process (making steel by blowing air through molten iron) in the 19th century, and Henry Ford’s car assembly line in the 20th all dramatically increased efficiency.

The industrial revolution has evolved as efficiency improved, from the development of coal mines in the 18th century to Henry Ford’s car assembly line in the 20th century.
Parilov/Shutterstock

Yet none of these efficiency gains reduced society’s overall consumption of resources. Rather, they underpinned successive waves of industrial expansion, fossil-fuel use and environmental degradation.

AI is no different.

My research shows how digital technologies provide a historical example of this dynamic.

For decades, improvements in computers, telecommunications and data storage have allowed companies to spread different stages of production across several countries. They can now use real-time digital networks to share information and coordinate manufacturing and trade around the world.

These technologies have made possible today’s highly integrated global supply chains, allowing firms to source components from thousands of suppliers and move goods across continents with extraordinary speed and precision.

The environmental consequences are immense.

Digital technologies have helped companies produce and sell more goods around the world. This has increased the demand for raw materials, pollution from transport and damage to the natural environment. International trade in goods is now linked to around 30% of threats to the world’s species

Rather than reversing these trends, AI is deepening them. It is making supply chains faster, more responsive and more geographically extensive. From a business perspective, this is progress. Environmentally, it accelerates ecological breakdown.

Cleaner technology, more fossil fuels

The same contradiction can be seen in the energy sector. Much discussion of AI and green technology assumes that cleaner technologies replace dirtier ones. Yet, as the historian Jean-Baptiste Fressoz shows, new energy systems tend to accumulate on top of rather than substitute for each other.

Wood, coal, oil, gas and renewables have largely been added to one another rather than replacing one another. Green technologies are making fossil-fuel industries more efficient, rather than replacing them.

Many of the technologies being promoted as climate solutions, including AI, are actually accelerating the extraction of fossil fuels that is driving climate change.

In Guyana, since commercial oil production began in 2019, the country has become one of the world’s fastest-growing producers of oil, with targets to produce 1.3 million barrels per day by 2027. AI-enabled drilling and “geosteering” – the real-time adjustment of a well’s path to keep it within oil-bearing rock – are increasing the rate of oil extraction.

So, can a technology designed to increase productivity, competitiveness and growth solve a crisis rooted in relentless profit-oriented expansion of production and consumption on a finite planet? Until that question is confronted, greener AI is likely to make ecological destruction more efficient rather than bring it to an end.

Benjamin Selwyn works for the University of Sussex.

articles.title: Recruiting new trustees for The Conversation UK
articles.summary:
The Conversation Trust UK is the charity which operates the UK edition of The Conversation. Its Board of Trustees has overall responsibility for the charity, setting its strategy and overseeing its operations. The Board is chaired by Professor Paul Boyle, Vice-Chancellor of Swansea University. As several of our Trustees reach the end of their terms over the next 12 months, we are looking for new Trustees to join the board.

Role specification

As a Trustee you will work closely with fellow trustees and staff to make important decisions about The Conversation’s operations and strategy, and advise and support our team in doing the best work possible. It meets 4-5 times per year, both in person and virtually. Some Trustees also serve on subcommittees which meet between Board meetings, and all are encouraged to represent the charity externally. The Trustees are also supported by The Conversation’s Editorial Board.

We welcome expressions of interest from anyone who shares our commitment to the democratisation of knowledge and public engagement with research.

Trustees are asked to commit to a three year term, which can be extended for a further three year period by mutual agreement. Most trustees step down at the end of six years on the board.

Given The Conversation’s vision to be an inclusive and diverse organisation, including among our staff and contributors, we would welcome applications from under-represented groups, particularly people from Black, Asian or other minority ethnic backgrounds. We welcome applications from everyone regardless of age, gender, ethnicity, sexual orientation, faith or disability. All appointments will be made on merit, following a fair and transparent process. In line with the Equality Act 2010, however, The Conversation may employ positive action where diverse candidates can demonstrate their ability to perform the role equally well.

Application

To apply, please send a CV and brief supporting statement explaining your interest and relevant skills and experience to: uk-jobs@theconversation.com

If you would like an informal discussion about trusteeship, The Conversation or need further information, please contact Imogen Clark on uk-admin@theconversation.com to arrange a time to speak with the Editor or Chief Executive.

articles.title: Eminem and Damien Hirst collaboration shows the relationship between art and music is alive and well
articles.summary:
Few of even Eminem’s staunchest fans would have expected the rapper to find a home in a fine art gallery. Yet in 2026, when truth is often stranger than fiction, what was once inconceivable became a reality.

American Dream was a collaboration between the rapper and the artist Damien Hirst consisting of paintings and installations inspired by Eminem’s album covers. It was recently on display at London’s HENI gallery.

For centuries, western tradition has placed the visual arts at the top of an intellectual ladder, treating sight and sound as separate domains. Today however, artists, curators and researchers are increasingly interested in how our senses of sight and sound overlap, interact and enrich one another.

As a researcher of music, I find the combination of visual art and music to be one of the most fascinating pairings. At their core, the two art forms may be distinct forms of human expression, but they are deeply connected by how their use of space, rhythm and movement can express emotional responses and experiences for their viewers, listeners, or even the creators themselves.

Indeed, the two go together so well that they can be found sitting together on millions of shelves in millions of homes all over the world.

Ever since 1938, when graphic designer Alex Steinweiss created the first illustrated 78rpm record album cover (Smash Song Hits by Rodgers & Hart, which featured the songwriters’ names in lights on a shimmering marquee) popular music and visual art have been inseparable.

In his 2008 book A Brief History of Album Covers, author Jason Draper observed that some album covers are genuine pieces of high-class art that should be revered as much as the music. He cites The Beatles’ Sgt. Pepper’s Lonely Hearts Club Band, Sex Pistols’ Never Mind the Bollocks and Cindi Lauper’s She’s So Unusual as examples.

Perhaps due to its ability to reach vast audiences, the medium has appealed to several revered visual artists over the years. Andy Warhol, Peter Blake, Banksy and Takashi Murakami have all created cover art across a range of musical genres.

In my new book Reading Eminem, I explain that the album format has always been Eminem’s primary form of expression. The artwork found on his front and back covers, booklets and tray inserts has been a significant part of that.

From the grotesque cartoon imagery of 1999’s The Slim Shady LP through to the “body bag” image on 2024’s The Death of Slim Shady (Coup de Grâce), Eminem has used visuals art as a way to enhance the stories and characters contained within the songs themselves.

With 2004’s Encore CD booklet photographs, Eminem has even provided fans with an additional narrative, appearing to shoot at his audience at the end of a performance.

Album art in galleries

In recent years, the humble album cover has even been deemed worthy of promotion to art gallery status. Exhibitions such as For the Record: Photography & the Art of the Album Cover at The Photographers’ Gallery, London, Art & Vinyl at Fraenkel Gallery, San Francisco and Playback: Art Of The Album Sleeve at Lincoln Castle have underscored the medium as a serious artform.

In 2022, the Los Angeles County Museum of Art collaborated with Interscope, commemorating the label’s 30th anniversary by displaying reinterpretations of Interscope album art from an intergenerational group of visual artists. Among them was Hirst, who re-imagined album covers from Eminem’s discography based on their themes and lyricism.

Described by the HENI gallery as “a landmark collaboration that unites two of the most influential forces in contemporary art and music”, the show American Dream combined Hirst’s trippy interpretations of 12 Eminem album covers with a series of pharmaceutical-themed installations and visual motifs inspired by the rapper’s lyrics.

On the face of it, the exhibition may not have offered anything ground-breaking. But the fact that album covers, once considered part of a “low” culture medium, are being displayed in settings previously reserved for highbrow cultural capital is significant. I for one hope this trend continues.

This article features references to books that have been included for editorial reasons, and may contain links to bookshop.org. If you click on one of the links and go on to buy something, The Conversation UK may earn a commission.

Glenn Fosbraey does not work for, consult, own shares in or receive funding from any company or organisation that would benefit from this article, and has disclosed no relevant affiliations beyond their academic appointment.

articles.title: Grand Theft Auto 6: how gaming technology is helping everyone from scientists to filmmakers
articles.summary:
In Grand Theft Auto 6 (GTA 6), released on November 19, players can explore the streets of Vice City and the surrounding fictional US state of Leonida. The game’s detailed environments reflect years of work to make digital experiences feel as close as possible to real life.

Aside from what hopefully amounts to great gameplay, this sort of realism is likely to be surprisingly useful in other fields. A US-German team of researchers has already used images from GTA 5 to help AI systems recognise roads, cars and buildings for technologies like self-driving cars. Because the game already contained data on the objects within it, the team were able to use this to label 25,000 images for training their AI system in just 49 hours. It would have taken several years to hand-label the same number of real photographs.

Many ways of benefiting from gaming technology relate to their engines, which are the software platforms used to build and run a game. GTA uses a proprietary engine developed by its maker Rockstar Games, but other prominent engines include Unity and Unreal Engine. These are helping everyone from engineers to designers to researchers to understand, test and interact with the real world in new ways.

One example comes from a project I worked on with colleagues exploring the diving tradition associated with Mostar’s old bridge in Bosnia and Herzegovina. Using Unity, we created a reconstruction that allowed users to explore the site in virtual reality, hear from a local diver and even experience a simulated dive from the bridge. The aim was to help people who weren’t familiar with Mostar to engage with this tradition and understand its significance.

That sense of being in a place also depends on what we hear. The way a voice echoes
around a church can convey something about its size and atmosphere. With colleagues, I have explored how to recreate the acoustics of historic buildings alongside their appearance.

This includes a case study of Panagia Angeloktisti, a Byzantine church in Cyprus. Our team used filtering techniques employed in game audio to recreate how sound behaves within a virtual space like this church. The sound appeared to be affected by the environment in which it was generated, like in a real building.

Virtual diving off the old bridge in Mostar.

Yet creating a convincing digital simulation is only part of the challenge. Understanding how people interact with these experiences is just as important as building them.

During the Mostar project, we carried out user testing to see if participants used the virtual environment in the way we had expected. The results led us to change an aspect of the interface that helped users to move around in the virtual setting.
It was a small adjustment, but it showed why researchers cannot assume people will interpret digital experiences as intended. Testing with real users remains essential.

The same principle applies in engineering and robotics. In a project with the UK-based visualisation engineer Marius Matulis, we trained an AI system to operate a virtual robot arm inside Unity, enabling the AI system to move objects around. We then linked the robot arm’s movements to a physical, 3D-printed arm. The goal was to see whether skills learned by the AI in a digital environment could transfer to the physical world.

This approach is known as “sim-to-real” transfer. Researchers can repeat tasks and try different approaches in simulation before testing them on a real machine. Similar techniques have been used, for instance, to train drones to navigate unfamiliar environments, including forests and damaged buildings.

That said, the physical world rarely behaves exactly like a simulation. Sensors make errors, movements can be delayed and conditions change. Researchers call this the “reality gap”.
